lessons.title: Connecting an app: pools, ORMs, migrations & transactions
glossary: A reusable set of open DB connections, avoiding the cost of connecting per request.
Object-Relational Mapper — query the DB via code objects/methods instead of raw SQL (Prisma, Sequelize).
A versioned, code-tracked change to the schema, applied reproducibly across environments.
A group of statements that commit together or roll back together (all-or-nothing).
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees a relational transaction provides.

blocks.html: Your API talks to the database over a pooled connection. You can write raw SQL or use an ORM for convenience and type-safety. Either way, the endpoint from the backend module now persists for real — with parameterized queries and error handling.

When several statements must succeed or fail together, wrap them in a transaction. The canonical example is a transfer: debit one account, credit another. If the credit fails after the debit, money vanishes — unless both are in one atomic transaction that rolls back on error.

blocks.label: Migrations keep every environment in sync
blocks.html: A migration is a versioned script that evolves the schema (add a column, a table, an index). Tracking migrations in code means your laptop, staging, and production can all reach the identical schema reproducibly — and roll back if needed. It's how real teams change a live database without chaos or 'works on my machine.'

blocks.q: Why wrap a debit-then-credit money transfer in a single transaction?
options: So both statements commit together or roll back together, preventing money from being lost mid-way
blocks.explain: Transactions give atomicity (the A in ACID): if the second update fails, the first is rolled back, so you never end up with money debited but not credited. Anything that must be all-or-nothing belongs in one transaction.

blocks.q: An ORM primarily lets you…
options: Query the DB through code objects/methods instead of hand-writing SQL
blocks.explain: An Object-Relational Mapper maps tables to objects/methods so you work in your language, often adding type-safety and integrated migrations. You can still drop to raw SQL when needed.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Prisma — Getting Started & Migrate
A modern typed ORM many freelancers use, with first-class migrations.
PostgreSQL — Transactions & Concurrency Control
The authoritative treatment of ACID, isolation levels, and locking.

questions.q: A safe default database for structured, related app data is…
options: A relational database such as Postgres
questions.explain: Relational databases handle typed, related, consistent data with powerful queries and transactions — the default for most business apps.

questions.q: A primary key…
questions.explain: The primary key uniquely identifies rows; foreign keys reference it to form relationships.

questions.q: To combine rows from related tables you use…
questions.explain: JOIN merges rows across tables on a matching key (e.g. bookings.customer_id = customers.id).

questions.q: An index on a filtered column changes a lookup from…
options: O(n) scan to O(log n) search
questions.explain: A B-tree index lets the database binary-search instead of scanning every row — at the cost of slower writes and extra storage.

questions.q: SQL injection is prevented by…
questions.explain: Parameters send data separately from SQL code, so malicious input is treated as a literal value, not executable SQL.

questions.q: A transaction guarantees that a group of statements…
options: Commit together or roll back together (atomicity)
questions.explain: Transactions provide all-or-nothing atomicity (the A in ACID), essential for operations like transfers that must not partially complete.

questions.q: A migration is…
options: A versioned, code-tracked schema change applied reproducibly across environments
questions.explain: Migrations version schema changes so development, staging, and production converge on the same schema and can roll back safely.

modules.title: Testing, AI, Deployment & Practice
modules.tagline: Automated tests, integrating an LLM safely, shipping to production, and running it as a business.
objectives: Write unit, integration, and end-to-end tests and place them sensibly on the testing pyramid.
Call an LLM from a server with guardrails, and sketch a retrieval-augmented (RAG) flow.
Deploy a frontend, backend, and database across environments with CI/CD.
Scope, price, and protect freelance projects professionally.

lessons.title: Automated testing
glossary: Tests one function/module in isolation; fast and numerous.
Tests several units together (e.g. a route plus its database).
Tests the whole app through the UI as a user would (Playwright, Cypress).
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few slow E2E tests.
A statement that must hold; a failing assertion fails the test.
A stand-in for a dependency (network, DB) so a test stays fast and deterministic.

blocks.html: Tests are how you change code without fear. They encode the behavior you promised, catch regressions before users do, and let you refactor confidently. Professionals treat an untested feature as unfinished — and clients are paying, in part, for that reliability.

blocks.caption: The testing pyramid: many cheap unit tests, fewer integration tests, a thin E2E layer. In

blocks.label: Test behavior and edge cases, not implementation
blocks.html: Good tests assert what a function returns for meaningful inputs — including empty, zero, negative, and boundary cases — not how it computes internally. Tests coupled to internals break on every refactor and stop protecting you; tests coupled to behavior survive refactors and catch real regressions.

blocks.title: Two habits of a well-tested codebase

cards.label: Pure where possible
cards.html: Functions with no side effects (same input → same output) are the easiest to test. Push side effects (I/O, DOM) to the edges and keep the core pure.

cards.label: Mock the boundaries
cards.html: Stub the network and the clock so tests are fast and deterministic. A test that hits a real API is slow, flaky, and fails when you're offline.

blocks.q: According to the testing pyramid, you should have…
options: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few E2E tests
blocks.explain: The pyramid puts many cheap, fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of slow, brittle E2E tests. Inverting it (the 'ice-cream cone') makes the suite slow and flaky.

blocks.q: Why mock the network in a unit test?
options: To keep the test fast, deterministic, and independent of being online
Because mocking is required by JavaScript
blocks.explain: Mocking the boundary removes slowness and flakiness and lets the test run offline with predictable inputs, so it exercises your logic rather than a third party's uptime.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Vitest / Jest docs & Playwright docs
The standard unit and end-to-end testing tools with getting-started guides.
Kent C. Dodds — 'Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.'
A pragmatic, widely cited essay on where to invest test effort.

lessons.title: Integrating AI (LLM APIs)
glossary: Large Language Model — the AI you call via an API (Claude, GPT).
The instruction and context you send the model.
A chunk of text the model bills and reasons in; cost and limits scale with tokens.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — fetch relevant data, put it in the prompt, then ask.
A confident but fabricated model output; mitigated by grounding and validation.
Receiving the response incrementally for a responsive UI.

blocks.html: Adding AI is, mechanically, just another API call — made from your server so the key stays secret (the security lesson applies directly). You send messages, you get text back. The engineering is in the guardrails, not the call.

blocks.title: RAG in four steps ('a chatbot that knows our docs')
steps: Index
Split the client's documents into chunks and store vector embeddings.
Retrieve
For a question, find the most semantically relevant chunks.
Augment
Insert those chunks into the prompt as grounding context.
Generate
Ask the model to answer using only that context — grounded, not guessed.

blocks.label: Cost, trust & guardrails
blocks.html: LLM calls bill per token and can be confidently wrong (hallucinate). Cap max_tokens, bound and validate user input, cache repeats, and never let the model take irreversible actions (payments, deletes, emails) without a human or a validation gate. Treat model output as an untrusted suggestion, not a command.

blocks.q: Why call the LLM from your server rather than directly from the browser?
options: To keep the API key secret and add guardrails (limits, validation, logging)
blocks.explain: Frontend code is public, so a key there would be stolen and drained. Calling from the server keeps the secret safe and gives you a place to cap tokens, validate input/output, cache, and log.

blocks.q: RAG improves answer accuracy by…
options: Retrieving relevant data and feeding it into the prompt as grounding context
blocks.explain: RAG grounds the model in retrieved, relevant source material so it answers from your data rather than from parametric memory alone, reducing hallucination.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Anthropic / OpenAI API docs & prompt-engineering guides
The message format, parameters, pricing, and practical prompting patterns.
'Retrieval-Augmented Generation' (original paper + any vendor RAG guide)
How grounding works and where it fails.

lessons.title: Deployment, environments & CI/CD
glossary: Putting your app on infrastructure the public can reach.
A named context (development, staging, production) with its own config and data.
Continuous Integration/Delivery — automatically test and deploy on every push.
Serves frontend files from edge locations worldwide (Netlify, Vercel, Pages).
Bundling/transpiling source into optimized, fingerprinted assets to serve.
Reverting to a previous known-good deploy when something breaks.

blocks.html: "It works on my machine" is not shipped. Deployment puts your static frontend on a CDN, your backend on a server or serverless platform, and your database on a managed host — each reading configuration from environment variables, per environment.

blocks.label: Three environments prevent disasters
blocks.html: Keep development (your laptop), staging (a production-like rehearsal), and production (real users) separate, each with its own database and keys. You validate risky changes in staging so a bad deploy never touches real customer data. This discipline is a large part of what clients are really paying a professional for.

blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — run tests on every push, deploy on main
name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test          # fail the build if tests fail
      # deploy step runs only on main, after tests pass

blocks.label: A deploy you can't undo is a liability
blocks.html: Always have a rollback path — most platforms keep previous deploys one click away — and gate deploys behind passing tests in CI. The goal is that shipping is boring: automated, reversible, and low-drama, so you deploy often and small rather than rarely and huge.

blocks.q: Why keep staging and production as separate environments?
options: To validate changes in a production-like setting before real users and real data are exposed to risk
blocks.explain: Staging is a safe rehearsal with its own database and keys, so you can catch breakage before it reaches customers. Mixing them means every experiment risks real user data.

blocks.q: The main purpose of CI running your test suite on every push is…
options: To catch regressions automatically before code is merged or deployed
blocks.explain: Continuous Integration runs the tests on every change so failures surface immediately, keeping the main branch deployable and making shipping safe and routine.

items: The Twelve-Factor App
Timeless principles for configuration, environments, and reproducible deploys.
Vercel / Netlify docs & GitHub Actions docs
One-command deploys and simple CI pipelines with real examples.

lessons.title: The business of freelancing
glossary: The written list of what a project will and won't include.
A short contract defining scope, price, timeline, and ownership.
Upfront payment before work begins; filters non-serious clients.
A recurring fee for ongoing maintenance and updates.
Uncontrolled additions to a project beyond the agreed scope.
Transferring accounts, code, and documentation to the client.

blocks.html: The code is half the job; running it as a business is the other half. The habits that keep freelancers solvent are unglamorous, non-optional, and rarely taught in a coding course.

items: Write the scope down and get sign-off; treat every new ask as separate, paid work to prevent scope creep.
Take a deposit (30–50%) before starting; it filters tire-kickers and funds your time.
Use a simple statement of work covering price, timeline, deliverables, and who owns the code and IP.
Keep hosting, domain, and database accounts in the client's name so you aren't personally liable for their bills.
Sell retainers for maintenance — predictable monthly income beats chasing one-off projects.

blocks.label: Your positioning
blocks.html: "I build small businesses a custom app and give them the codebase knowledge to maintain and extend it" is a stronger, higher-paid pitch than no-code assembly. The depth you've built across this course — HTTP, security, databases, testing — is exactly the differentiator that justifies professional rates.

blocks.q: Before starting paid client work you should have…
options: Nothing in writing — trust is enough
A written scope/SOW and a deposit
blocks.explain: A written scope and a deposit protect your time, set professional expectations, and give you a contractual basis to charge for changes beyond the agreed work.

blocks.q: The steadiest freelance income typically comes from…
blocks.explain: Retainers convert delivered projects into predictable recurring revenue — the closest thing to a salary in freelancing — smoothing the feast-or-famine cycle of one-offs.

No tests if the code is simple

questions.q: You should call an LLM API from…

Your server, keeping the key in env vars and adding guardrails
questions.explain: Server-side calls keep the secret safe and provide a place to cap tokens, validate, cache, and log.

questions.q: RAG grounds an LLM by…

questions.explain: Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplies relevant source text so the model answers from your data, reducing hallucination.

questions.q: Staging exists to…

questions.explain: Staging is a safe rehearsal with its own data and keys, catching problems before they reach customers.

modules.title: Capstone: Ship a Full-Stack Feature
modules.tagline: Design, build, secure, test, and deploy a real booking feature end to end — then defend it in review.
objectives: Translate a written brief into a data model, API contract, and UI.
Implement a full CRUD slice across frontend, API, and database with real error handling and security.
Add automated tests and deploy to a live environment with separate config.
Justify your engineering decisions the way you would in a code review or to a client.

lessons.title: The brief & how to approach it
glossary: The agreed request/response shape of each endpoint — the interface between frontend and backend.
One feature built through every layer (UI → API → DB) rather than one layer built fully.
The explicit checklist a feature must meet before it's considered complete.
A peer reading your change and asking why — the forcing function for defensible decisions.

blocks.html: This capstone ties every module together. You'll build a small but complete vertical slice: a class-booking feature for a fictional studio, spanning the database, a REST API, and an accessible frontend — deployed and tested. The goal isn't size; it's that every layer is done properly and you can explain why.

The scenario. "Studio 7" runs classes. Customers should be able to view available class times, book a spot with their name and email, and see their bookings. Staff must not be able to double-book a full class. The studio owner wants it live, on their own hosting, maintainable by whoever they hire next.

blocks.title: A professional approach, in order
steps: Model the data
Design tables: classes (id, title, starts_at, capacity) and bookings (id, class_id FK, name, email, created_at). Decide constraints and indexes.
Define the API contract
GET /classes, GET /classes/:id/bookings, POST /classes/:id/bookings (201 or 409 when full). Write the request/response shapes before coding.
Build the slice
Implement the endpoints with parameterized queries and validation, then the frontend that consumes them with proper loading/error states.
Secure it
Validate on the server, escape output, parameterize queries, keep secrets in env, set sensible status codes.
Test & deploy
Unit-test the capacity logic, integration-test the POST route, then deploy frontend + API + DB across environments with CI.

blocks.label: Write the contract first
blocks.html: Deciding the exact request and response JSON — and the status codes, including the 409 Conflict when a class is full — before you write code forces the hard questions early and lets the frontend and backend be built in parallel against the same agreement. This is how real teams work.

blocks.q: Why decide the API contract (paths, request/response shapes, status codes) before writing code?
options: It surfaces hard questions early and lets frontend and backend be built in parallel against one agreement
blocks.explain: A contract-first approach forces decisions like 'what happens when a class is full?' (a 409) up front, documents the interface, and decouples the two sides so they can progress independently and integrate cleanly.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: OpenAPI (Swagger) Specification
A standard, machine-readable way to write and share the API contract you designed here.
MDN — HTTP conditional & status codes (409 Conflict)
When to use 409 and other precise codes for domain errors like a full class.

lessons.title: Modeling the data & building the frontend slice
glossary: UI shown while an async request is in flight, so the interface never appears frozen or empty.
UI shown when a request fails, giving the user a message and a way to recover.
Building a baseline that works, then layering on richer behavior.
Updating the interface before the server confirms, then reconciling on the response.

blocks.html: With the contract agreed, build both halves against it. Start at the database: a normalized schema with the constraints and index the queries need. Everything upstream depends on getting this shape right, so it's worth drawing before typing.

blocks.caption: The capstone model: one class has many bookings via the indexed class_id foreign key that

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE classes (
  id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title     TEXT NOT NULL,
  starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  capacity  INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (capacity > 0)
);
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  class_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES classes(id),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  email      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_class ON bookings(class_id);  -- every query filters on this

blocks.html: Now the frontend consumes the API. The pattern from the DOM and async modules applies directly: keep state, render from state, and — critically for a real product — show honest loading and error states rather than a blank screen or a silent failure.

blocks.label: Loading and error states are not optional polish
blocks.html: A screen that shows nothing during a slow network, or silently does nothing on failure, reads as broken to users. The three states — loading, success, error — are part of the feature's definition of done, not a nicety. This is a frequent gap between a demo and a shippable product.

blocks.q: Why build the class list with createElement + textContent instead of innerHTML with the class titles?
options: textContent prevents any HTML in the data from executing (XSS) while innerHTML would run it
blocks.explain: Class titles ultimately come from data that may include user or admin input; textContent renders them as literal text, closing the XSS hole that innerHTML would open. It's the same output-safety rule from the DOM and security modules.

items: web.dev — Loading, empty, and error states
Patterns for the UI states real features must handle.
MDN — FormData & fetch with a POST body
Wiring the booking form to the create endpoint cleanly.

lessons.title: Build, test, ship — and defend it
glossary: A bug where concurrent requests interleave to produce an invalid state (e.g. two bookings exceeding capacity).
Making a repeated request safe — relevant if a user double-submits the booking form.
The explicit criteria your finished work is evaluated against.

blocks.html: Below is the capacity check at the heart of the feature. Note the subtlety: checking the count and then inserting in two separate steps is a race condition — two simultaneous requests can both pass the check and overfill the class. The professional fix is to enforce it in one atomic step (a transaction with a constraint, or a conditional insert), exactly the transaction reasoning from the database module.

blocks.label: The check-then-act trap
blocks.html: A tempting first draft reads the count, compares in JavaScript, then inserts. Between the read and the insert, another request can slip in — both see space, both insert, capacity is exceeded. Any "check then act" on shared state needs a transaction or a database constraint to be correct under concurrency. This is the kind of bug a code reviewer will look for.

blocks.title: Assignment: Ship the Studio 7 booking feature
blocks.brief: Build and deploy the full vertical slice described in this module: a database schema for classes and bookings, a REST API (list classes, list a class's bookings, create a booking with a capacity check), and an accessible frontend that lists classes and lets a user book one. Deploy it live with separate configuration, and write a short README explaining your decisions. Then be ready to defend every choice as if in a code review.
items: A strong result models data correctly: a bookings.class_id foreign key, sensible types/constraints, and an index on the column you filter/join on.
A strong result uses correct HTTP semantics: GET to read, POST to create, 201 on success with a Location, 400 on invalid input, 409 when the class is full, 404 for a missing class.
A strong result enforces capacity atomically (transaction or conditional insert), demonstrably free of the check-then-act race condition.
A strong result is secure: parameterized queries throughout, server-side validation, output escaped in the UI (no innerHTML with user data), and all secrets in environment variables.
A strong result is accessible: labeled form controls, keyboard-operable, visible focus, and AA-contrast text.
A strong result handles async honestly: loading and error states in the UI, res.ok checked, and failures surfaced to the user rather than swallowed.
A strong result includes automated tests: at least a unit test of the capacity rule and an integration test of the create-booking route (including the 409 path).
A strong result is deployed and reproducible: frontend on a static host/CDN, API and database hosted, config per environment, and a README that justifies the key engineering decisions.

blocks.q: Reading a class's booking count, comparing it in JavaScript, then inserting the booking is unsafe because…
options: Two concurrent requests can both pass the check before either inserts, overfilling the class (a race condition)
blocks.explain: Between the read and the insert, another request can interleave; both see available space and both insert, exceeding capacity. Enforce the limit atomically with a transaction or a single conditional insert so the check and the act cannot be split.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: PostgreSQL — Transaction Isolation & row locking (SELECT … FOR UPDATE)
The tools to make capacity checks correct under concurrency.
Google — Web Vitals & Lighthouse
Audit your deployed capstone for performance and accessibility, and iterate on the scores.

questions.q: When a client POSTs a booking to a class that is already full, the most correct status code is…
questions.explain: 409 Conflict signals that the request conflicts with the current state of the resource (no capacity). 201 would falsely claim success; 500 wrongly blames the server for a valid, expected domain condition.

questions.q: Enforcing class capacity by counting in JavaScript and then inserting risks…
options: A race condition under concurrent requests
questions.explain: Check-then-act on shared state lets concurrent requests both pass the check and insert, exceeding capacity. Use a transaction or conditional insert to make it atomic.

questions.q: In the capstone, secrets like the database URL should live…
options: In server-side environment variables, never committed
questions.explain: Frontend code is public; connection strings and keys belong in server environment variables, kept out of the repo and the client.

questions.q: Designing the API contract before coding primarily helps by…
options: Surfacing edge cases early and letting frontend and backend proceed in parallel
Removing the need for a database
questions.explain: A contract-first approach forces decisions (like the full-class 409) up front and decouples the two sides so they integrate against one shared agreement.

questions.q: Which test best protects the capacity feature from regressions?
options: An automated integration test asserting the (capacity+1)th booking returns 409
questions.explain: An automated test that books to capacity and asserts the next request is rejected with 409 locks in the exact behavior and fails loudly if a future change breaks it.

questions.q: Displaying a booker's name in the confirmation UI should use…
options: textContent (or escaped output) to prevent XSS
questions.explain: User-provided names are untrusted; textContent or output escaping prevents injected markup/script from executing — the XSS defense from the security module.

questions.q: Which HTTP method is both safe and idempotent?
questions.explain: GET neither changes state (safe) nor differs on repetition (idempotent). DELETE is idempotent but not safe; POST is neither.

questions.q: A POST that creates a resource should ideally return…
questions.explain: 201 is the precise creation code; Location points to the new resource.

questions.q: A logged-in user requests a document they're not permitted to see. The semantically correct status is…
questions.explain: Authenticated but not allowed is 403. 401 means unauthenticated.

questions.q: The specificity of the selector #save .btn is…
questions.explain: One id and one class gives (1,1,0); the id column dominates any class-only selector.

questions.q: box-sizing: border-box makes the declared width…
questions.explain: border-box folds padding and border into the width for predictable sizing.

questions.q: Which comparison avoids type-coercion surprises?
questions.explain: === compares value and type with no coercion.

questions.q: What does this log in order? console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
questions.explain: Sync first (1,4), then microtasks drain (3) before the next macrotask (2).

questions.q: Filtering an array with .includes() against another array is…
questions.explain: An O(n) scan performed n times is O(n²); a Set makes membership O(1), yielding O(n).

questions.q: To display untrusted user text safely in the DOM, assign it to…
questions.explain: textContent inserts literal text and cannot execute injected markup — an XSS defense.

questions.q: Event delegation works because DOM events…
options: Bubble up from the target through ancestors
questions.explain: One ancestor listener catches bubbling events from many descendants via event.target.

questions.q: fetch() rejects its promise when…
options: The request can't complete (offline, DNS, CORS)
questions.explain: fetch resolves on any completed HTTP exchange, including 4xx/5xx; only network-level failure rejects.

questions.q: To run three independent async calls concurrently and collect all results, use…
questions.explain: Promise.all launches them together; total time is the slowest call, not the sum.

questions.q: In REST, creating a booking is…
options: POST /bookings with a JSON body, returning 201
questions.explain: Create maps to POST on the collection, returning 201; the verb lives in the method, not the path.

questions.q: A CORS error is resolved…
options: On the server, by allowing your origin (or via your own proxy)
questions.explain: The browser enforces same-origin; the server grants exceptions via CORS headers.

questions.q: Passwords must be stored as…
questions.explain: Store only a salted one-way hash; Base64 is encoding, not security.

questions.q: Putting untrusted input into element.innerHTML risks…
questions.explain: innerHTML parses input as HTML, executing injected script — cross-site scripting.

questions.q: SQL injection is prevented with…
questions.explain: Parameters separate data from SQL code so injected input can't execute.

questions.q: Adding a B-tree index on a filtered column changes lookups from…
options: O(n) scan to O(log n) search
questions.explain: The index enables binary search instead of a full scan, at the cost of slower writes.

questions.q: A database transaction guarantees that grouped statements…
options: Commit together or roll back together (atomicity)
questions.explain: Atomicity (the A in ACID) makes operations like transfers all-or-nothing.

questions.q: The testing pyramid recommends…
options: Many unit, fewer integration, few E2E
questions.explain: A wide base of fast unit tests keeps the suite fast and reliable; keep slow E2E tests few.

questions.q: You should call an LLM API from…
options: The browser with the key exposed
Your server, key in env vars, with guardrails
questions.explain: Server-side keeps the secret safe and enables limits, validation, and logging.

questions.q: Enforcing class capacity by counting then inserting in two steps risks…
questions.explain: Check-then-act on shared state lets concurrent requests overfill; make it atomic with a transaction or conditional insert.

questions.q: Under WCAG AA, normal body text needs a contrast ratio of at least…
questions.explain: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 is only allowed for large text.

questions.q: The steadiest freelance income comes from…
questions.explain: Retainers create predictable recurring revenue, smoothing project volatility.

title: Reading Stock Charts: Technical Analysis & Market Microstructure
subtitle: A rigorous, university-level course in price action, indicators with real formulas, microstructure, and the risk math that actually keeps traders solvent.
tagline: Candlesticks, structure, RSI/MACD math, bid/ask microstructure, R-multiples, expectancy, and a backtested capstone — taught quantitatively, with a standing reminder that this is education, not financial advice.
author: Oboros
certificateDesc: has completed a rigorous, university-level educational course on reading stock charts — covering candlestick anatomy, trend structure and support/resistance, price-action patterns and their statistics, volume and moving averages, the RSI and MACD formulas, market microstructure (bid/ask, liquidity, order flow), risk management and position sizing (R-multiples, expectancy, Kelly), trading psychology, and a backtested rules-based capstone. This certifies structured study of market analysis — not trading skill, profitability, or any recommendation to trade. Trading carries a high risk of loss.
disclaimer: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose.

modules.title: Chart & Candle Basics
modules.tagline: The atoms of price: OHLC, chart encodings, and why timeframe changes everything.
objectives: Decode the four prices (OHLC) inside any candlestick and read body/wick ratios as conviction.
Compare line, bar, candle, and Heikin-Ashi encodings and state what each one hides.
Explain gaps and why unfilled gaps attract attention.
Apply top-down multi-timeframe analysis: context from the high timeframe, timing from the low.

lessons.title: The anatomy of a candlestick
glossary: A mark encoding four prices for one time period: open, high, low, close (OHLC).
The first traded price of the period.
The last traded price of the period; the most information-rich of the four.
The extreme prices reached during the period.
The rectangle spanning open to close; its length measures net directional conviction.
The thin lines to the high and low; they mark prices that were reached but rejected.
Open-High-Low-Close, the four numbers summarizing a period's trading.

blocks.label: Read this first
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. We will repeat this because it matters more than any pattern in this course.

A price chart is a compressed record of a negotiation. Every candle is the market answering one question: at what price did buyers and sellers agree, and how far did they wander getting there? The candlestick chart, formalized by Japanese rice traders and popularized in the West by Steve Nison, packs four numbers into one glyph.
Each candle covers a fixed time slice (1 minute, 5 minutes, 1 day…). It encodes the open (first price), the close (last price), and the high and low reached in between — collectively OHLC.

blocks.title: One candle, four prices
blocks.caption: The thick part is the body (open-to-close). The thin lines are wicks (shadows) reaching to the high and low. Body length = |close − open|; here the body is 2.0 and the total range (high − low) is 3.2.

items.label: Body
items.html: The rectangle between open and close. A long body means one side clearly won; the ratio body/range (here 2.0/3.2 ≈ 0.63) is a rough conviction score.

items.label: Wicks / shadows
items.html: The thin lines above and below. They mark prices reached but rejected — the period travelled there but did not settle. Long wicks are footprints of a fight.

items.label: Colour
items.html: Green/hollow = close > open (buyers netted the period). Red/filled = close < open (sellers netted it). Colour tells you direction, not magnitude — read the body for that.

blocks.html: Think of a candle as the box score of one inning. The open and close are who was ahead at the start and end of the inning; the high and low are the biggest leads either side ever held. A tie game with wild swings (long wicks, tiny body) tells a very different story than a blowout (long body, no wicks).

blocks.label: The close is king
blocks.html: Of the four prices, the close carries the most information: it is where the market settled after all the day's information was digested, and it is the price most institutional benchmarks and end-of-day systems use. When analysts say 'the level held,' they almost always mean on a closing basis, not an intrabar wick.

blocks.q: On a green candlestick, which is necessarily true?
options: The close is below the open
The close is above the open
blocks.explain: Green means price finished higher than it started: close > open, so buyers netted the period. It says nothing about the size of the wicks or the volume.

blocks.q: A candle has open 50, high 55, low 49, close 50.2. Its body is small relative to its range. This best describes a…
options: Near-doji: lots of movement, almost no net change
blocks.explain: Body = |50.2 − 50| = 0.2 while range = 55 − 49 = 6. A tiny body on a wide range is indecision — the market travelled six points net two-tenths.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Nison, "Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques"
The canonical Western text on candle construction and psychology; start here for primary-source rigor.
Bulkowski, "Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts"
Statistical break-even and reliability rates for individual patterns — rare quantitative treatment.
CME Group / Investopedia: "Candlestick"
Free reference glossaries for confirming definitions and OHLC conventions.

lessons.title: Chart types and why they disagree
glossary: A chart connecting only closing prices; hides intrabar range.
A Western bar showing the same four prices as a candle with ticks for open/close.
A smoothed candle type using averaged prices; better for trend, worse for exact levels.
A jump between one period's close and the next period's open, leaving no trading in between.

blocks.html: Candles are one of several encodings of the same OHLC data. Knowing what each hides is part of literacy.

blocks.title: Three ways to draw the same data

tabs.label: Line
tabs.html: Connects closes only. Cleanest for spotting the big trend, but it discards the high, low, and open — you lose all intrabar drama and every wick.

tabs.label: OHLC bar
tabs.html: A vertical bar for the range with a left tick (open) and right tick (close). Same information as a candle, less visually loud. Preferred by some quants who find candle bodies distracting.

tabs.label: Heikin-Ashi
tabs.html: Each 'candle' uses averaged prices (close = average of OHLC; open = average of prior HA open/close). This smooths noise and makes trends obvious, but the plotted prices are no longer real prices — never place a stop off a Heikin-Ashi wick.

blocks.label: Heikin-Ashi hides real prices
blocks.html: Because Heikin-Ashi averages prices, the values you see are synthetic. It is a trend visualizer, not a source of executable levels. Beginners who set stops from HA charts are stopping off numbers that never traded.

A gap is a discontinuity: the open of a period sits away from the prior close with no trades in between, usually from news released while the market (or that symbol) was thin. Gaps matter because unfilled orders pile up behind them, and 'gap fill' — price returning to the pre-gap level — is a heavily watched tendency.

blocks.title: An overnight gap up

annotations.label: gap up — opens far above prior close

blocks.caption: Between candle 2's close (20.2) and candle 3's open (21.6) no trading occurred. The shaded band is the gap; many traders watch whether price later 'fills' it.

blocks.q: Why can a line chart make a stock look calmer than it was?
options: It plots only closes, hiding the intrabar highs, lows, and wicks
blocks.explain: A line chart connects closing prices only. All the intrabar range — the spikes and rejections captured by wicks — is discarded, so violent sessions can look smooth.

lessons.title: Timeframes and multi-timeframe context
glossary: Reading a higher timeframe for context and a lower one for timing.
The property that price structure looks similar across timeframes.
Small, mostly random price movement that carries little information.

blocks.html: The same stock is a different animal on a 1-minute chart versus a daily. Price structure is roughly fractal — trends and ranges recur at every scale — but the meaning of a move depends entirely on which scale you are on. A $0.30 swing can be the whole story on the 1-minute and invisible on the daily.

head: Timeframe
Typical use
Signal-to-noise
rows: Intraday entries and exits, scalping timing
Low — lots of noise, fast decisions
Intraday trend and key levels for the session
Overall trend, major support/resistance, position context
High — each bar is heavily traded

blocks.label: Top-down is a discipline
blocks.html: Professionals read top-down: establish the higher-timeframe trend and levels first, then drop to a lower timeframe only to time an entry already justified by the bigger picture. This one habit prevents most 'reacting to noise' errors.

blocks.caption: Higher timeframe gives context; a scary intraday drop is one wick on the daily.

blocks.q: Why do disciplined traders check the daily before trading the 5-minute?
options: To fix the higher-timeframe trend and key levels as context before timing an entry
blocks.explain: Top-down analysis: the higher timeframe supplies trend and levels; the lower one only times an entry that the context already supports. It prevents overreacting to noise.

blocks.q: Price structure being roughly 'fractal' means…
options: Similar trend/range structure recurs across timeframes
Wicks disappear when you zoom in
blocks.explain: Fractal structure means the same building blocks — trends, ranges, support/resistance — appear at every scale, which is why the same reading skills transfer across timeframes.

questions.q: The body of a candlestick spans…
questions.explain: Body = open-to-close; wicks reach to the high and low.

questions.q: Which price carries the most information and is used by most end-of-day benchmarks?
questions.explain: The close reflects where the market settled after digesting the session's information; most benchmarks and 'level held' claims are closing-based.

questions.q: A candle with open 50, close 50.2, high 55, low 49 is best called…
questions.explain: Tiny body (0.2) on a wide range (6.0) is indecision — lots of travel, almost no net change.

questions.q: Heikin-Ashi candles are dangerous for stop placement because…
options: Their plotted prices are averaged and synthetic, not real traded prices
questions.explain: HA averages prices, so its wicks show numbers that never actually traded — a bad basis for a real stop.

questions.q: An unfilled 'gap' is…
options: A jump from one close to the next open with no trading between
questions.explain: A gap is a price discontinuity where no trades occurred; the untraded band is watched for a later 'fill'.

questions.q: Top-down multi-timeframe analysis means…
options: Establish trend/levels on a higher timeframe, then time entries on a lower one
questions.explain: Context from the higher timeframe, timing from the lower — the standard disciplined workflow.

questions.q: A line chart can understate volatility because it…
options: Plots only closes and discards intrabar highs/lows/wicks
questions.explain: Connecting closes hides all the intrabar range that candles show through their wicks.

modules.title: Trend Structure, Support & Resistance
modules.tagline: The skeleton of every chart: swings, structure breaks, levels, and the polarity flip.
objectives: Define trend objectively via swing structure (HH/HL, LH/LL) and identify BOS vs ChoCh.
Locate support and resistance as zones and explain the order-flow reason levels react.
Apply polarity: predict when broken resistance becomes support and distinguish a real break from a trap.
Draw trendlines and channels with discipline, avoiding overfitting.

lessons.title: Trend as market structure
glossary: The prevailing direction of price: up, down, or sideways.
A local peak/trough that anchors trend structure.
The swing sequence defining an uptrend.
The swing sequence defining a downtrend.
A close beyond the prior swing that confirms trend continuation.
The first swing that breaks the trend's pattern, hinting at reversal.

blocks.html: Price does three things: trend up, trend down, or range. Naming the current regime is the first decision a trader makes because the correct strategy inverts between them. We define trend not by a feeling but by the sequence of swing points.

An uptrend is a sequence of higher highs (HH) and higher lows (HL): each pullback bottoms above the last. A downtrend is the mirror — lower highs and lower lows. The trend is intact until a swing violates the pattern.

blocks.title: Uptrend: HH and HL, then a break of structure
blocks.caption: Each dip bottoms higher (rising green line = dynamic support). A close above the prior swing high (candle 6) is a break of structure confirming continuation.

blocks.html: The moment the pattern first breaks — an uptrend printing a lower low, say — is a change of character (ChoCh). It is not proof of reversal, but it is the earliest structural warning that control may be shifting.

cards.label: BOS (continuation)
cards.html: A close beyond the last swing in the trend's direction — uptrend takes out the prior high. Confirms the trend is still working.

cards.label: ChoCh (warning)
cards.html: A close beyond the last swing against the trend — uptrend prints a lower low. First hint the regime may be turning.

blocks.q: An established uptrend prints its first lower low. Structurally this is a…
options: Break of structure confirming the uptrend
Change of character warning of a possible reversal
blocks.explain: A lower low against an uptrend breaks the HH/HL pattern — a change of character. It warns of, but does not guarantee, a reversal.

blocks.q: The cleanest objective definition of a downtrend is…
options: A sequence of lower highs and lower lows
blocks.explain: Trend is defined by swing structure: lower highs and lower lows is a downtrend, independent of candle colour or indicators.

lessons.title: Support, resistance, and the flip
glossary: A price zone where buying has repeatedly halted declines.
A price zone where selling has repeatedly capped advances.
The tendency for broken resistance to become support and vice versa.
Sideways price oscillating between support and resistance.
Clustered stop and limit orders resting just beyond an obvious level.

blocks.html: Support is a price zone where buyers have repeatedly stepped in; resistance is where sellers have repeatedly capped a rise. They are zones, not lines — draw them with a highlighter, not a razor.

blocks.title: A range between support and resistance
blocks.caption: Price oscillates between a ~49.2 floor and ~50.9 ceiling. Range traders fade the edges (buy near support, sell near resistance) until a breakout ends the range.

blocks.label: Why levels 'work'
blocks.html: Levels are partly self-fulfilling: because many participants watch the same round numbers, prior highs, and session opens, resting orders cluster there. That clustering — a liquidity pool — makes a reaction more likely. It is order flow, not magic.

When a level breaks decisively, it often reverses roles: old resistance becomes new support and old support becomes new resistance. The mechanism is human: buyers who missed the breakout wait to buy the retest, and trapped sellers cover there. That confluence of orders defends the flipped level.

blocks.label: Levels break — plan for it
blocks.html: Support and resistance are tendencies, not walls. A break on rising volume flips polarity; a false break (poke without a close beyond) traps traders. Always pre-decide what a genuine break looks like (usually a close beyond the zone) versus a wick.

blocks.q: After resistance breaks decisively and price retests it from above and holds, that old resistance is now acting as…
blocks.explain: Polarity: broken resistance frequently flips to support because missed-breakout buyers and trapped sellers both create buying at the retest.

blocks.q: A 'false break' or bull trap is characterized by…
options: A decisive close beyond the level
Price poking beyond a level but closing back inside, trapping breakout traders
blocks.explain: A false break wicks beyond the level without a confirming close, then reverses — stranding those who chased the breakout.

lessons.title: Trendlines, channels, and drawing discipline
glossary: A sloped line connecting swing lows (up) or swing highs (down) acting as dynamic support/resistance.
A pair of parallel trendlines bracketing price.
Forcing a trendline through wicks to fit the past, reducing its predictive value.

blocks.html: A trendline is dynamic support or resistance: in an uptrend, connect successive higher lows; in a downtrend, connect lower highs. A second parallel line forms a channel that brackets the move.

blocks.title: An up-channel
blocks.caption: Two parallel lines bracket the advance. Traders buy pullbacks to the lower rail and trim near the upper rail while structure holds.

blocks.label: Don't overfit the line
blocks.html: Any three points can be connected if you cheat through wicks. A trendline earns trust by being touched and respected on a closing basis multiple times without being redrawn. If you find yourself moving the line to fit each new bar, it has no predictive value — you are overfitting the past.

blocks.title: Drawing a trustworthy trendline
steps: Anchor
Start from two clear swing points in the trend direction (lows for up, highs for down).
Extend
Project the line forward; do not adjust it to chase price.
Validate
Count clean touches. Two points define a line; the third respected touch validates it.
Invalidate
Decide in advance: a decisive close through the line ends it. That is also a logical stop location.

blocks.q: What most reduces a trendline's usefulness?
options: Drawing it once and leaving it
Constantly redrawing it through wicks to fit new bars (overfitting)
blocks.explain: A line you keep moving to fit the past has no forward value. Trustworthy lines are anchored, extended, and left alone to be tested.

blocks.q: In an up-channel, a disciplined trader typically…
options: Buys the upper rail and sells the lower
Buys pullbacks toward the lower rail and trims near the upper rail while structure holds
Only trades the breakout of the daily
blocks.explain: In an up-channel you buy weakness (pullbacks to the rising lower rail = support) and take profits into strength (upper rail = resistance), until structure breaks.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Edwards & Magee, "Technical Analysis of Stock Trends"
The foundational classic on trendlines, channels, and classical chart patterns — primary source for level-drawing discipline.
Murphy, "Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets"
The standard comprehensive reference tying trend structure and support/resistance together.
Brooks, "Trading Price Action Trends"
Bar-by-bar treatment of trend structure, swings, and breaks for serious price-action study.

questions.q: An uptrend is defined structurally by…
questions.explain: Trend = swing structure. HH + HL is an uptrend regardless of colour or indicators.

questions.q: A 'change of character' (ChoCh) in an uptrend is…
options: The first lower low that breaks the HH/HL pattern
questions.explain: The first swing that violates the trend's structure warns of a possible regime change.

questions.q: Broken resistance that price retests from above and holds becomes…
questions.explain: Polarity: trapped sellers and missed-breakout buyers create support at the retest of old resistance.

questions.q: A bull trap / false break is…
options: A poke above a level that closes back inside, trapping breakout buyers
questions.explain: No confirming close beyond the level; price reverses back into the range.

questions.q: The order-flow reason levels react is that…
options: Resting orders cluster at widely watched levels (liquidity pools)
questions.explain: Clustered orders at watched levels make reactions more likely — partly self-fulfilling order flow.

questions.q: The best practice for a decisive break of a level is to require…
options: A close beyond the zone, ideally on rising volume
questions.explain: A closing break filters out wick-only false breaks; volume adds conviction.

questions.q: Overfitting a trendline means…
options: Anchoring it to two swings and leaving it
Repeatedly redrawing it through wicks to fit each new bar
questions.explain: A constantly redrawn line fits the past but predicts nothing.

modules.title: Candlestick Patterns & Price Action
modules.tagline: High-signal shapes, the psychology they encode, and the statistics that keep you honest.
objectives: Identify doji, hammer, shooting star, marubozu, engulfing, and inside bars and state the psychology each encodes.
Rank a pattern's reliability by location, trend fit, confirmation, and volume (confluence).
Treat any pattern as a conditional probability measured against its base rate.
Recognize confirmation, survivorship, and small-sample biases that manufacture false edges.

lessons.title: Single-candle signals and their psychology
glossary: A candle with open ≈ close (tiny body); indecision.
Small body up top, long lower wick; rejection of lower prices.
Small body at the bottom, long upper wick; rejection of higher prices.
A candle with little or no wick; one side dominated wire-to-wire.
A sharp move pushed back, leaving a long wick.

blocks.html: Some single candles hint that control is shifting. They are clues, not prophecies, and only carry weight in the right context: at a tested level, after an extended move, and confirmed by what follows.

items.label: Doji
items.html: Open ≈ close. Buyers and sellers fought to a draw. After a long trend, a stalemate warns momentum is tiring.

items.label: Hammer
items.html: Small body up top, long lower wick. Price fell then buyers reclaimed it by the close — rejection of lower prices. Meaningful at support.

items.label: Shooting star
items.html: Small body low, long upper wick. Buyers pushed up then sellers slammed it back — rejection of higher prices. Meaningful at resistance.

items.label: Marubozu
items.html: Almost no wick. One side controlled from open to close — maximal conviction for the period.

blocks.title: Hammer defending support
blocks.caption: Sellers drove price to ~9.9 but buyers reclaimed almost all of it by the close, printing a hammer right at support — a footprint of defense.

blocks.label: The wick tells the story
blocks.html: On a hammer, the long lower wick is the message: price was offered much lower and buyers absorbed it. The location (at support) and the follow-through (next candle) decide whether that absorption matters.

blocks.q: A shooting star at resistance suggests…
options: Sellers rejected higher prices — possible stall of the advance
blocks.explain: A long upper wick means price was pushed up then sold back down; at resistance that rejection warns the advance may stall. It is a clue, not a certainty.

blocks.q: A doji is most informative when it appears…
options: After an extended trend or at a tested level
blocks.explain: Indecision matters where a decision was expected — after a strong trend or at a key level — not in the middle of chop.

lessons.title: Multi-candle patterns and confirmation
glossary: A candle whose body fully covers the prior candle's body.
A candle whose whole range sits within the prior candle's range; compression.
Waiting for a following candle, close, or volume to validate a signal.

blocks.html: A bullish engulfing is two candles: a small red one, then a larger green one whose body fully covers it. It says sellers were decisively overpowered — strongest after a downtrend into support.

blocks.title: Bullish engulfing at a level
blocks.caption: The final green candle opens near the prior close and closes above the prior open — its body swallows the red body. Buyers overwhelmed sellers.

blocks.html: An inside bar is the opposite: a candle whose entire range sits inside the prior candle. It signals compression — a coiled spring — and traders often watch for the break of the mother bar's range.

head: Pattern
Reads as
Best context
rows: At support/resistance, with the higher-timeframe trend
In a trend as a continuation coil
After an extended move as an exhaustion warning
At a tested level, confirmed next candle

blocks.label: Context is everything
blocks.html: The identical candle shape means little in open space. Weight a pattern only when it appears at a tested level, aligns with the higher-timeframe trend, and comes with supportive volume. A pattern alone is a weak signal — Bulkowski's statistics show many patterns barely beat a coin flip in isolation.

blocks.title: How a trader actually uses a pattern
steps: Location
Is it at a meaningful level? If not, ignore it.
Trend fit
Does it agree with the higher-timeframe direction?
Confirmation
Wait for the next candle / a confirming close / volume rather than front-running.
Risk plan
Define the invalidation (stop) and target before entering.

blocks.q: Why is a bullish engulfing at support more meaningful than one in open space?
options: Confluence — a tested level plus the pattern is a stronger, corroborated signal
blocks.explain: Confluence: the pattern lining up with a meaningful level and the trend makes it far more reliable than the shape alone.

blocks.q: An inside bar primarily signals…
options: Compression — reduced range that often precedes an expansion
blocks.explain: An inside bar's range sits within the prior bar: volatility is contracting, a coil that frequently precedes a directional break.

lessons.title: The base-rate problem: patterns need statistics
glossary: The unconditional frequency of an outcome, ignoring the signal.
Seeking evidence that fits a belief and ignoring the rest.
Judging a method only from the winners that survived, ignoring failures.
The number of observations; small samples mislead.

blocks.html: The dangerous thing about patterns is that our brains are pattern-completion machines: we see hammers everywhere after price rose and forget the hammers that failed. Rigor means treating a pattern as a conditional probability, not a promise.

Ask: after this pattern in this context, how often does price move my way within N bars, and by how much versus the base rate? If a hammer is followed by a bounce 55% of the time but price bounces 52% of the time anyway, the hammer's edge is nearly nothing.

blocks.label: Three biases that fake an edge
blocks.html: (1) Confirmation bias — remembering wins, forgetting losses. (2) Survivorship bias — studying only the charts where the pattern 'worked.' (3) Small samples — ten trades prove nothing; noise dominates until dozens of trades accumulate.

blocks.caption: One hammer-at-support pattern, twelve times: about half bounce, half fail.

blocks.q: A pattern is followed by a bounce 55% of the time, but the market bounces 53% of the time regardless. The pattern's edge is…
options: About 2 percentage points — tiny, and easily noise in a small sample
blocks.explain: Edge is the lift over the base rate: 55% − 53% = 2 points. That is small and could vanish once you account for costs and sampling error.

blocks.q: Studying only the charts where a pattern worked is…
blocks.explain: Cherry-picking the survivors (the winners) inflates a method's apparent reliability — survivorship bias.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Bulkowski, "Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts"
Publishes measured performance and break-even failure rates per pattern — the antidote to anecdote.
Nison, "Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques"
Authoritative on pattern definitions and the psychology behind them.
Aronson, "Evidence-Based Technical Analysis"
A rigorous, skeptical statistical treatment of whether TA signals have real edge.
Kahneman, "Thinking, Fast and Slow"
Why humans over-see patterns — base rates, small samples, and cognitive bias.

questions.q: A hammer's long lower wick shows that during the period…
options: Price fell but buyers reclaimed it by the close
Sellers closed it at the low
questions.explain: Long lower wick = rejection of lower prices; buyers absorbed the sell-off before the close.

questions.q: A shooting star at resistance suggests…
options: Rejection of higher prices — possible stall
questions.explain: A long upper wick at resistance means sellers slammed price back down — the advance may stall.

questions.q: A bullish engulfing candle is…
options: A larger green body that fully covers the prior red body
questions.explain: Buyers decisively overpower sellers; the green body engulfs the prior red body.

questions.q: An inside bar signals…
options: Compression that often precedes a directional expansion
questions.explain: Its range sits inside the prior bar — contracting volatility, a coil before a break.

questions.q: The single biggest factor making a pattern trustworthy is…
options: Context — location, trend fit, confirmation, and volume
questions.explain: Confluence matters far more than the raw shape.

questions.q: A pattern works 56% of the time; the base rate is 54%. Its edge is…
options: About 2 percentage points — small and possibly noise
questions.explain: Edge is lift over base rate: 56% − 54% = 2 points, easily within sampling noise.

questions.q: Judging a pattern only from charts where it worked is…
questions.explain: Ignoring the failures inflates apparent reliability — survivorship bias.

questions.q: Before acting on a reversal candle a disciplined trader first…
options: Waits for confirmation and defines stop and target
questions.explain: Confirmation plus a pre-planned invalidation and target is the disciplined process.

modules.title: Volume & Moving Averages
modules.tagline: Participation and trend tools — with the actual formulas, used sparingly.
objectives: Use volume and relative volume to judge conviction, and recognize climax/exhaustion.
Compute and contrast SMA, EMA (k = 2/(N+1)), and VWAP, and state what each measures.
Explain why moving averages lag and where crossovers whipsaw.
Assemble genuine multi-source confluence instead of redundant, correlated indicators.

lessons.title: Volume: the conviction gauge
glossary: Shares (or contracts) traded in a period; a measure of participation.
Current volume vs the average for that time of day; flags unusual activity.
An extreme volume spike often marking exhaustion at a move's end.
A breakout that fails and reverses, typically on weak volume.

blocks.html: Volume is how many shares changed hands, drawn as bars beneath price. It is the closest thing to a lie-detector for a move: price up on high volume shows real participation; price up on thin volume can be a fragile drift.

Raw volume is less useful than relative volume (RVOL) — today's volume divided by the typical volume for this time of day. RVOL of 3× means three times normal participation; that is what makes a breakout credible or a spike suspicious.

blocks.title: Breakout confirmed by a volume surge
blocks.caption: Price chops under resistance on ~40 units, then breaks out as volume triples. The surge signals broad agreement, not a thin push.

blocks.label: Volume confirms, it doesn't lead
blocks.html: Volume is context for the price move, read together with it. A breakout on rising volume is more trustworthy; a breakout on falling volume more often becomes a fakeout and snaps back. But beware climax volume — a huge spike after an extended run can mark exhaustion, not continuation.

blocks.q: A breakout above resistance on 3× relative volume is generally read as…
options: More trustworthy — broad participation behind the move
blocks.explain: High RVOL signals many participants agreeing, making the move more credible than a thin, low-volume push.

blocks.q: A massive volume spike after a long, extended rally can indicate…
blocks.explain: Climax volume after an extended move can mark the last rush of buyers — exhaustion — rather than fresh continuation. Context and follow-through decide.

lessons.title: Moving averages: SMA, EMA, and VWAP
glossary: Simple moving average: the unweighted mean of the last N closes.
Exponential moving average: a weighted mean that reacts faster to recent price.
Volume-weighted average price; an intraday fair-value line, reset daily.
A fast MA crossing above / below a slow MA.

blocks.html: A moving average summarizes recent price as a line. The simple moving average (SMA) is just the mean of the last N closes; it weights every period equally and therefore lags.
The exponential moving average (EMA) weights recent prices more, so it turns faster. It uses a smoothing constant k = 2/(N+1):

blocks.code:
k = 2 / (N + 1)
EMA_t = P_t * k + EMA_{t-1} * (1 - k)

# Example, N = 10 -> k = 2/11 = 0.1818
# Newest close gets ~18% weight; the rest decays exponentially.

blocks.title: Price riding above a rising average
blocks.caption: The blue line is a 3-period average. Price holding above a rising average is a quick read that buyers are in control; the average also acts as dynamic support.

blocks.html: When a fast MA crosses above a slow MA (e.g. 50 over 200) traders call it a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. These are lagging, popular, and prone to whipsaw in ranges — useful as trend filters, poor as precise timing.

VWAP weights each price by the volume traded there and resets each day. It answers 'what is the average dollar's entry price today?' — the benchmark institutions grade their fills against, which is exactly why it attracts orders.

blocks.code:
VWAP = sum(price_i * volume_i) / sum(volume_i)   # cumulative from the day's open
# 'price_i' is typically the bar's typical price (H+L+C)/3.

blocks.label: MAs lag — by construction
blocks.html: Every moving average is built from past prices, so it always trails. It summarizes trend; it does not predict. In a choppy range, MA crossovers generate a stream of false signals — the classic 'whipsaw.'

blocks.q: The EMA reacts faster than the SMA of the same length because it…
options: Weights recent prices more heavily via k = 2/(N+1)
blocks.explain: The EMA's exponential weighting gives the newest close more influence, so it turns toward price sooner than the equally weighted SMA.

blocks.q: VWAP is reset…
blocks.explain: VWAP accumulates from the day's open and resets each session — it is an intraday fair-value benchmark.

blocks.q: For a 20-period EMA, the smoothing constant k equals…
blocks.explain: k = 2/(N+1) = 2/21 ≈ 0.0952 — the weight applied to the newest close.

lessons.title: Combining volume and MAs without over-tooling
glossary: Independent tools agreeing on the same read.
Stacking so many indicators that contradictory signals prevent action.
Whether a tool trails price (MA, MACD) or attempts to anticipate (RSI extremes).

blocks.html: Indicators add context to price; they do not replace it. Two or three that measure different things (trend via MA, participation via volume, momentum via an oscillator) beat ten that all restate price with a lag.

blocks.label: Redundant indicators are not confluence
blocks.html: Three momentum oscillators agreeing is not confluence — they are the same measurement three times. Real confluence combines different information sources. Stacking similar tools produces false confidence and analysis paralysis.

blocks.q: Which set is genuine multi-source confluence?
options: RSI, Stochastic, and Williams %R all oversold
A rising 20-EMA, a reclaim of VWAP, and a volume surge
The same signal on three timeframes only
blocks.explain: RSI, Stochastic, and %R are all momentum oscillators — one signal thrice. Trend + fair value + participation are three different information sources.

head: Information source
Example tool
What it adds
rows: Where price is relative to value
Whether the move is backed by size
Whether thrust is building or fading

blocks.label: Two or three, no more
blocks.html: A practical toolkit picks at most one tool per information source and stops. Adding a fourth momentum oscillator does not add information — it adds correlated noise and hesitation.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Murphy, "Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets"
Standard reference on moving averages, volume, and combining indicators without over-tooling.
Grimes, "The Art and Science of Technical Analysis"
A quantitatively grounded guide to which tools actually add information.
Investopedia: "VWAP", "Moving Average", "Volume"
Free, reliable references for confirming formulas and definitions.

questions.q: Relative volume (RVOL) of 3× means…
options: Three times the normal volume for that time of day
questions.explain: RVOL compares current volume to the typical volume for that time — 3× flags unusual participation.

questions.q: An EMA reacts faster than an equal-length SMA because…
options: It weights recent prices more via k = 2/(N+1)
It ignores old prices entirely after N bars
questions.explain: Exponential weighting gives newer closes more influence, so the EMA turns sooner.

questions.q: For a 10-period EMA, k ≈…
VWAP is…
options: The volume-weighted average price, reset each day
questions.explain: VWAP weights price by volume and resets each session — the institutional fair-value benchmark.

questions.q: A death cross is…
options: A fast MA crossing above a slow MA
A fast MA crossing below a slow MA
questions.explain: Fast below slow (e.g. 50 below 200) is a death cross; the reverse is a golden cross. Both lag.

questions.q: Moving averages lag because…
options: They are computed from past prices
questions.explain: Built from historical prices, MAs always trail current price — they summarize, not predict.

questions.q: Which is genuine confluence rather than redundancy?
options: Rising EMA + VWAP reclaim + volume surge
questions.explain: The oscillators measure the same thing; trend + fair value + participation are three distinct sources.

modules.title: Oscillators: RSI & MACD
modules.tagline: Momentum with the real formulas — and the regime-awareness to use them.
objectives: State and apply the RSI formula (RSI = 100 − 100/(1+RS)) and interpret overbought/oversold correctly.
Construct MACD from EMAs (12, 26, 9) and read the line, signal, zero-line, and histogram.
Detect divergence and explain why it warns of fading momentum.
Match oscillator interpretation to regime (fade in ranges, buy dips in trends) and avoid repainting/look-ahead.

lessons.title: RSI: measuring momentum and its formula
glossary: A bounded indicator that swings within a fixed range to gauge momentum.
Relative Strength Index; momentum on a 0–100 scale over N periods (default 14).
RSI above 70 / below 30 — stretched, not an automatic reversal.
Price makes a new extreme but the oscillator does not — a momentum warning.

blocks.html: An oscillator is a bounded momentum gauge. The Relative Strength Index (RSI), from J. Welles Wilder (1978), compresses the ratio of average gains to average losses over N periods (default 14) onto a 0–100 scale.

blocks.code:
# 1. Over N periods, split each change into gains and losses.
# 2. Average them (Wilder's smoothing):
RS = AverageGain / AverageLoss
RSI = 100 - ( 100 / (1 + RS) )

# If AverageLoss = 0, RSI = 100.
# RS = 1 (equal gains/losses) -> RSI = 50.

blocks.html: Intuition: RSI = 50 means gains and losses balanced. Above 70 is conventionally overbought (recent gains dominate); below 30 is oversold. Crucially these are stretched, not sell/buy buttons — in a strong trend RSI can pin above 70 for a long time.

head: RSI reading
Interpretation
Trap to avoid
rows: Shorting a strong uptrend just because RSI is 'high'
Catching a falling knife in a strong downtrend

blocks.html: Divergence is often more useful than raw levels: price prints a higher high but RSI prints a lower high (bearish divergence), hinting the new price extreme lacks momentum. It is a warning of weakening thrust, not a timing trigger by itself.
