blocks.q: RSI is calculated as 100 − 100/(1+RS), where RS is…
options: Average gain divided by average loss over N periods
blocks.explain: RS = AverageGain/AverageLoss over the lookback (default 14); plugging into the formula maps momentum onto 0–100.

blocks.q: Price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. This is…
options: Bearish divergence — the new high lacks momentum
blocks.explain: Diverging slopes — price up, momentum down — warn that thrust is fading behind the new price extreme.

blocks.q: RSI above 70 in a strong uptrend most reliably means…
options: Momentum is stretched, but it can stay overbought for a long time
blocks.explain: Overbought is 'stretched,' not 'reverse now.' Strong trends routinely hold RSI above 70; blindly shorting it is a classic error.

lessons.title: MACD: trend-momentum from EMAs
glossary: EMA(12) minus EMA(26); measures momentum via the gap between two EMAs.
EMA(9) of the MACD line; a smoothed trigger.
MACD line minus signal line; visualizes momentum acceleration.
Where MACD = 0, i.e. the two EMAs are equal.

blocks.html: The MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence), from Gerald Appel, turns two EMAs into a momentum reading. It has three parts:

blocks.code:
MACD line   = EMA(12) - EMA(26)     # gap between fast and slow EMA
Signal line = EMA(9) of the MACD line
Histogram   = MACD line - Signal line

# MACD > 0  -> fast EMA above slow EMA (up-momentum)
# MACD crossing above Signal -> momentum turning up
# Histogram growing -> momentum accelerating

items.label: MACD line
items.html: EMA(12) − EMA(26). Positive means the fast average is above the slow one — upward momentum. It crosses zero when the two EMAs are equal.

items.label: Signal line
items.html: A 9-period EMA of the MACD line — a smoothed trigger. MACD crossing above it is a bullish signal; below, bearish.

items.label: Histogram
items.html: MACD − Signal, drawn as bars. Growing bars = momentum accelerating; shrinking bars = momentum fading even before a cross.

blocks.html: Two distinct signals live in MACD: the signal-line cross (MACD crosses its own signal) and the zero-line cross (MACD crosses 0, i.e. the EMAs flip order). Like all EMA-derived tools, MACD lags and whipsaws in ranges; its histogram is the most forward-looking piece because it turns before the crosses.

blocks.label: MACD is not bounded
blocks.html: Unlike RSI, MACD has no fixed 0–100 range — its scale depends on the instrument's price, so 'MACD is high' is meaningless across different stocks. Read it for crosses, zero-line, and histogram shape, not absolute value.

blocks.q: The MACD line itself is defined as…
blocks.explain: MACD line = EMA(12) − EMA(26): the gap between a fast and slow EMA, a momentum measure.

blocks.q: The MACD histogram equals…
blocks.explain: Histogram = MACD line − signal line; its bars grow as momentum accelerates and shrink as it fades, often before a cross.

blocks.q: Why is comparing one stock's MACD value to another's meaningless?
options: MACD is unbounded and scales with the instrument's price
blocks.explain: MACD is in price units and unbounded, so its magnitude depends on the instrument. Read crosses and histogram shape, not absolute level.

lessons.title: Using oscillators without fooling yourself
glossary: The tendency for stretched prices to snap back toward an average.
Trading in the direction of momentum rather than fading it.
Repeated false signals in a choppy, directionless market.
When an indicator's past values change as new data arrives, faking hindsight accuracy.

blocks.html: The deepest mistake with oscillators is using a mean-reversion tool (fade the extreme) inside a trend where you should be trend-following — or vice versa. RSI 'overbought' is a sell in a range and a buy-the-dip signal in a strong uptrend. The regime decides the meaning.

tabs.label: In a range
tabs.html: RSI > 70 near range resistance is a fade: sell the stretched move back toward the middle. Oscillators shine in choppy, mean-reverting conditions.

tabs.label: In a strong trend
tabs.html: RSI > 70 is just strength. Fading it fights the tape. Here you use pullbacks (RSI dipping to ~40 then turning) to join the trend, not to counter it.

blocks.label: Match the tool to the regime
blocks.html: First classify the regime (trend vs range) from structure and MAs. Then choose the oscillator interpretation that fits: fade extremes in ranges, buy dips in trends. Skipping the regime step is why beginners get chopped up.

blocks.label: Beware repainting and hindsight
blocks.html: Some indicators (and many social-media 'signals') repaint — their past values change as new bars arrive, so backtests look magically accurate. Always test on data the indicator could actually have known at the time (no look-ahead).

blocks.q: RSI hits 75. When is that a sell signal rather than 'just strength'?
options: In a range near resistance (mean-reversion regime), not in a strong uptrend
blocks.explain: Interpretation depends on regime: fade the extreme in a range; in a strong trend RSI 75 is strength, and fading it fights the trend.

blocks.q: An indicator that 'repaints' is dangerous because…
options: Its historical values change as new data arrives, faking hindsight accuracy
blocks.explain: Repainting means past signals were not actually available in real time, so any backtest of it is contaminated by look-ahead bias.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Wilder, "New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems"
The primary source that introduced RSI, ATR, and more — read the formulas from the inventor.
Appel, "Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors"
MACD from its creator, with construction and application.
Murphy, "Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets"
The standard comprehensive reference tying indicators to structure.
Aronson, "Evidence-Based Technical Analysis"
How to test whether an oscillator signal has edge without fooling yourself.

questions.q: RSI is defined as…
questions.explain: RSI = 100 − 100/(1+RS) where RS is the ratio of average gains to average losses over N periods.

questions.q: RSI = 50 corresponds to…
questions.explain: RS = 1 gives RSI = 100 − 100/2 = 50: balanced momentum.

questions.q: The MACD line equals…
questions.explain: MACD line = EMA(12) − EMA(26), the gap between a fast and slow EMA.

questions.q: The MACD histogram equals…
questions.explain: Histogram = MACD − signal; it accelerates/decelerates before the crosses.

questions.q: Bearish divergence is…
options: Price and RSI both higher highs
Price higher high while RSI makes a lower high
questions.explain: Opposing slopes — price up, momentum down — warn the new high lacks thrust.

questions.q: RSI > 70 in a strong uptrend most safely means…
options: Momentum is stretched but can stay overbought a long time
questions.explain: Overbought is 'stretched,' not a reversal trigger; strong trends hold RSI high.

questions.q: A repainting indicator is dangerous because…
options: Its past values change with new data, faking backtest accuracy
questions.explain: Repainting injects look-ahead: the historical signals were never actually available in real time.

questions.q: Comparing MACD magnitude across two different stocks is meaningless because MACD…
options: Is unbounded and scales with each instrument's price
questions.explain: MACD is in price units and unbounded, so absolute levels are not comparable across instruments.

modules.title: Market Microstructure
modules.tagline: Under the candle: bid/ask, the order book, liquidity, slippage, and who trades against you.
objectives: Define bid, ask, spread, mid, and NBBO, and read an order book / depth ladder.
Contrast market vs limit orders (taker vs maker) and quantify spread and slippage as real costs.
Explain how liquidity varies and why thin markets punish market orders.
Interpret liquidity grabs, adverse selection, and structural rules (PDT, margin) from an order-flow view.

lessons.title: Bid, ask, spread, and the order book
glossary: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
Ask minus bid; the immediate cost of a round trip and a liquidity gauge.
The stack of resting limit orders at each price level.
National Best Bid and Offer — the best bid and ask across all US venues.

blocks.html: Beneath every candle is a live auction. At any instant there is a bid (highest price buyers will pay) and an ask (lowest price sellers will accept). The gap between them is the spread — the immediate, invisible cost of trading.
The full stack of resting orders at each price is the order book (or depth-of-market). It shows how many shares wait to buy below and sell above — the supply/demand ledger that price walks through.

blocks.label: The spread is a real cost
blocks.html: If you buy at the ask (10.02) and immediately sell at the bid (10.00), you lose the 2-cent spread before any price move. Over hundreds of trades, spreads and commissions are a headwind that a genuine edge must overcome — they are why high-frequency 'scalping' is brutally hard for retail.

blocks.q: The spread is…
options: Ask − bid, the immediate round-trip cost
blocks.explain: Spread = ask − bid. Cross it to trade immediately; it is a real cost paid before any price move.

blocks.q: The order book (depth-of-market) shows…
options: Resting limit orders (size) waiting at each price level
blocks.explain: The book displays resting supply and demand — how many shares wait to buy and sell at each level.

lessons.title: Liquidity, order types, and slippage
glossary: The ease of trading size without moving price much.
An order to execute immediately at the best available price; crosses the spread.
An order to trade only at a stated price or better; may not fill.
The difference between expected and actual fill price.
Taking liquidity (crossing the spread) vs posting it (resting a limit).

blocks.html: Liquidity is how easily you can trade size without moving price. A deep book with tight spreads (a large, popular stock) is liquid; a thin book with a wide spread (a small-cap at lunch) is not. Liquidity is not constant — it evaporates around news and near the open/close.

blocks.title: Two order types you must understand

cards.label: Market order
cards.html: 'Fill me now at whatever's available.' You take liquidity and cross the spread — guaranteed execution, uncertain price. In thin markets it can walk the book and fill badly.

cards.label: Limit order
cards.html: 'Fill me only at X or better.' You post liquidity — certain price, uncertain execution (it may never fill). Safer for price, but you can miss the move.

blocks.html: Slippage is the gap between the price you expected and the price you got. A market order for more shares than sit at the best ask walks the book — filling at progressively worse prices. In illiquid names, slippage can dwarf the spread and quietly destroy a strategy that looked profitable on paper.

blocks.title: Why a big market order slips in a thin book

annotations.label: market buy walks the thin ask stack

blocks.caption: With little resting size, a large market buy consumes each ask level in turn and fills far above the touch — that jump is slippage, not a 'move' you predicted.

blocks.label: Liquidity is when you need it least
blocks.html: Spreads widen and depth vanishes exactly when volatility spikes — news, halts, the first minutes of the session. That is when market orders slip worst and stops fill far from their trigger. Prefer limits in thin conditions, and size down.

blocks.q: You send a market buy larger than the size resting at the best ask. You will likely…
options: Walk the book and fill at progressively higher prices (slippage)
blocks.explain: A market order takes whatever liquidity exists; exceeding the top level walks up the ask stack, producing slippage above the quoted price.

blocks.q: A limit order trades price certainty for…
options: Execution uncertainty — it may never fill
blocks.explain: Limits fill only at your price or better, so you control price but risk not being filled at all.

blocks.q: Which best describes a 'taker'?
options: Sends a marketable order that crosses the spread and removes liquidity
blocks.explain: A taker crosses the spread with a marketable order, consuming resting liquidity; a maker posts a resting limit that adds it.

lessons.title: Who is on the other side: participants and games
glossary: A firm continuously quoting both bid and ask, earning the spread for providing liquidity.
A push to trigger clustered stops, generating fills before reversing.
The risk that whoever trades against you knows more than you do.
US pattern-day-trader rule: 4+ day trades/5 days needs $25k equity in a margin account.

blocks.html: Every fill has a counterparty. Some are market makers earning the spread for providing liquidity; some are institutions working large orders over hours; some are algorithms hunting the very stop clusters this course taught you to see. Understanding the game changes how you place orders.

A liquidity grab (colloquially 'stop hunt') is a sharp poke beyond an obvious level — just past yesterday's low, say — where retail stops cluster. Triggering those stops creates a burst of market sell orders that larger players buy into, then price reverses. This is exactly the false-break trap from Module 2, viewed from the order-flow side.

blocks.label: Adverse selection
blocks.html: When your limit order fills instantly, ask why someone was so eager to take the other side. Often it is because news you haven't seen is arriving — adverse selection. Being filled is not the same as being right; informed flow tends to pick off stale quotes.

blocks.label: Rules of the game (US)
blocks.html: The Pattern Day Trader rule requires ≥$25,000 equity in a margin account to place 4+ day trades within 5 business days. Leverage, margin calls, and locate requirements for shorting are structural constraints — know your venue's rules before, not after.

blocks.q: A sharp poke just below an obvious support (yesterday's low) that triggers stops then reverses is a…
blocks.explain: Larger players push through clustered stops to source liquidity, absorbing the triggered market orders before price reverses — the order-flow view of a false break.

blocks.q: Your resting limit fills instantly right before a sharp adverse move. This illustrates…
options: Adverse selection — the counterparty likely knew more
blocks.explain: Eager counterparties are often trading on information; being filled by informed flow is adverse selection, not a good sign.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Harris, "Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners"
The definitive, readable text on how real markets, orders, and participants work.
O'Hara, "Market Microstructure Theory"
The rigorous academic foundation for spreads, adverse selection, and price formation.
SEC investor.gov: "Day Trading" & "Pattern Day Trader"
Authoritative rules on PDT, margin, and the regulator's risk warnings.
Bouchaud et al., "Trades, Quotes and Prices"
Modern empirical microstructure: order books, impact, and liquidity dynamics.

questions.q: The spread equals…
questions.explain: Spread = ask − bid; crossing it is the immediate round-trip cost of trading.

questions.q: A market order gives you…
questions.explain: A market order fills immediately (execution certain) at whatever price is available (price uncertain).

questions.q: Slippage is…
options: The gap between expected and actual fill price
questions.explain: Slippage is how far your fill differs from the expected price, e.g. when a big order walks the book.

questions.q: A 'maker' in an order book…
options: Crosses the spread with a market order
Posts a resting limit order that adds liquidity
questions.explain: Makers post resting limits (add liquidity); takers cross the spread with marketable orders (remove it).

questions.q: A liquidity grab / stop hunt is…
options: A poke beyond an obvious level to trigger clustered stops, then reverse
questions.explain: It sources liquidity from triggered stops — the order-flow view of a false break.

questions.q: Adverse selection means…
options: You always get a good fill
The counterparty who eagerly trades against you may be better informed
questions.explain: Being filled quickly by informed flow often means the other side knows something you don't.

questions.q: The US Pattern Day Trader rule requires…
options: ≥$25,000 equity in a margin account for 4+ day trades in 5 days
questions.explain: PDT: 4+ day trades within 5 business days in a margin account requires maintaining at least $25,000 equity.

modules.title: Risk Management & Position Sizing
modules.tagline: The actual edge: R-multiples, expectancy, drawdown math, and the Kelly ceiling.
objectives: Compute position size from a fixed-fractional rule and express outcomes in R-multiples.
Calculate expectancy = (W×avgWinR) − (L×avgLossR) and the breakeven win rate 1/(1+b).
Explain drawdown recovery asymmetry and why small fixed risk ensures survival.
Use the Kelly fraction f* = W − (1−W)/b as a ceiling, not a target.

lessons.title: R-multiples and position sizing
glossary: The dollar distance from entry to stop × shares — the amount risked on the trade.
A trade's result expressed in units of R (a +2R trade made twice the amount risked).
Risking a constant fraction (e.g. 1%) of equity per trade.
Planned reward divided by planned risk before entering.

blocks.html: You cannot control whether a trade wins. You can control how much you lose when it doesn't. That single asymmetry is why professionals obsess over risk, and it is best expressed in R-multiples.

R is your initial risk: the distance from entry to stop, times shares. Every outcome is then measured in R. Lose exactly to your stop = −1R. Make twice what you risked = +2R. Thinking in R makes trades comparable across different prices and account sizes.

blocks.code:
R (per share) = |entry - stop|
Shares       = (account * risk_fraction) / R_per_share
R ($)        = shares * R_per_share  = account * risk_fraction

# Example: $25,000 account, risk 1% = $250 per trade.
# Entry 20.00, stop 19.50  ->  R_per_share = 0.50
# Shares = 250 / 0.50 = 500 shares
# If it hits the stop: loss = 500 * 0.50 = $250 = 1R (the planned 1%).

blocks.label: Size is set by the stop, not by excitement
blocks.html: Notice what the formula does: a wider stop forces fewer shares, a tighter stop allows more, but the dollar risk stays fixed at 1% either way. You decide where you're wrong first, then arithmetic decides size. This is fixed-fractional sizing.

blocks.q: Your account is $20,000 and you risk 1% per trade. Entry 30.00, stop 29.60. How many shares?
A trade that makes three times what you risked is…
blocks.explain: Expressed in R-multiples, making three times the initial risk is a +3R result, regardless of the dollar amounts.

blocks.q: If you widen your stop but keep risk at 1% of equity, your share count…
blocks.explain: Wider stop = larger R/share = fewer shares to keep dollar risk fixed at 1%. Size and stop move inversely.

lessons.title: Expectancy: the equation of an edge
glossary: Average profit/loss per trade in R; the core measure of an edge.
Fraction of trades that are winners.
Average winning R divided by average losing R.
The win rate at which expectancy is zero for a given payoff.

blocks.html: A method's edge is captured by one number: expectancy — the average R you make per trade over many trades. It fuses win rate and payoff into a single verdict.

blocks.code:
Expectancy (in R) = (W * avgWinR) - (L * avgLossR)
  where L = 1 - W, and if losers = 1R then avgLossR = 1.

# Simplified when losers are exactly 1R:
Expectancy = (W * b) - (1 - W)          # b = avgWinR (payoff)

# Example: W = 0.40, average winner = +2R, average loser = -1R
Expectancy = (0.40 * 2) - (0.60 * 1) = 0.80 - 0.60 = +0.20R per trade

blocks.html: That +0.20R means: risking 1% per trade, you net about +0.20% of equity per trade on average, before costs. Over 200 trades that compounds meaningfully — but only on average, and only if you actually take the setup the same way every time.
For a given payoff b, the breakeven win rate — where expectancy = 0 — is W* = 1/(1+b). This is why a high win rate is not the goal:

head: Payoff b (avg win in R)
Breakeven win rate W* = 1/(1+b)
Meaning
rows: Must win over half just to break even
Can be wrong 2 of 3 times and still profit
Wrong 3 of 4 times and still profit
Small winners demand a very high win rate

blocks.label: Costs eat expectancy
blocks.html: The formula above ignores spread, commissions, and slippage. A gross +0.20R edge can become negative once you subtract, say, 0.05R of costs per trade × many trades. Always compute expectancy net of realistic costs — this is why overtrading a thin edge loses.

blocks.q: A system wins 40% of the time; winners average +2R, losers −1R. Its expectancy is…
With a 2:1 average payoff, the breakeven win rate is…
blocks.explain: W* = 1/(1+b) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 ≈ 33.3%. Above that, the system is profitable.

blocks.q: Why can a 35% win rate still be highly profitable?
options: If the payoff ratio is large enough (e.g. 3:1), breakeven is only 25%
Win rate is all that matters
blocks.explain: Expectancy blends win rate and payoff. With 3:1 winners, breakeven is 25%, so 35% wins yields positive expectancy.

lessons.title: Drawdown, ruin, and the Kelly ceiling
glossary: A peak-to-trough decline in account equity.
The probability of losing enough capital to be unable to continue.
The bet size maximizing long-run growth; f* = W − (1−W)/b.
Random clustering of losses even in a positive-expectancy system.

blocks.html: Positive expectancy is necessary but not sufficient: path matters. Even a good system suffers losing streaks, and a drawdown that is too deep ends the game before the edge can compound. Survival is the first objective.

Losing streaks are longer than intuition suggests. With a 40% win rate, runs of 5–8 consecutive losers are ordinary over a few hundred trades. If each loss is 1% of equity, an 8-loss streak is roughly an 8% drawdown — survivable. At 5% risk per trade, that same streak is a devastating ~34% drawdown that needs a +52% gain to recover.

blocks.label: The recovery math is merciless
blocks.html: Losses and the gains needed to undo them are asymmetric: down 50% needs +100% just to break even. This asymmetry is the entire argument for small, fixed risk per trade — it keeps drawdowns in the shallow, recoverable zone.

The Kelly fraction gives the bet size maximizing long-run growth: f* = W − (1−W)/b. It is best used as a ceiling, not a target: full Kelly produces wild swings, and any error in estimating W or b (which are always uncertain) can push you past the growth-optimal point into decline. Most professionals trade a small fraction of Kelly — 'half-Kelly' or less.

blocks.code:
Kelly f* = W - (1 - W)/b

# W = 0.40, b = 2:  f* = 0.40 - 0.60/2 = 0.40 - 0.30 = 0.10 (10%)
# Full Kelly here says 'risk 10% per trade' -> enormous swings.
# Practitioners use a fraction (e.g. 1-2%), trading growth for smoother equity
# and a large safety margin against mis-estimated W and b.

blocks.q: Recovering from a 50% drawdown requires a gain of…
blocks.explain: From half your capital you must double it: +100% just to return to the prior peak. The asymmetry is why small risk matters.

blocks.q: Full-Kelly sizing is usually avoided because…
options: It produces large swings and any error in estimating W or b can push you past the optimum
blocks.explain: Full Kelly maximizes theoretical growth but is highly volatile and unforgiving of the inevitable estimation error in W and b; fractional Kelly is safer.

blocks.q: Why is small, fixed per-trade risk (e.g. 1%) the core survival tool?
options: It keeps ordinary losing streaks in the shallow, recoverable drawdown zone
blocks.explain: Small fixed risk means even a long losing streak produces only a modest, recoverable drawdown, keeping you in the game for the edge to compound.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Van Tharp, "Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom"
Origin of R-multiples and expectancy thinking; the practical playbook for position sizing.
Thorp, "The Kelly Capital Growth Investment Criterion" (and "A Man for All Markets")
Kelly sizing from the mathematician who applied it in markets and casinos.
Ralph Vince, "The Mathematics of Money Management"
Rigorous treatment of optimal-f, drawdown, and risk of ruin.
Barber & Odean, "Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth"
Empirical evidence that most active traders underperform after costs — the sobering base rate.

questions.q: Account $20,000, risk 1%, entry 30.00, stop 29.60. Shares =
questions.explain: Risk $200; R/share 0.40; 200/0.40 = 500 shares.

questions.q: A +2R trade means you made…
options: twice the amount you initially risked
questions.explain: R-multiples express result in units of initial risk; +2R = twice what was risked.

questions.q: Expectancy with W=0.40, avg win +2R, avg loss −1R is…
Breakeven win rate for a 3:1 payoff is…
Recovering from a 33% drawdown needs about…
questions.explain: From 67% of capital back to 100% is a +50% gain — the asymmetry of losses.

questions.q: The Kelly fraction is…
questions.explain: f* = W − (1−W)/b, the growth-optimal fraction — used as a ceiling, not a target.

questions.q: Full Kelly is usually avoided because…
options: it is very volatile and unforgiving of errors in estimating W and b
questions.explain: Fractional Kelly trades some growth for far smoother equity and a safety margin against estimation error.

questions.q: Fixed-fractional sizing means size is set by…
options: the stop distance and a constant risk fraction of equity
questions.explain: You fix risk as a % of equity; the stop distance then determines share count.

modules.title: Psychology & Statistics of Trading
modules.tagline: Why edges live in samples and lose in emotions — variance, bias, and the journal.
objectives: Explain variance, sample size, and the law of large numbers, and why small samples mislead.
Identify loss aversion, the disposition effect, recency bias, gambler's fallacy, and revenge trading.
Use a written plan and journal to pre-commit decisions and separate process from outcome.
Compute realized expectancy from journalled trades to verify (or reject) an edge.

lessons.title: Probability, variance, and the law of large numbers
glossary: Averages converge to expectancy only over many trials.
Dispersion of outcomes around the mean; the source of streaks.
Number of trades; small samples are dominated by luck.
Confusing one lucky path with the true long-run expectation.

blocks.html: A trading edge is a statistical claim, and statistics only speaks over samples. Expectancy is the long-run average; any short run is dominated by variance. The law of large numbers promises convergence to your edge only after many trades — dozens at minimum, ideally hundreds.

Concretely: a +0.2R edge over 10 trades is invisible — a couple of unlucky losers swamp it. The same edge over 300 trades is a smooth uptrend in equity. Judging a method (or yourself) on a handful of trades is a category error.

blocks.caption: Many random paths, one +0.2R edge: early dips are variance, drift wins.

blocks.label: Small samples lie in both directions
blocks.html: A losing system can look brilliant for 15 trades; a winning system can look broken for 15. Never conclude from a small sample — and never let a hot streak convince you to abandon your rules or size up.

blocks.q: Why can a positive-expectancy system show a loss over 12 trades?
options: Variance dominates small samples; the edge only emerges over many trades
blocks.explain: Over few trades, random dispersion (variance) swamps a small average edge. The law of large numbers only guarantees convergence over many trials.

blocks.q: The minimum reasonable sample to start judging a discretionary edge is closer to…
blocks.explain: Meaningful conclusions need dozens to hundreds of trades so that variance averages out and expectancy shows through.

lessons.title: Cognitive biases at the trading desk
glossary: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good.
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long.
Over-weighting the most recent trades or events.
Believing a streak makes the opposite outcome 'due'.
Trading emotionally to recoup a loss, abandoning the plan.

blocks.html: The market is an engine for exploiting predictable human error. Kahneman and Tversky's work shows our decision-making is systematically biased — and every bias has a direct, expensive analog at the trading desk.

blocks.title: Five biases and their trading cost

items.label: Loss aversion
items.html: Losses feel ~2× as bad as equal gains. Result: we cut winners fast (to bank a good feeling) and let losers run (to avoid the pain of realizing them) — the exact opposite of 'let winners run, cut losers.'

items.label: Disposition effect
items.html: The direct consequence of loss aversion: selling winners too early, holding losers too long. It quietly inverts your payoff ratio.

items.label: Recency bias
items.html: Over-weighting the last few trades — sizing up after a hot streak, freezing after losses — instead of trusting the tested edge.

items.label: Gambler's fallacy
items.html: 'Five reds, so green is due.' Independent outcomes have no memory; a losing streak does not make a winner 'owed.'

items.label: Revenge trading
items.html: Trading to 'get back' at the market after a loss — oversized, unplanned, emotional. The single fastest route to ruin.

blocks.label: The plan is a bias-defeating device
blocks.html: A written plan — fixed entry, stop, size, and target decided before the trade — exists precisely to overrule the in-the-moment brain. You pre-commit while calm so the emotional you can't renegotiate. This is why journals and checklists work: they externalize discipline.

blocks.q: Selling winners quickly but holding losers too long is called the…
blocks.explain: The disposition effect — driven by loss aversion — inverts the ideal payoff by cutting winners early and nursing losers.

blocks.q: After five straight losing trades, believing a win is now 'due' is the…
blocks.explain: Independent trades have no memory; a streak does not make the opposite outcome more likely. Believing so is the gambler's fallacy.

blocks.q: A pre-written trade plan primarily helps by…
options: Pre-committing decisions while calm so the emotional brain can't renegotiate mid-trade
blocks.explain: Deciding entry/stop/size/target in advance overrules in-the-moment biases like loss aversion and revenge trading.

lessons.title: The trading journal as a scientific instrument
glossary: A structured log of every trade's plan, execution, and outcome for later analysis.
Judging decision quality separately from the (partly random) result.
Computing realized expectancy from journalled results to verify an edge.

blocks.html: Because outcomes are noisy, you cannot improve by staring at your P&L. You improve by treating trading as an experiment: log a falsifiable plan, execute it, and analyze the record. The journal is the instrument that turns gambling into science.

The key discipline is separating process from outcome. A trade can be well-executed and lose (good process, bad luck) or reckless and win (bad process, good luck). Rewarding yourself for lucky wins trains disaster. Grade the decision, then let statistics grade the results over many trades.

head: Log this per trade
Why
rows: Group results by setup to find which actually has edge
Makes the trade falsifiable and checks discipline
Feeds realized expectancy and slippage analysis
Separates process errors from bad luck

blocks.label: What the journal computes for you
blocks.html: With ~30+ logged trades you can compute realized win rate, average win R, average loss R, and expectancy — and compare planned vs actual to isolate slippage and discipline leaks. That is a feedback loop; raw P&L is not.

blocks.q: Grading a reckless trade as 'good' because it happened to win trains you to…
options: Repeat bad process that got lucky — eventually costly
blocks.explain: Rewarding lucky outcomes reinforces poor decisions. Grade process independently of the noisy result.

blocks.q: The main reason to journal is to…
options: Create a data feedback loop to measure edge and isolate discipline errors
blocks.explain: A structured journal lets you compute realized expectancy and separate process from outcome — the only reliable path to improvement.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Kahneman, "Thinking, Fast and Slow"
The foundational account of the biases (loss aversion, base-rate neglect) that wreck traders.
Thaler, "Misbehaving"
Behavioral finance from a Nobel laureate: the disposition effect and mental accounting.
Douglas, "Trading in the Zone"
The classic on probabilistic thinking and executing an edge without emotional interference.
Odean, "Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?"
The primary empirical paper documenting the disposition effect.

questions.q: A positive-expectancy system can lose over 12 trades because…
questions.explain: Small samples are ruled by variance; the edge shows only over many trades.

questions.q: Selling winners early and holding losers too long is the…
questions.explain: The disposition effect, driven by loss aversion, inverts the payoff ratio.

questions.q: Believing a win is 'due' after five losses is the…
questions.explain: Independent trades have no memory; expecting a correction is the gambler's fallacy.

questions.q: Loss aversion means losses feel roughly…
options: twice as painful as equal gains feel good
questions.explain: Empirically losses hurt about 2× as much as equivalent gains please — driving many trading errors.

questions.q: Grading a reckless but winning trade as 'good' trains you to…
questions.explain: Rewarding lucky outcomes reinforces poor decisions; grade process, not the noisy result.

questions.q: A written plan defeats bias mainly by…
questions.explain: Deciding entry/stop/size/target in advance overrules the in-the-moment emotional brain.

questions.q: The minimum sample to begin trusting a discretionary edge is closer to…
questions.explain: Variance requires dozens to hundreds of trades before expectancy is visible.

modules.title: Capstone: Build & Backtest a Rules-Based Setup
modules.tagline: Synthesize everything into one mechanical setup, then test it honestly — on paper.
objectives: Specify a fully mechanical setup (universe/timeframe, entry trigger, stop, target, size).
Backtest without look-ahead bias, overfitting, or ignoring costs.
Journal 10+ trades and compute net expectancy in R.
Interpret results with correct regard for sample size, and accept a null/negative result honestly.

lessons.title: Specifying a rules-based setup
glossary: Entry/exit conditions specific enough that two people would trade them identically.
The precise event that initiates entry (e.g. a close beyond a level).
The condition that proves the idea wrong (the stop).
Gradually bending 'rules' in the moment, destroying testability.

blocks.label: Capstone disclaimer
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. This capstone builds a testing discipline, not a money-making system. The goal is the process of specification, backtesting, and honest evaluation — most simple retail setups have little or no edge after costs, and finding that out is a successful outcome.

A setup is only testable if it is mechanical: written so precisely that two people reading it would place the same trade. Vague rules ('buy when it looks strong') cannot be backtested and invite discretion creep. We will fully specify one classic setup: the support-flip breakout retest, synthesizing the whole course.

blocks.title: The five things every rule set must define
steps: Universe & timeframe
Which instruments, which chart (e.g. liquid large-caps, 5-minute, regular hours only).
Entry trigger
The exact event: e.g. price breaks resistance on RVOL ≥ 2, pulls back, and prints a bullish confirmation candle holding above the flipped level.
Stop (invalidation)
Exact location: e.g. a close back below the flipped level.
Target / exit
Exact rule: e.g. fixed 2R target, or trail under each new higher low.
Position size
Fixed-fractional: 1% of equity / (entry − stop).

blocks.q: Why must a setup be fully mechanical to backtest it?
options: So the rules are unambiguous and two people would trade them identically — otherwise results aren't reproducible
blocks.explain: Backtesting requires unambiguous rules; any discretion means the historical results can't be reproduced or trusted.

blocks.q: In this setup, the invalidation (stop) is…
options: A close back below the flipped level
blocks.explain: The idea is that the flipped level holds as support; a close back below it proves the idea wrong — that is the logical stop.

lessons.title: Backtesting honestly and computing expectancy
glossary: Applying rules to historical data to estimate performance.
Using information not available at decision time, inflating results.
Tuning rules to past noise so they fail on new data.
Data withheld from tuning, used to honestly test the rules.

blocks.html: A backtest applies your mechanical rules to historical bars and records each trade's R-multiple. Done honestly it estimates expectancy; done carelessly it manufactures a fantasy. Three traps ruin most amateur backtests:

head: Trap
What goes wrong
Guard
rows: Using the day's close to 'decide' an entry that happened intraday
Only use information available at the bar you act on
Tuning parameters until the past looks perfect
Keep rules simple; test on out-of-sample data
Subtract realistic per-trade costs from every result

blocks.html: The output you care about is realized expectancy in R, computed exactly as in Module 7, plus the distribution: win rate, average win R, average loss R, largest drawdown, and number of trades. One number without the sample size and drawdown is meaningless.

blocks.code:
# Pseudocode for scoring a journal of trades (each stored as an R-multiple)
results_R = [+2.0, -1.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0]

n        = len(results_R)
wins     = [r for r in results_R if r > 0]
losses   = [r for r in results_R if r <= 0]
win_rate = len(wins) / n
avg_win  = sum(wins)/len(wins)          # +2.0R
avg_loss = sum(losses)/len(losses)      # -1.0R

expectancy = sum(results_R) / n         # average R per trade
# = (4*2.0 + 6*-1.0)/10 = (8 - 6)/10 = +0.20R per trade (gross)

# Now subtract realistic costs, e.g. 0.05R/trade -> net +0.15R.
print(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, expectancy)

blocks.label: A negative result is a real result
blocks.html: If your honest, cost-inclusive backtest shows expectancy ≤ 0, the correct action is to not trade it — that is the system working. Discovering an edge doesn't exist before risking real money is exactly what this discipline is for. Do not 'fix' it by curve-fitting until the past looks good.

blocks.q: Using the day's closing price to justify an entry that occurred mid-session is…
blocks.explain: You used information (the close) not available when the entry decision was made — look-ahead bias, which inflates backtest results.

blocks.q: Ten trades produce R-multiples summing to +2.0R. The expectancy is…
blocks.explain: Expectancy = total R / number of trades = 2.0 / 10 = +0.20R per trade (before costs).

blocks.q: An honest backtest shows expectancy of −0.1R after costs. You should…
options: Not trade it — the negative result is the system working
blocks.explain: A negative net expectancy means no edge; declining to trade it is the correct, disciplined outcome. Curve-fitting to fix it is self-deception.

lessons.title: Capstone assignment: build, journal, evaluate
glossary: Simulated trading with no real capital, to test execution and rules.
Testing rules on new data going forward, after the backtest.

blocks.html: Now you assemble everything: specify the rules, journal at least 10 trades (backtested on historical charts or paper-traded forward), and compute your expectancy honestly. This is the capstone deliverable.

blocks.label: Paper money, real discipline
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. Do this on paper or in a simulator. The point is to practice specification, record-keeping, and honest evaluation — never to justify risking real capital on an unproven setup.

blocks.title: Do this
steps: Specify
Write the five rule components (universe/timeframe, entry trigger, stop, target, size) so precisely a stranger could execute them.
Sample
Collect 10+ trades that met your entry trigger, backtested or paper-traded — include the losers you'd rather forget.
Journal
For each: planned entry/stop/target/size, actual result in R, followed-plan Y/N, one-line note.
Compute
Win rate, avg win R, avg loss R, and expectancy = total R / trades. Subtract realistic costs.
Evaluate
State whether the net expectancy is positive, and — critically — whether 10 trades is enough to trust it (it usually isn't).

blocks.title: Assignment: Build & backtest a rules-based setup
blocks.brief: Specify one fully mechanical setup, journal at least 10 trades (backtested or paper-traded), and compute its net expectancy in R. Submit the rule set, the 10-row journal, and your evaluation. Everything is simulated — no real capital.
items: A strong result states the universe, timeframe, exact entry trigger, stop (invalidation), target, and fixed-fractional size precisely enough that a stranger would trade identically.
A strong result includes a 10+ row journal with, per trade: planned entry/stop/target/size, actual R-multiple, followed-plan (Y/N), and a one-line note — losers included, not cherry-picked.

A strong result computes win rate, average win R, average loss R, and expectancy = (total R)/(number of trades), then subtracts realistic costs (spread + commission + slippage) to report NET expectancy.

A strong result correctly interprets sample size: it acknowledges that ~10 trades is dominated by variance and cannot confirm an edge, and proposes a larger forward/out-of-sample test before any conclusion.
A strong result treats a zero-or-negative net expectancy as a valid, honest finding (do not trade it) rather than curve-fitting the rules until the past looks profitable.
A strong result reflects on process vs outcome: identifies any trades that followed the plan yet lost (good process) or broke the plan yet won (bad process).

blocks.q: Your capstone's 10-trade backtest shows +0.3R expectancy. The most rigorous conclusion is…
options: The system is proven profitable — trade it live
Promising, but 10 trades is too small to trust; forward-test on more data before any conclusion
Win rate is all that matters
blocks.explain: Ten trades are dominated by variance; a positive figure is encouraging but not confirmation. Rigor demands a larger out-of-sample/forward test before trusting the edge.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Pardo, "The Evaluation and Optimization of Trading Strategies"
The professional standard on backtesting, walk-forward analysis, and avoiding overfitting.
Bergstra & Bengio / Lopez de Prado, "Advances in Financial Machine Learning"
Rigorous treatment of overfitting, cross-validation, and honest evaluation in finance.
Van Tharp, "Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom"
Ties R-multiples, expectancy, and journaling into one practical evaluation loop.
Investopedia / SEC investor.gov: "Backtesting" & "Paper Trading"
Accessible references and the regulator's reminders on the limits of simulated results.

questions.q: A setup must be 'mechanical' so that…
options: two people would trade it identically, making it reproducible/testable
questions.explain: Unambiguous rules are the precondition for a reproducible backtest.

questions.q: Using the day's close to justify a mid-session entry is…
questions.explain: You used information not available at decision time — inflating results.

questions.q: Ten trades sum to +2.0R. Expectancy is…
questions.explain: Expectancy = total R / trades = 2.0/10 = +0.20R.

questions.q: An honest, cost-inclusive backtest showing −0.1R expectancy means you should…
options: not trade it — the null result is the process working
questions.explain: No net edge; declining to trade is the correct disciplined outcome.

questions.q: Tuning parameters until the past looks perfect is…
questions.explain: Fitting to past noise produces rules that fail on new data.

questions.q: A +0.3R result over just 10 trades should be treated as…
options: promising but statistically inconclusive; forward-test more
questions.explain: Small samples are dominated by variance; more out-of-sample data is needed before trusting it.

questions.q: Including your losing trades in the journal is important because…
options: excluding them is survivorship bias and corrupts expectancy
questions.explain: Cherry-picking winners inflates expectancy — survivorship bias; honest evaluation needs every qualifying trade.

questions.q: The body of a candlestick spans…
questions.explain: Body = open-to-close; wicks reach the high and low.

questions.q: Of a candle's four prices, the most information-rich is generally the…
questions.explain: The close reflects where the market settled after digesting the session; most benchmarks are closing-based.

questions.q: An uptrend is defined structurally by…
questions.explain: Trend is swing structure: HH + HL regardless of colour or indicators.

questions.q: Broken resistance that price retests and holds from above becomes…
questions.explain: Polarity flip: trapped sellers and missed buyers create support at the retest.

questions.q: A shooting star at resistance signals…
options: rejection of higher prices — possible stall
questions.explain: A long upper wick at resistance means sellers slammed price back down.

questions.q: Judging a pattern only from charts where it worked is…
questions.explain: Ignoring failures inflates apparent reliability.

questions.q: For a 10-period EMA, the smoothing constant k =…
VWAP is…
options: the volume-weighted average price, reset each day
questions.explain: VWAP weights price by volume and resets each session.

questions.q: RSI is computed as…
questions.explain: RSI maps the gain/loss ratio onto 0–100 via 100 − 100/(1+RS).

questions.q: The MACD line equals…
questions.explain: MACD line = EMA(12) − EMA(26); signal is its EMA(9); histogram is MACD − signal.

questions.q: Bearish divergence is…
options: price and RSI both higher highs
price higher high while RSI makes a lower high
questions.explain: Opposing slopes warn the new price high lacks momentum.

questions.q: The spread equals…
questions.explain: Ask − bid is the immediate round-trip cost of trading.

questions.q: A market order gives…
questions.explain: It fills immediately at whatever price is available.

questions.q: Slippage is…
options: the gap between expected and actual fill price
questions.explain: How far your fill differs from expectation, e.g. when a large order walks the book.

questions.q: Account $20,000, risk 1%, entry 30.00, stop 29.60. Shares =
questions.explain: Risk $200; R/share 0.40; 200/0.40 = 500 shares.

questions.q: Expectancy with W=0.40, avg win +2R, avg loss −1R is…
Breakeven win rate for a 3:1 payoff is…
Recovering from a 50% drawdown requires…
questions.explain: From half your capital you must double it: +100%.

questions.q: The Kelly fraction is…
questions.explain: f* = W − (1−W)/b — used as a ceiling, not a target.

questions.q: A positive-expectancy system can lose over 12 trades because…
questions.explain: Variance rules small samples; the edge shows only over many trades.

questions.q: Selling winners early and holding losers too long is the…
questions.explain: Loss aversion drives the disposition effect, inverting the payoff.

questions.q: Using the day's close to justify a mid-session entry in a backtest is…
questions.explain: Using information unavailable at decision time inflates backtest results.

questions.q: An honest, cost-inclusive backtest showing −0.1R expectancy means you should…

questions.q: The single most realistic statement about day trading is…
options: most active day traders lose money over time and consistency is rare
questions.explain: Empirical studies (e.g. Barber & Odean) show the large majority lose after costs.

title: Personal Finance: A Quantitative Foundation
subtitle: Budgeting, the time value of money, debt, taxes, investing, and retirement — with the actual math.
tagline: Decisions you can run the numbers on, and habits that compound for life.
author: Oboros
certificateDesc: has completed a rigorous, collegiate-level foundation in personal finance, including the mathematics of compounding, debt, taxes, and investing.
disclaimer: Educational content only — not individualized financial, tax, legal, or investment advice. Dollar figures, contribution limits, and tax brackets are illustrative and change over time; verify current numbers with the IRS, the CFPB, and a qualified professional before acting. Examples ignore many real-world details (state taxes, fees, phase-outs) to keep the arithmetic clear.

modules.title: Cash Flow & Budgeting
modules.tagline: Know where your money goes before you tell it where to go.
objectives: Distinguish gross pay, take-home pay, fixed and variable expenses, and discretionary spending
Build a percentage-based budget and compute a personal savings rate
Construct a monthly cash-flow statement and read it for leaks
Set an emergency-fund target using real monthly expenses

lessons.title: The anatomy of a budget
glossary: A forward-looking plan for expected income and expenses over a period, usually a month.
A cost that stays roughly constant each period, such as rent or a loan payment.
A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries, fuel, or utilities.
Optional spending you could reduce or cut without an immediate crisis.
Income remaining after taxes, payroll deductions, and benefit premiums — the money you can actually budget.

blocks.html: A budget is a plan for the money you expect to receive and spend over a period — usually a month. It converts vague intentions (I should save more) into concrete numbers you can check against reality. A budget is not a punishment; it is a decision you make once so you do not have to re-decide every purchase.

blocks.text: Gross pay is not your budget

blocks.html: The number on a job offer is gross pay. What lands in your account is take-home pay — gross minus income tax withholding, payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare), retirement contributions, and insurance premiums. Budget the money you actually control, not the headline salary.

Most durable budgets split take-home pay into three broad buckets: <mark>needs</mark> (housing, food, transport, minimum debt payments, utilities), <mark>wants</mark> (dining out, subscriptions, hobbies, travel), and <mark>savings</mark> (emergency fund, investing, extra debt payoff).

blocks.label: A starting ratio
blocks.html: The 50/30/20 guideline — 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings — is a useful default, not a law. In high-cost cities needs alone may exceed 50%; the response is to widen the gap elsewhere, not to abandon the framework.

items.label: Rent / mortgage
items.html: Need — housing is non-negotiable, though its size is a choice.

items.label: Streaming subscriptions
items.html: Want — discretionary and easy to pause.

items.label: Minimum loan payment
items.html: Need — skipping it triggers fees and credit damage.

items.label: Roth IRA deposit
items.html: Savings — paying your future self first.

blocks.html: The single most important habit is not the exact percentages — it is tracking. You cannot manage what you never measure, and almost everyone underestimates variable spending until they write it down for one full month.

blocks.q: In the 50/30/20 guideline, which bucket does a streaming subscription fall into?
blocks.explain: A subscription is discretionary — you could cancel it tomorrow without a crisis — so it belongs in 'wants'.

lessons.title: Building a cash-flow statement
glossary: A record of money in versus money out over a period; positive cash flow means income exceeds spending.
Total income minus total expenses for the period.
A method where every dollar of income is assigned a job until income minus assignments equals zero.

blocks.html: A budget is a plan; a cash-flow statement is the scoreboard. It lists every dollar that came in and every dollar that went out over the month, and the difference is your net cash flow. Positive net cash flow is the raw material of wealth — it is the money available to save, invest, or repay debt.

blocks.title: Build it in five steps
steps: List income
Sum all take-home pay and any side income for the month.
List fixed expenses
Rent, insurance, loan minimums, subscriptions — costs you can predict.
List variable expenses
Groceries, fuel, dining, utilities — pull from bank and card statements.
Subtract
Net cash flow = income - (fixed + variable).
Assign the surplus
Give every leftover dollar a job: emergency fund, investing, or extra debt payoff.

blocks.html: In this example the household ends the month with $857 unassigned. In a zero-based budget that surplus is not left to drift — it is deliberately routed (say $457 to the Roth IRA and $400 to extra loan payoff) so income minus assignments equals zero.

blocks.label: The leak test
blocks.html: If your statement shows a surplus but your bank balance never grows, the surplus is leaking through untracked cash, buy-now-pay-later, or forgotten subscriptions. Reconcile the plan against your actual ending balance.

A cash-flow statement is a pre-flight checklist. Pilots do not skip it because they feel confident; they run it because small unnoticed problems compound at altitude. Your money is the same — the ten-minute monthly review catches the leak before it drains the tank.

blocks.q: Net cash flow is best defined as:
options: Total income minus total expenses for the period
The balance in your checking account
blocks.explain: Net cash flow is simply money in minus money out over the period. A positive figure is what you have available to save, invest, or repay debt.

lessons.title: Savings rate and the emergency fund
glossary: The share of take-home (or gross) income you save or invest, expressed as a percentage.
Liquid cash set aside to cover unexpected costs or income loss without borrowing.
How quickly an asset can be turned into spendable cash without loss of value.

blocks.html: Your savings rate — the percentage of income you keep — is the single most predictive number in personal finance, more than your salary and more than your investment returns in the early years. Savings rate = amount saved ÷ income.

From the earlier statement, routing $857 of $3,367 take-home gives a savings rate of 857 ÷ 3,367 ≈ 25%. A higher savings rate does two things at once: it builds the pile faster and lowers the pile you need, because you have trained yourself to live on less.

blocks.text: How big should the emergency fund be?

blocks.html: The target is measured in months of essential expenses, not months of income. Add up needs only — housing, food, utilities, transport, minimum debt payments, insurance — and multiply.

head: Situation
Recommended buffer
rows: Single income or some job risk
Variable income, freelance, or sole earner with dependents

blocks.html: If essentials are $2,510/month, a six-month fund is 6 × $2,510 = $15,060. Keep it in a high-yield savings account — high liquidity, insured, and boring on purpose. This money is not an investment; its job is to exist the day you need it.

blocks.label: Order of operations
blocks.html: A common sequence: (1) a $1,000 starter buffer, (2) capture any employer 401(k) match, (3) pay off high-interest debt, (4) build the full 3-6 month fund, (5) invest for long-term goals. The match comes early because it is an instant 50-100% return.

blocks.q: A household with $3,000/month of essential expenses wants a five-month emergency fund. What is the target?
blocks.explain: Five months of essentials = 5 x $3,000 = $15,000. The fund is sized on essential expenses, not gross income.

questions.q: What is the first habit that makes any budget work?
questions.explain: Tracking reveals reality. The percentages are just a target to steer toward once you know your real numbers.

questions.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
questions.explain: Rent is contractually the same each month, so it is fixed. The others fluctuate and are variable.

questions.q: Which figure should a monthly budget be built on?
questions.explain: Take-home pay is the money you actually receive and control after taxes and deductions — that is what you can assign.

questions.q: A savings rate is calculated as:
questions.explain: Savings rate = amount saved / income. It is the most predictive early-career wealth metric.

questions.q: An emergency fund's size should be based on:
questions.explain: The fund must cover essential expenses during a disruption, so it is measured in months of essentials, not income.

questions.q: What is the common name for liquid cash set aside to cover surprises without borrowing? (two words)
questions.explain: An emergency fund is your first savings priority and is kept liquid and insured, not invested.

questions.q: Which of these typically count as 'needs'?
questions.explain: Concert tickets are discretionary wants. Housing, minimum debt payments, and basic groceries are needs.

questions.q: In a ______-based budget, every dollar of income is assigned a job until the leftover equals zero. (one word)
questions.explain: A zero-based budget assigns every dollar a purpose so nothing drifts unallocated.

modules.title: The Time Value of Money
modules.tagline: A dollar today outranks a dollar tomorrow — and the gap is math you can compute.
objectives: State why money has time value and define present and future value
Apply the compound-interest formula FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) to real numbers
Use the future-value-of-an-annuity formula to value regular contributions
Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and reason about inflation

lessons.title: Present value, future value, and compounding
glossary: The principle that a sum available now is worth more than the same sum later, because it can earn a return.
What a future sum is worth today, discounted at a given rate.
What a present sum will grow to by a future date at a given rate.
When investment returns themselves earn further returns over time.
The original amount invested or borrowed, before interest.

blocks.html: The <mark>time value of money</mark> is the idea that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's dollar can be put to work and earn a return. Every serious money decision — loans, investing, retirement, even lottery payouts — is an application of this one principle.

Think of a snowball rolling downhill. It does not collect snow at a steady rate — the bigger it gets, the more surface it has to gather even more. Time on the hill matters more than how hard you push at the top. Compound interest is that snowball made of money.
Future value from a single lump sum is:

blocks.code:
FV = P * (1 + r/n)^(n*t)

P = principal (starting amount)
r = annual interest rate (as a decimal)
n = compounding periods per year
t = number of years

blocks.html: Worked example. Invest P = $10,000 at r = 7% (0.07), compounded annually (n = 1), for t = 30 years:

blocks.title: Compute FV of $10,000 at 7% for 30 years
steps: Set up
Simplify the base
Evaluate the power
Multiply

blocks.html: The $10,000 became about $76,123 without adding another cent — roughly 7.6x. Of that gain, the overwhelming majority is interest earning interest, not the original deposit.

blocks.label: The cost of waiting
blocks.html: Because compounding rewards time, starting five years earlier often beats saving twice as much later. The same $10,000 for only 20 years grows to about $38,700 — less than half — even though you waited just a third less time. The most expensive mistake is delay.

blocks.caption: Growth is trivial early, dominant late — time in the market beats a bigger late deposit.

blocks.q: In FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), which variable does compounding reward most dramatically because it sits in the exponent?
blocks.explain: Time t appears in the exponent, so small increases in years produce large increases in future value. That is why starting early is so powerful.

lessons.title: Valuing regular contributions and doubling time
glossary: A series of equal payments made at regular intervals.
What a stream of equal periodic contributions grows to by a future date.
A shortcut: dividing 72 by the annual percent return estimates the years to double.
An investment return after subtracting inflation; it reflects true gain in purchasing power.

blocks.html: Most people do not invest one lump sum — they contribute a fixed amount every month. A stream of equal payments is an <mark>annuity</mark>, and its future value has its own formula:

blocks.code:
FV = PMT * [ ((1 + r)^N - 1) / r ]

PMT = payment per period
r   = rate per period
N   = total number of periods

blocks.html: Worked example. Contribute PMT = $500 per month, at 7% annual (r = 0.07/12 ≈ 0.005833 per month), for 30 years (N = 360 months):

blocks.title: FV of $500/month at 7% for 30 years
steps: Growth factor
Subtract 1
Divide by r
Multiply by PMT

blocks.html: Contributions total $500 × 360 = $180,000, but the account holds roughly $610,000. About $430,000 — more than two-thirds — is growth. Consistency plus time did the heavy lifting.

blocks.html: To estimate how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the annual percent return. At 7%, 72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10.3 years to double. At 9%, about 8 years. This mental shortcut lets you sanity-check any growth claim without a calculator.

blocks.label: Inflation runs the clock backward
blocks.html: If investments return 7% but inflation is 3%, your <mark>real return</mark> is only about 4%. Purchasing power, not the raw balance, is what buys groceries in 30 years. Always reason in real terms for long horizons.

blocks.q: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at a 6% annual return?
blocks.explain: 72 / 6 = 12 years. The Rule of 72 is an estimate but is accurate enough for quick planning at typical rates.

questions.q: The time value of money says that:
options: Money loses value in a safe
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later
questions.explain: A dollar today can earn a return, so it is worth more than the same dollar received later.

questions.q: In FV = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), what does n represent?
questions.explain: n is how many times per year interest compounds; monthly is 12, quarterly is 4, annually is 1.

questions.q: $10,000 invested at 7% compounded annually for 30 years grows to approximately:
Compounding accelerates over time primarily because:
questions.explain: Growth stacking on prior growth is the engine of compounding, which is why the curve steepens with time.

questions.q: If your investments return 7% and inflation is 3%, your approximate real return is:
questions.explain: Real return is roughly nominal return minus inflation: 7% - 3% = 4% of true purchasing-power gain.

questions.q: The shortcut that divides 72 by the annual percent return to estimate doubling time is called the Rule of ______. (number)
questions.explain: The Rule of 72 estimates years to double; 72 divided by the rate gives the answer.

questions.q: Which factors increase the future value of a lump-sum investment?
questions.explain: Higher rate, more time, and more frequent compounding all increase FV. A lower principal decreases it.

questions.q: Contributing $500/month at 7% for 30 years yields roughly $610,000 on $180,000 contributed. The extra ~$430,000 is:
questions.explain: The gap between contributions and ending balance is compound growth — returns earning further returns.

modules.title: Debt, Credit & Amortization
modules.tagline: The same compounding that builds wealth can bury you when it runs in reverse.
objectives: Interpret APR, interest, and the difference between good and bad debt
Read an amortization schedule and compute a fixed loan payment
Compare minimum payments against aggressive payoff on a credit card
Explain what drives a credit score and how to protect it

lessons.title: APR, interest, and the two kinds of debt
glossary: Annual Percentage Rate — the yearly cost of borrowing, including certain fees, expressed as a percentage.
The outstanding amount borrowed on which interest is charged.
Interest charged on both the principal and previously accrued interest.
Borrowing that funds an appreciating asset or higher future income, ideally at a low rate.
High-rate borrowing for depreciating consumption, where interest outruns any benefit.

blocks.html: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the yearly price of borrowing money. A 22% APR credit card charges roughly 22 ÷ 12 ≈ 1.83% per month on the balance you carry. Because that interest is added to the balance and then itself charged interest, compound interest works against you exactly as hard as it works for an investor.

items.label: Mortgage (3-7%)
items.html: Often 'good' — funds an asset that may appreciate; interest may be tax-deductible.

items.label: Federal student loan (4-8%)
items.html: Can be good if it raises lifetime income; borrow deliberately.

items.label: Auto loan (5-10%)
items.html: Neutral to bad — the car depreciates while you pay interest.

items.label: Credit card / payday (20-400%)
items.html: Almost always bad — high-rate borrowing for consumption. Attack first.

blocks.html: The distinction between <mark>good debt</mark> and <mark>bad debt</mark> is not moral — it is arithmetic. Debt is defensible when the rate is low and the money buys something that appreciates or raises your income. It is destructive when a high rate compounds against a purchase that is losing value.

blocks.label: The rate hurdle
blocks.html: Paying off a 22% credit card is a guaranteed, tax-free 22% return — better than almost any investment can promise. This is why high-interest debt payoff usually beats investing on a pure-numbers basis.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 240" role="img" aria-label="Two mirrored exponential arrows: compounding growing an investment versus growing a debt" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="24" y="22" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="var(--ink)">Same math, opposite direction</text><text x="147" y="46" font-size="11.5" font-weight="800" fill="var(--fig)" text-anchor="middle">Compounding FOR you</text><text x="147" y="60" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="var(--muted)" text-anchor="middle">investment returns</text><line x1="44" y1="196" x2="250" y2="196" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1.25"/><path d="M50,192 C134,190 190,166 242,78" fill="none" stroke="var(--fig)" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round" marker-end="url(#arrUp)"/><text x="242" y="70" font-size="12" font-weight="800" fill="#2fb57f" text-anchor="middle">$$$</text><text x="413" y="46" font-size="11.5" font-weight="800" fill="#ef5f6b" text-anchor="middle">Compounding AGAINST you</text><text x="413" y="60" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="var(--muted)" text-anchor="middle">credit-card interest</text><line x1="310" y1="74" x2="516" y2="74" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1.25"/><path d="M316,78 C400,80 456,104 508,192" fill="none" stroke="#ef5f6b" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round" marker-end="url(#arrDn)"/><text x="508" y="206" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#ef5f6b" text-anchor="middle">debt</text><line x1="280" y1="52" x2="280" y2="210" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1.25" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><defs><marker id="arrUp" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="4" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,8 L4,0 L8,8 Z" fill="var(--fig)"/></marker><marker id="arrDn" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="4" refY="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,1 L4,9 L8,1 Z" fill="#ef5f6b"/></marker></defs><text x="280" y="228" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="var(--muted)" text-anchor="middle">identical exponential shape — only the sign flips</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Compound interest is direction-agnostic: it multiplies investments up and debt down.

blocks.q: Why is paying off a 22% APR credit card often described as a guaranteed 22% return?
options: Every dollar of balance eliminated avoids 22% of future interest you would otherwise pay
blocks.explain: Eliminating a 22% balance avoids 22% in future interest with certainty — an outcome no ordinary investment can guarantee.

lessons.title: Amortization: how a fixed payment splits
glossary: Paying off a loan through equal periodic payments that cover interest first, then reduce principal.
A table showing, for each payment, how much goes to interest versus principal and the remaining balance.
A loan whose interest rate and payment stay constant for the full term.

blocks.html: A fixed-rate loan is repaid through <mark>amortization</mark>: equal payments, each split between interest (charged on the current balance) and principal (which shrinks the balance). Early payments are mostly interest; later payments are mostly principal. The monthly payment comes from this formula:

blocks.code:
M = P * [ r(1 + r)^N ] / [ (1 + r)^N - 1 ]

M = monthly payment
P = loan principal
r = monthly interest rate (APR / 12)
N = total number of payments

blocks.html: Worked example. A $20,000 auto loan at 6% APR (r = 0.005/month) over 5 years (N = 60):

blocks.title: Compute the monthly payment
steps: Growth factor
Numerator
Denominator
Divide

blocks.html: Total paid = $386.66 × 60 ≈ $23,200, so interest costs about $3,200 on a $20,000 loan. Watch how the first and last payments split:

blocks.label: Why extra principal payments are powerful early
blocks.html: An extra $100 applied to principal in month 1 removes that dollar from every future interest calculation for the rest of the term. The earlier in an amortization schedule you overpay, the more total interest you erase.

blocks.caption: Fixed payments shift gradually from mostly interest to mostly principal.

blocks.q: In an amortization schedule, why is the first payment mostly interest?
options: Interest is charged on the balance, which is largest at the start
The rate is higher early on
blocks.explain: Interest each month is the rate times the current balance. Early on the balance is largest, so the interest portion is largest.

lessons.title: Minimum payments vs aggressive payoff
glossary: The smallest amount a lender requires each month, often ~2% of the balance, designed to maximize interest collected.
Paying minimums on all debts and throwing extra cash at the highest-APR debt first.
Paying minimums on all debts and clearing the smallest balance first for psychological momentum.

blocks.html: The <mark>minimum payment</mark> on a credit card — often about 2% of the balance — is engineered to keep you in debt as long as legally comfortable. Consider a $5,000 balance at 22% APR (1.833%/month).

blocks.caption: Minimum-only drags on for years; a fixed $200/mo clears it in ~34 months.

blocks.html: Paying a fixed $200/month clears the $5,000 in about 34 months with roughly $1,750 of interest. Paying only the 2% minimum (which shrinks as the balance shrinks) can stretch repayment past a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchase — a textbook case of compounding running against you.

tabs.label: Avalanche
tabs.html: Pay minimums everywhere, then attack the highest-APR debt first. This minimizes total interest paid — it is the mathematically optimal strategy.

tabs.label: Snowball
tabs.html: Pay minimums everywhere, then clear the smallest balance first. It costs slightly more interest but delivers a quick win that keeps many people motivated to continue.

blocks.label: Which to choose
blocks.html: The <mark>debt avalanche</mark> wins on math; the <mark>debt snowball</mark> wins on psychology. The best plan is the one you will actually finish — a completed snowball beats an abandoned avalanche.

blocks.q: The debt avalanche method directs extra payments toward the debt with the:
blocks.explain: The avalanche targets the highest APR first, which minimizes total interest paid across all debts.

lessons.title: Credit scores and how to protect them
glossary: A number (commonly 300-850) estimating the likelihood you will repay borrowed money on time.
The share of your available revolving credit you are using; lower is better.
A lender's credit check when you apply for new credit, which can slightly lower your score.
A detailed record of your credit accounts, payment history, and inquiries maintained by credit bureaus.

blocks.html: A <mark>credit score</mark> (typically 300-850 on the FICO scale) is a lender's estimate of your reliability. It affects loan approvals, interest rates, insurance premiums, apartment applications, and sometimes hiring. A higher score can mean tens of thousands of dollars less in lifetime interest.

head: FICO factor
Approx. weight
What it measures
rows: Whether you pay on time — the single biggest factor
How much of your available credit you are using
Variety of credit types (cards, installment loans)
Recently opened accounts and hard inquiries

blocks.html: The two dominant levers are within your control. Pay every bill on time (35%) and keep credit utilization low (30%). Utilization is your balance divided by your limit — if you have a $10,000 limit and carry $3,000, that is 30% utilization. Aim to keep it under about 30%, and under 10% is even better.

cards.label: Do: automate minimums
cards.html: One missed payment can drop a good score by 50-100 points and linger for years. Autopay the minimum so you are never late by accident.

cards.label: Don't: close old cards
cards.html: Closing an old card shortens your average account age and cuts your total limit, raising utilization. Usually keep old no-fee cards open.

cards.label: Do: check reports free
cards.html: You can pull your reports from the three bureaus at no cost via AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors.

cards.label: Don't: chase every offer
cards.html: Each application is a hard inquiry. A cluster of inquiries signals risk and dents your score.

blocks.label: Carrying a balance does NOT help your score
blocks.html: A persistent myth: you do not need to carry credit-card debt to build credit. Using the card and paying it in full every month builds history and avoids all interest. Utilization is measured at the statement date, not by how much interest you pay.

blocks.q: Which two factors carry the most weight in a FICO score?
options: Length of history and credit mix
blocks.explain: Payment history (~35%) and amounts owed/utilization (~30%) together account for about two-thirds of the score.

questions.q: A 22% APR corresponds to roughly what monthly interest rate on a carried balance?
questions.explain: APR divided by 12: 22% / 12 is about 1.83% charged per month on the balance.

questions.q: In an amortizing loan, early payments consist mostly of:
questions.explain: Interest is charged on the balance, which is largest at the start, so early payments are mostly interest.

questions.q: The debt avalanche method minimizes total interest by targeting:
questions.explain: Attacking the highest APR first eliminates the most expensive interest, minimizing the total paid.

questions.q: Credit utilization is defined as:
questions.explain: Utilization is the balance you carry divided by your available limit; lower is better for your score.

questions.q: Which single factor has the largest weight in a FICO score?
questions.explain: Payment history is about 35% of the score — paying on time matters more than anything else.

questions.q: Paying off a fixed-rate loan through equal periodic payments that cover interest then reduce principal is called ______. (one word)
questions.explain: Amortization spreads repayment into equal payments, front-loaded with interest and back-loaded with principal.

questions.q: Which habits generally help a credit score?
options: Applying for many cards at once
questions.explain: On-time payments and low utilization help. Closing old cards and rapid applications hurt.

questions.q: Carrying a credit-card balance month to month:
options: Costs interest with no scoring benefit
questions.explain: You build credit by using the card and paying in full; carrying a balance only adds interest cost.

modules.title: Taxes: The Basics Everyone Needs
modules.tagline: You are taxed on what you keep — knowing the rules changes what you keep.
objectives: Distinguish gross income, adjusted gross income, and taxable income
Explain marginal versus effective tax rates and progressive brackets
Contrast the standard deduction with itemizing and use tax-advantaged accounts
Describe how withholding, credits, and deductions differ

lessons.title: How income tax actually works
glossary: Total income from all sources before any deductions.
Gross income minus specific 'above-the-line' adjustments; AGI drives many phase-outs.
AGI minus the standard or itemized deduction; the amount brackets are applied to.
The rate applied to your next dollar of income — your top bracket.
Total tax divided by total income — your true average rate.
A system where higher income is taxed at higher marginal rates, bracket by bracket.

blocks.html: The most common tax misconception is that moving into a higher bracket taxes all your income at that rate. It does not. The U.S. federal income tax is progressive: each bracket's rate applies only to the income within that bracket. This is the difference between your marginal tax rate and your effective tax rate.

blocks.label: Numbers change every year
blocks.html: Bracket thresholds and the standard deduction are indexed to inflation and revised annually. The figures below use 2026 single-filer brackets — always confirm the current year's values with the IRS.
Worked example (single filer, 2026 brackets). Suppose taxable income is $60,000 and the brackets are: 10% up to $12,400; 12% to $50,400; 22% to $105,700.

This filer's marginal rate is 22% (their next dollar is taxed at 22%), but their effective rate is only $7,912 ÷ $60,000 ≈ 13.2%. Earning one more dollar never lowers your total take-home — only the newest dollars sit in the top bracket.
