False. A loss is a flow; insolvency is about the balance sheet or the ability to pay debts as they fall due. Loss-making companies with strong balance sheets are entirely solvent.
questions.explain: Every option except the last is not merely possible but routine. The one to reject is the assumption that a loss says anything definitive about solvency.

questions.q: Retained earnings opened at $412m. The company earned net income of $95m, paid $28m of dividends, and issued $60m of new shares. What is closing retained earnings, in $m?
questions.hint: Only two of these four numbers touch retained earnings.
questions.explain: 412 + 95 − 28 = $479m. The $60m share issue increases total equity but lands in share capital and share premium; it is contributed capital, not earned profit, and never passes through retained earnings.

questions.q: A company buys a $6m machine for cash. What is the immediate effect on the accounting equation?
options: Total assets are unchanged; only their composition changes
why: Nothing has been earned. Equity moves only through profit, loss or transactions with owners.
No obligation was created — the machine was paid for in cash.
Correct. Cash falls $6m and equipment rises $6m. The business has swapped one asset for another.
This would be the effect of an expense, not an asset purchase. The $6m has not been consumed; it has been converted.
questions.explain: Capital expenditure is a swap, not a cost, at the moment it happens. The cost is recognised later through depreciation as the machine is consumed — which is the matching principle applied to a long-lived asset.

questions.q: Match each timing mismatch to the item it creates.
pairs: Cash paid before the benefit is consumed
Service delivered before cash is received
Cost incurred before it is paid
questions.explain: Two questions resolve every case: has the economic activity happened, and has the cash moved? Whichever came first determines whether the balancing entry is an asset or a liability.

questions.q: An unmodified audit opinion asserts that the financial statements…
options: Present fairly in all material respects under the applicable framework
Show the company is a sound investment
Have been checked transaction by transaction
why: Immaterial errors are known to exist and are deliberately not pursued. Absolute accuracy is not the standard and never has been.
Correct. Three qualifiers do the work: fairly, materially, and in accordance with the framework.
The auditor expresses no view on the merits of the business. Companies with clean opinions fail regularly.
Audits are sample-based. Examining every transaction in a large company would be neither affordable nor useful.
questions.explain: Reading the three qualifiers precisely is the difference between using the opinion correctly and over-relying on it.

questions.q: Which disclosure most directly signals doubt about a company surviving the next twelve months?
options: A material uncertainty related to going concern
A material weakness in internal control
why: A qualified opinion flags one material but non-pervasive issue. It may have nothing to do with survival.
Correct. This paragraph exists precisely to disclose events casting significant doubt on the twelve-month outlook.
A material weakness concerns the reliability of the reporting machinery, which is serious but is not itself a survival question.
A restatement says the past figures were wrong. It damages credibility but is not a forward-looking solvency signal.
questions.explain: Going concern language is one of the highest-signal sentences in an annual report and is usually placed where casual readers will not reach it.

questions.q: Under which circumstances is book value a reasonable first approximation of economic value? Select all that apply.
options: A bank whose assets are mostly loans and securities
A property company carrying investment property at fair value under IFRS
A consultancy whose value is its staff and client relationships
A pharmaceutical company whose pipeline was developed in-house
why: Reasonable. A bank’s balance sheet contains nearly all of its productive capacity, much of it marked close to fair value.
Reasonable. IFRS permits investment property at fair value, so the carrying amount is a current estimate rather than a historical residue.
Poor. Staff and relationships never appear as assets, so book value omits essentially everything that makes the firm valuable.
Poor. Internally generated R&D is largely expensed as incurred under US GAAP, so a valuable pipeline can be almost invisible on the balance sheet.
questions.explain: Book value works where the balance sheet captures the productive assets and carries them near current value. It fails wherever value is intangible and internally generated — which is most of the modern economy.

questions.q: A retailer reports rising net income for three consecutive years while operating cash flow falls each year. Give three distinct, plausible explanations, and state what you would examine in the filings to distinguish between them.
questions.model: Three families of explanation, all consistent with rising profit and falling operating cash flow. (1) Working capital absorption. Receivables, inventory or both are growing faster than sales — perhaps because credit terms were loosened to book revenue, or because inventory is not selling. I would compute DSO and DIO for each year from the balance sheet and income statement and see whether the deterioration matches the cash gap, and I would check the inventory footnote for a rising provision or a shifting mix toward slow-moving goods. (2) Revenue quality. Revenue may be recognised earlier than cash is collected — bill-and-hold arrangements, longer-dated contracts, channel stuffing near period end, or growth in unbilled receivables and contract assets. I would read the revenue recognition policy, look at the split between billed and unbilled receivables, and compare fourth-quarter revenue against the other three. (3) Composition of profit. Net income may be flattered by items that are non-operating or non-recurring — asset disposal gains, fair-value remeasurements, reversal of prior provisions, or capitalising costs that were previously expensed. I would reconcile net income to operating cash flow line by line in the indirect-method statement, since every non-cash and non-operating item must be added back there, and check whether capitalised development or capitalised interest has risen. Distinguishing them: the reconciliation in the cash flow statement is the fastest single test, because it names the gap explicitly. If the gap sits in working capital lines, explanation 1 or 2 applies and the receivables ageing and revenue policy separate them. If the gap sits in add-backs and non-cash items, explanation 3 applies. Persistent divergence over three years is the important feature — a single year is often just timing.

modules.title: The Balance Sheet
modules.tagline: What the company holds, who has a claim on it, and the large parts of the business it leaves out.
objectives: Read a classified balance sheet and explain why current and non-current are separated.
Interpret each major asset line, including what measurement basis it uses and how much judgement that basis admits.
Distinguish debt from other liabilities, and compute net debt and invested capital from a published balance sheet.
Name the material economic assets and obligations that a balance sheet systematically omits, and explain the consequence for analysis.

lessons.title: A photograph, not a film
glossary: One that separates current from non-current items on both sides.
Expected to be realised or settled within twelve months, or within the operating cycle if longer.
Listing assets from most to least readily convertible into cash. US practice; IFRS often reverses it.
Total borrowings less cash and equivalents.

blocks.html: The balance sheet is the only statement that describes a moment. The income statement and the cash flow statement cover a period — twelve months of activity. The balance sheet says: as at 31 December, here is what we held and who had a claim on it. One instant, chosen by the company.

blocks.label: The consequence of being an instant
blocks.html: Every balance sheet figure is a closing balance on a date the company selects. Retailers commonly close their year in January, when Christmas stock has sold and receivables are collected — the leanest, healthiest-looking day of their year. This is legal, sensible and entirely disclosed. It also means a single balance sheet flatters seasonal businesses, and that averaging opening and closing balances is the right move whenever you compute a ratio that mixes a balance with a flow.

Almost every balance sheet you will meet is classified: assets and liabilities are each split into current and non-current. "Current" means expected to turn into cash, or be settled, within twelve months — or within the operating cycle if that is longer, which matters for shipbuilders and distillers.

Within those groups, US filers order assets by liquidity, cash first. IFRS filers frequently reverse it, opening with property and ending with cash. Neither is more correct; recognising the convention stops you misreading an unfamiliar layout.

Here is the company we will follow for the rest of the course. Meridian Tools plc makes and distributes precision hand and power tools. Every number in Modules 2 through 7 comes from this one set of statements, so when a later module claims a ratio you can find its ingredients here.

Read the two right-hand columns as a pair, always. A single year is a photograph; two years is the beginning of a film. The most informative thing on this page is not any level but the direction: receivables up 20.0, inventory up 21.0, long-term debt down 15.0, retained earnings up 60.0.

blocks.text: Two derived numbers worth computing immediately

blocks.html: Working capital is current assets less current liabilities — the cushion between what is coming in within a year and what must go out within a year.
Working capital = 358.0 − 183.0 = $175.0m (FY1: $139.0m)

Net debt is borrowings less cash. It answers the question a lender actually asks: if you liquidated your cash tomorrow against your debt, what would remain? Note that only borrowings count — payables and accruals are operating liabilities, not debt, and lumping them in is one of the most common beginner errors.

blocks.q: Meridian’s working capital rose from $139.0m to $175.0m. Is that unambiguously good news?
options: Yes — more cushion is always better
No — it depends entirely on which lines drove the increase
Yes, provided the current ratio also rose
No, because working capital should always fall
blocks.explain: Rising working capital driven by cash is a strengthening balance sheet. Rising working capital driven by receivables and inventory — which is what happened here, up 41.0 between them — means cash has been absorbed into the operating cycle. The headline number is identical; the economics are opposite. Module 6 is devoted to this distinction.

blocks.text: What the balance sheet cannot tell you

items: Nothing about the period. A balance sheet does not say how much was sold or earned. Two companies with identical balance sheets can have utterly different income statements.
Nothing about quality within a line. "Trade receivables $138.0m" does not distinguish an invoice raised last week from one 200 days overdue. The ageing analysis in the footnotes does.

Nothing about the other 364 days. A company can repay a revolving facility on 30 December and redraw it on 2 January. The balance sheet shows low debt; the average balance was high. This is called window dressing and it is why lenders look at average and peak drawings, not year-end.

blocks.html: A balance sheet is a still frame from a security camera. It tells you exactly who was in the room at 11:47pm and nothing about how they got there or where they went. Two frames a year apart start to suggest a plot. The income statement and cash flow statement are the footage in between.

lessons.title: Reading the asset side
glossary: A contra-asset reducing receivables to the amount expected to be collected.
An account that offsets an asset, such as accumulated depreciation.
The excess of an acquisition price over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired.
A write-down when an asset’s recoverable amount falls below its carrying value.
The asset recognised by a lessee representing its right to use a leased item.

blocks.html: Assets are not measured on a single basis. Each line uses a different rule, and knowing which rule applies tells you how much judgement — and therefore how much room for distortion — sits inside the number.

head: Line
Measurement basis
Judgement involved
rows: Almost none. Check the footnote for restricted cash and cash trapped in subsidiaries abroad.
Invoiced amount less expected credit losses
Moderate. The allowance is an estimate of who will not pay.
Lower of cost and net realisable value
High. Cost depends on the flow assumption (FIFO, weighted average, LIFO under GAAP); NRV requires a view on what will still sell.
Cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment
High. Useful life and residual value are chosen by management.
Moderate. The discount rate and any renewal options assumed are management estimates.
Very high. Never amortised under current standards; written down only when management concludes it must be.
High. Only assets that were purchased appear; internally generated ones mostly do not.
High. Recognised only to the extent future profits are considered probable.

blocks.text: Receivables: the allowance is the interesting part

blocks.html: Meridian reports trade receivables of $138.0m. That figure is already net — the gross invoiced amount less an allowance for the customers who will not pay. Two questions matter more than the headline:

items: How does the allowance compare with the gross balance, and is that ratio moving? A falling allowance percentage while receivables grow is a classic soft spot: either credit quality genuinely improved, or the provision is being under-fed to support profit. Both look identical on the face of the balance sheet.

What does the ageing analysis look like? The footnote splits receivables by how overdue they are. A shift of weight into the 90-plus bucket is a leading indicator of write-offs, and it will show up in the footnote a year before it shows up in earnings.

blocks.label: The current expected credit loss regime
blocks.html: Since ASC 326 in the US and IFRS 9 internationally, the allowance is forward-looking: companies must provide for losses they expect over the life of the receivable, not only those already incurred. This made allowances larger and more sensitive to macroeconomic assumptions, which means the same book of customers can be provided very differently by two managements with different views of the coming year.

blocks.text: Inventory: two levers in one line

blocks.html: Meridian carries inventory of $152.0m, up from $131.0m. Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value, and both halves of that rule are choices.

Cost depends on the flow assumption. FIFO charges the oldest costs to the income statement; weighted average smooths; LIFO — permitted in the US, prohibited under IFRS — charges the newest. Under rising prices LIFO reports lower profit and a balance sheet inventory figure that can be decades out of date. US LIFO filers must disclose the LIFO reserve, the difference between LIFO and FIFO carrying value; adding it back is the standard way to compare a US filer with a foreign peer.

Net realisable value is a judgement about what will actually sell and for how much. Write-downs are irreversible under US GAAP; under IFRS they must be reversed if the circumstances reverse. A company sitting on obsolete stock has every incentive to postpone the write-down, and inventory growing faster than sales is the single most reliable early warning of one.
Meridian: inventory +16.0% against revenue +10.2% — stock is building faster than sales.

blocks.q: A distributor reports inventory up 22% while revenue is up 4% and gross margin is flat. What is the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: The company negotiated better purchase prices
Stock is not selling and a write-down may be pending
blocks.explain: Inventory growing five times faster than sales, with margin unchanged, points to product sitting still rather than to a pricing or purchasing effect. Flat gross margin is the tell: if the build were a deliberate cheap-buying opportunity you would eventually expect margin to improve. Check the inventory ageing and provision footnotes, and the split between raw materials, work in progress and finished goods — a build concentrated in finished goods is the worst case.

blocks.html: PP&E is shown gross, less accumulated depreciation. Meridian's note ties like this:

Two derived facts fall straight out of this note. First, the disposed asset had a net book value of $6.0m and was sold for $14.0m, producing the $8.0m gain that appears in the income statement — a real cash event, but not an operating one. Second, the ratio of accumulated depreciation to gross cost, 45%, says the asset base is roughly 45% through its accounting life. A company whose assets are 85% depreciated is facing a replacement cycle whether or not it has budgeted for one.

blocks.label: A quick reality check on depreciation
blocks.html: Divide gross PP&E by the annual depreciation charge to get the implied average useful life: $470.0m ÷ $32.0m ≈ 14.7 years for Meridian. If a competitor with identical equipment implies 25 years, one of the two is depreciating too slowly — and the slow one is reporting higher profit for no economic reason. Changes in implied life at the same company are more suspicious still.

Goodwill arises only from acquisitions. When one company buys another for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets, the excess is recorded as goodwill. It is not amortised under current US GAAP or IFRS for public companies; instead it is tested for impairment at least annually.

This creates a distinctive pattern. Goodwill sits unchanged at $96.0m year after year, and then in some future year drops by a large amount all at once. That drop is a non-cash admission that an acquisition did not deliver what was paid for. It tells you nothing new about cash — the money left years ago — but a great deal about the quality of past capital allocation, which is one of the few durable signals about a management team.

Other intangibles — purchased customer lists, brands, patents, capitalised software — are amortised. Meridian's fell from $40.0m to $34.0m, exactly the $6.0m amortisation charge, so no additions or impairments occurred this year.

blocks.label: The asymmetry to remember
blocks.html: If a company builds a brand, the spending is expensed and no asset appears. If it buys the identical brand, an asset appears. This means a serial acquirer and an organic grower with identical economics report very different balance sheets, very different returns on assets, and very different book values — and the acquirer will look worse on return-on-capital measures precisely because it recorded the price it paid.

lessons.title: Liabilities, equity, and what the balance sheet omits
glossary: An obligation arising from trading — payables, accruals, deferred revenue. Not debt.
Borrowings on which interest is paid. What "debt" means in a ratio.
A contractual test in a loan agreement; breaching it can make the debt immediately repayable.
Equity plus debt less cash — the capital on which a return should be measured.
A possible obligation disclosed but not recognised because it is not probable or not measurable.

blocks.html: The right side of the balance sheet is a ranking. In liquidation, claims are paid in order: secured creditors, then unsecured creditors, then preference shares, then ordinary equity. The balance sheet does not draw that ladder explicitly, but the classification hints at it, and the footnotes complete it.

blocks.text: Debt is not the same as liabilities

blocks.html: Meridian has total liabilities of $450.0m but debt of only $255.0m. The difference matters more than almost anything else on this page.

head: Liability
FY2 ($m)
Kind
Costs interest?
rows: No — settled in goods, not cash

blocks.html: Deferred revenue is the friendliest liability there is. The customer has already paid; the obligation is to deliver, not to hand back cash. A software or subscription business with large and growing deferred revenue is being financed, interest-free, by its own customers. Treating it as a burden because it appears under "liabilities" is a mistake beginners make constantly.

Deferred tax is not a bill from anyone. It records timing differences between accounting profit and taxable profit — most often because tax depreciation runs faster than book depreciation. The liability unwinds as those differences reverse, and for a company that keeps investing it may never unwind at all.

blocks.q: Which of these liabilities would you exclude when calculating net debt?
options: The current portion of long-term debt
blocks.explain: Net debt covers borrowings — anything on which interest accrues and principal must be repaid in cash. That includes the current portion, revolvers and finance leases. Trade payables and deferred revenue are operating liabilities that arise from trading and are settled in the ordinary course, so they belong in working capital, not in leverage.

blocks.text: What to read in the debt footnote

items: The maturity ladder. How much falls due in each of the next five years. A company with modest total leverage and a large maturity next year has a refinancing problem, not a leverage problem — and the two are managed completely differently.
Fixed versus floating. Floating-rate debt turns a rate move into an earnings move immediately.

Covenants. Typically a maximum net debt to EBITDA and a minimum interest cover. The distance between the current ratio and the covenant threshold — the headroom — is the number that determines whether a bad quarter is an inconvenience or a crisis.
Security and seniority. Which assets are pledged, and who ranks ahead of whom.

blocks.html: Meridian's headroom: net debt / EBITDA = 198.0 / 147.2 = 1.35×, against a typical covenant of 3.0×

For measuring returns, the useful denominator is not total assets and not equity but invested capital: the money actually put to work by all providers of finance, ignoring the cash that has not been deployed.
Invested capital = equity + debt − cash = 310.0 + 255.0 − 57.0 = $508.0m

This is the base for return on invested capital in Module 7. Excluding cash matters: a company holding a large idle cash pile is not employing it, and including it drags the measured return down for no operating reason.

The most important thing about a balance sheet is what is not on it. These are not loopholes; they are consequences of the recognition rules, disclosed and well known — and every one of them has been the source of a major failure of analysis.

tabs.label: Internal intangibles
tabs.html: Brands, trained workforces, customer relationships and internally developed software are largely expensed as incurred. A company whose entire competitive advantage is its brand can carry almost nothing for it. This is the main reason price-to-book ratios have drifted so far above 1 across the market over recent decades: the accounting base has stopped capturing what firms invest in.

tabs.label: Contingent liabilities
tabs.html: Litigation, guarantees, environmental obligations and regulatory exposure appear as narrative disclosure rather than a number, unless an outflow is probable and reliably measurable. The footnote is where a pending case that could exceed the company's market value lives.

tabs.label: Operating lease history
tabs.html: Before IFRS 16 and ASC 842 took effect around 2019, operating leases were entirely off balance sheet — retailers and airlines carried enormous unrecognised obligations. The standards brought most of them on. When comparing to pre-2019 figures, the jump in assets and liabilities is an accounting change, not a business one.

tabs.label: Pension and off-balance-sheet vehicles
tabs.html: Defined benefit pension deficits are recognised, but the assumptions behind them — discount rate, mortality, expected return — move the number enormously. Securitisations and joint ventures may keep debt outside the consolidated group entirely; the related-party and commitments notes are where to look.

blocks.label: The general lesson
blocks.html: The balance sheet answers "what did this company pay for, and who financed it?" It does not answer "what is this company worth?" Anyone who reaches for book value as a valuation without first asking which of these four omissions applies will systematically overvalue asset-heavy businesses and undervalue asset-light ones.

With the balance sheet read, the next question is what happened between the two photographs. That is the income statement, and it is the statement most exposed to judgement — which is why it gets a module of its own and then a second one, in Module 8, on the ways it can be bent.

questions.q: Why do retailers so often choose a January or February year end?
options: It is the point in the year when inventory and receivables are lowest, so the balance sheet looks strongest
It aligns with the calendar year for comparability
why: No tax regime mandates a retail year end. Companies choose within permitted rules.
Correct. Christmas stock has sold and been collected, so cash is high and inventory low. This is disclosed, legal, and a reason to be careful with single-date ratios.
A January year end deliberately does not align with the calendar year.
Auditor availability is a genuine practical factor in choosing a year end, but it is not why retailers specifically pick post-Christmas.
questions.explain: A balance sheet describes a date the company selects. For seasonal businesses this makes single-date leverage and liquidity ratios flattering, which is why averaging opening and closing balances is the right habit.

questions.q: Using Meridian’s FY2 figures — cash 57.0, current portion of debt 25.0, long-term debt 230.0, trade payables 96.0 — what is net debt in $m?
questions.hint: Only borrowings count as debt.
questions.explain: (25.0 + 230.0) − 57.0 = $198.0m. Trade payables are an operating liability and are excluded — including them is the most common error in this calculation and it inflates apparent leverage substantially.

questions.q: Goodwill of $96m has sat unchanged on a balance sheet for four years and is then written down by $60m. What has the company disclosed?
options: That it paid $60m of cash it should not have paid this year
That an acquisition made previously is no longer expected to deliver what was paid for it
That the acquired business has been sold
That its own share price has fallen
why: No cash moves on an impairment. The cash left at the time of the acquisition, possibly years earlier.
Correct. Impairment is the recognition that the recoverable amount of an acquired business has fallen below its carrying value.
A disposal would remove the goodwill entirely and produce a gain or loss on sale, which is disclosed differently.
A falling share price can be a trigger for testing goodwill, but the write-down is about the acquired unit, not the parent’s market value.
questions.explain: Goodwill impairment is a non-cash admission about a past capital allocation decision. It changes nothing about current cash generation and a great deal about how you should read management’s acquisition record.

questions.q: Which of these appear on a conventional balance sheet? Select all that apply.
options: A brand purchased in an acquisition
A brand built internally over thirty years
A right-of-use asset for a leased warehouse
A pending lawsuit where loss is possible but not probable
why: Appears. Purchased intangibles are recognised at cost and amortised.
Does not appear. Internally generated brands are expensed as incurred and never become assets.
Appears. Since IFRS 16 and ASC 842 lessees recognise a right-of-use asset and a corresponding lease liability.
Does not appear as a number. A possible but not probable loss is disclosed narratively in the contingencies note.
Appears. The net deficit is recognised, although the assumptions driving it can move the figure dramatically.
questions.explain: The pattern is that purchase and contract create recognition, while internal creation and uncertainty do not. That asymmetry is the single biggest reason book value diverges from economic value.

questions.q: A subscription business reports deferred revenue of $340m, up from $260m. How should this be read?
options: As a worsening of the balance sheet, since liabilities grew $80m
As customers prepaying for future service — interest-free financing and a leading indicator of revenue
As a sign that revenue was recognised too early
As debt that must be refinanced
why: Mechanically liabilities did grow, but the obligation is to deliver a service already paid for, not to repay cash.
Correct. Rising deferred revenue means more cash collected in advance and more contracted future revenue. It is one of the healthiest lines a subscription business can grow.
The opposite. Deferred revenue exists precisely because revenue was not recognised on receipt of cash.
It carries no interest and is never refinanced; it is settled by delivering the service.
questions.explain: Deferred revenue is customer-funded working capital. Companies that can collect a year in advance are structurally advantaged, and a decline in deferred revenue is a warning long before reported revenue turns.

questions.q: Meridian’s gross PP&E is $470.0m and the annual depreciation charge is $32.0m. What average useful life, in years, does that imply?
questions.hint: Gross cost divided by the annual charge.
questions.explain: 470.0 ÷ 32.0 ≈ 14.7 years. This crude estimate is most useful comparatively: against a peer with the same equipment, or against the same company’s own prior years. A lengthening implied life without a change in the asset mix means depreciation has been slowed, which raises reported profit without any economic improvement.

questions.q: Place these claims in the order they would be settled in a liquidation, from first paid to last.
items: Secured bank debt
Unsecured trade creditors
Subordinated notes
Preference shares
Ordinary shares
questions.explain: Ordinary equity is the residual claim, which is exactly what makes it equity — and why the accounting equation defines it as assets less liabilities rather than measuring it directly. The ladder also explains why the same set of accounts reads completely differently to a lender and to a shareholder.

questions.q: Which measure is the right denominator for return on invested capital?
why: Total assets includes operating liabilities such as payables, which were supplied free by suppliers rather than invested by financiers.
Equity alone ignores the debt capital that also funds the business, so the measure becomes a return on leverage rather than on operations.
Correct. This is the capital that providers of finance actually committed, net of the cash not yet deployed.
This equals total assets by definition, so it inherits the same problem.
questions.explain: Excluding cash matters: an idle cash pile is capital not put to work, and leaving it in the denominator understates the return the operating business is actually earning.

questions.q: A manufacturer reports gross PP&E of $1,200m, accumulated depreciation of $960m, and annual capital expenditure of $48m against a depreciation charge of $95m. What do these four numbers together suggest, and what would you check before drawing a conclusion?
questions.model: Two things stand out. First, accumulated depreciation is 80% of gross cost, so the asset base is heavily consumed on an accounting basis — the average asset is late in its recorded life. Second, capital expenditure is running at roughly half the depreciation charge, so the asset base is shrinking in net book terms and will continue to. Together these suggest a company that is under-investing relative to the rate at which its assets are being used up, which is sustainable for a year or two and then is not. The likely consequences are a future step-up in capital expenditure, rising maintenance costs and downtime in the interim, or a deliberate decision to run assets to failure ahead of an exit or a plant closure. Before concluding, I would check several things. Whether the asset mix has shifted toward leased or outsourced capacity, so that spending has moved from capex to operating cost and the right-of-use asset line has grown. Whether depreciation policy changed — a shortened useful life raises the charge without any change in spending. Whether the company recently completed a major investment programme, in which case a low-capex year is a normal pause rather than a trend; three to five years of capex-to-depreciation is far more informative than one. Whether the business is genuinely becoming less asset-intensive, for example by moving from manufacturing to distribution. And whether there is an impairment or restructuring plan disclosed, which would explain deliberate under-investment in assets about to be retired. The single most useful follow-up is the multi-year capex-to-depreciation ratio alongside revenue growth: capex below depreciation while revenue grows is the combination that most reliably precedes a period of catch-up spending.

questions.q: Match each asset to the measurement basis used for it.
pairs: Lower of cost and net realisable value
Invoiced amount less expected credit losses
Present value of the lease payments
questions.explain: No single basis governs the asset side. Knowing which rule applies to a line tells you immediately how much management judgement is embedded in it — and therefore where to look first when a balance sheet needs to be challenged.

modules.title: The Income Statement
modules.tagline: The statement that gets the headline, carries the most judgement, and is restated more often than any other.
objectives: Apply the five-step revenue model to decide when, and how much, revenue is recognised.
Distinguish principal from agent and explain why gross versus net presentation can change reported revenue by an order of magnitude with no change in economics.
Separate operating from non-operating results and compute a clean operating margin from a published statement.
Explain what EBITDA does and does not measure, and why the effective tax rate rarely equals the statutory rate.
Compute basic and diluted earnings per share and identify when EPS growth is coming from the denominator rather than the business.

lessons.title: Revenue: the hardest line to trust
glossary: A distinct promise to transfer a good or service to a customer.
The consideration a company expects to be entitled to in exchange for satisfying its obligations.
Amounts contingent on future events — rebates, refunds, bonuses, penalties.
A party that controls a good or service before transfer, and reports revenue gross.
A party that arranges for another to provide the good or service, and reports only its commission.
Revenue earned but not yet unconditionally billable.

blocks.html: Revenue is the top line, the number every headline quotes, the basis of most compensation plans, and the line most often at the centre of a restatement. It deserves the most scrutiny and usually gets the least, because it looks like the simplest number on the page.

blocks.label: Why revenue attracts manipulation
blocks.html: Revenue sits at the top, so a distortion there flows through every line below it and through almost every ratio. It is also the line where the underlying question — has the company done what it promised? — genuinely admits shades of grey, especially for long contracts, bundled products and anything sold through a channel. Where genuine ambiguity exists, pressure finds it.
ASC 606 in the US and IFRS 15 internationally converged on one framework. It is worth learning as a checklist, because most revenue questions dissolve once you identify which step is contested.

blocks.title: ASC 606 / IFRS 15
steps: Identify the contract
An agreement with enforceable rights and obligations, where collection is probable. If collection is not probable there is no contract and no revenue, however firmly the order was placed.
Identify the performance obligations
Each distinct promise is separated. Selling hardware bundled with three years of support is two obligations, not one, and they are recognised on different timetables.
Determine the transaction price
Including variable consideration — rebates, returns, volume discounts, penalties — constrained so that a significant reversal is not probable.
Allocate the price to the obligations
In proportion to standalone selling prices. This is where bundling gets interesting: allocate more to the hardware and revenue lands sooner.
Recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied
At a point in time when control transfers, or over time where the customer consumes as you perform.

blocks.html: Steps 2 and 4 do the most work in practice, and they are the ones an analyst can actually check, because the revenue recognition footnote must describe how obligations were identified and how price was allocated.

blocks.text: Gross versus net: the same business, ten times the revenue

blocks.html: Consider a marketplace that sells a $100 item and keeps $15. If it is a principal — it controls the item before transfer, sets the price, carries inventory risk — it reports revenue of $100 and cost of sales of $85. If it is an agent, it reports revenue of $15 and no cost of sales.

Gross profit and cash are identical. Revenue differs by a factor of nearly seven and gross margin by a factor of nearly seven in the other direction. Every revenue multiple, every growth rate, every margin comparison against a peer is transformed by a presentation choice that changes no economics whatsoever.

blocks.label: Where this bites
blocks.html: Travel, food delivery, advertising resale, ticketing, freight brokerage and payments have all seen major reclassifications between gross and net — sometimes reducing reported revenue by 80% overnight with no change in the business. Before comparing two companies on revenue growth or price-to-sales, confirm they are on the same basis. If one is gross and one is net, the comparison is meaningless.

blocks.q: Two food delivery companies each collect $1.00 per $10 order. One reports revenue of $10 and cost of sales of $9; the other reports revenue of $1. Which is more profitable?
options: The first, because revenue is higher
The second, because its margin is higher
Impossible to say without the cash flow statement
blocks.explain: Both keep $1.00 per order. One presents as principal, one as agent. Gross profit, cash and economics are identical; only the presentation differs. This is why revenue multiples across a sector are treacherous unless you have checked the principal-agent conclusion in each company’s revenue footnote.

items: Channel stuffing. Shipping more to distributors than they can sell, often with informal return rights. Revenue is recognised now and returns arrive later. The tell is receivables and channel inventory growing faster than end-market demand.
Bill and hold. Invoicing goods the customer has not taken delivery of. Permitted in narrow circumstances, all of which must be disclosed, and a persistent feature of accounting fraud cases.

Aggressive percentage of completion. On long contracts, revenue is recognised in proportion to progress. Overstating progress pulls revenue forward, and the correction arrives as a large loss late in the contract.
Under-providing for returns and rebates. Variable consideration is an estimate. A modest reduction in the expected return rate lifts revenue immediately.
Round-tripping. Two companies buy from each other in matched amounts. Both report revenue growth; neither has a real customer.

blocks.label: Three cheap checks
blocks.html: 1. Compare revenue growth with receivables growth over three years. Receivables persistently outgrowing revenue means the cash is not following the sale. 2. Look at fourth-quarter revenue as a share of the year, and whether that share is rising — quarter-end pushes cluster there. 3. Watch the contract asset or unbilled receivable balance. It is revenue the customer has not even been invoiced for yet, and rapid growth in it is the softest revenue a company can report.
Meridian: revenue +10.2%, receivables +16.9% — receivables are outgrowing sales, which Module 6 quantifies as 3.4 extra days of sales outstanding.

lessons.title: From gross margin down to net income
glossary: Gross profit as a percentage of revenue.
Profit from trading, before financing and tax. Also called EBIT.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.
Tax expense divided by pre-tax profit — rarely the statutory rate.
Gains and losses that bypass net income and go straight to equity.

blocks.html: The income statement is a funnel. Each stage strips out a different kind of cost, and each subtotal answers a different question. Reading it well means knowing which subtotal answers your question.

blocks.text: Gross margin: the pricing power line

blocks.html: Gross margin rose from 35.3% to 36.0%. Over any period longer than a year or two, gross margin is the most informative single ratio on the statement, because it reflects the intersection of pricing power and input cost — the two things a business either controls or does not.

It is also the least comparable, because what goes into cost of goods sold is not standardised. Some companies put distribution, warehousing and depreciation of production equipment in COGS; others put them in SG&A. Two firms with identical economics can report gross margins twenty points apart. Always read the accounting policy note before comparing gross margins across companies; within one company over time the measure is reliable, provided the policy has not changed.

blocks.text: Operating income, and what does not belong in it

blocks.html: Operating income of $109.2m is what the business earned from trading, before deciding how it is financed and before tax. It is the right starting point for comparing two companies with different capital structures, because interest depends on borrowing choices rather than on operations.

Below operating income sit items that are real but not repeatable or not operational. Meridian's $8.0m gain on the sale of a building is a good example: real cash, correctly recognised, and utterly irrelevant to what the tool business will earn next year.
The gain is 7.7% of pre-tax profit. Excluding it, pre-tax profit grew 25.8% rather than the headline 36.3%.

blocks.label: Do this every time
blocks.html: Before comparing any two years, scan for one-off items and restate both years without them. Gains and losses on disposal, restructuring charges, impairments, legal settlements, insurance recoveries and acquisition costs are all candidates. The point is not that they are fake — they are real — but that extrapolating them into the future is a forecasting error.

blocks.text: EBITDA, and the argument about it

blocks.html: EBITDA adds depreciation and amortisation back to operating income. For Meridian: $109.2m + $32.0m + $6.0m = $147.2m.

Its defenders point out that it strips away two things that differ between companies for reasons unrelated to operating skill: the depreciation policy chosen and the intangible amortisation created by past acquisitions. That is a fair argument, and it is why leverage covenants are almost universally written against EBITDA.

Its critics point out that depreciation is a real cost — machines wear out and must be replaced — and that calling EBITDA "cash flow" ignores both capital expenditure and working capital. Charlie Munger's remark that you should substitute "bullshit earnings" whenever you hear "EBITDA" is characteristically blunt but names something true: for a capital-intensive business, EBITDA systematically overstates what the owner can take out.

head: Metric
Meridian FY2 ($m)
What it ignores
rows: Capital replacement, working capital, interest, tax

blocks.html: The spread is the lesson. EBITDA of $147.2m against free cash flow of $29.3m is a difference of $117.9m — nearly 80% of the headline figure — consumed by capital expenditure, working capital, interest and tax, all of which are unavoidable.

blocks.q: A company with heavy machinery reports EBITDA of $400m, capital expenditure of $310m and interest of $60m. What does the EBITDA figure most obscure?
options: That nearly all of the operating cash is consumed by maintaining and servicing the asset base
That the tax rate is unusually low
blocks.explain: Capex of $310m and interest of $60m absorb $370m of the $400m. EBITDA is a legitimate measure of operating performance before capital structure, but quoting it without the capital intensity beside it presents a business with $30m of discretionary cash as though it had $400m.

blocks.html: Meridian's effective tax rate is 24.0%. Effective rates rarely equal the statutory rate, and the tax reconciliation footnote explains why. The usual drivers are the mix of jurisdictions, permanently disallowed expenses, tax credits such as R&D relief, prior-year adjustments, and the recognition or de-recognition of deferred tax assets.

blocks.label: A rate that moves is a signal
blocks.html: A company whose effective rate falls sharply for one year has usually recognised a one-off benefit — a settled dispute, a released provision, a newly recognised deferred tax asset. The earnings that result are real but not repeatable. Analysts who apply a normalised tax rate before forecasting are removing exactly this noise.

blocks.text: What bypasses the income statement entirely

blocks.html: Some gains and losses never pass through net income. They go directly to equity through other comprehensive income: foreign currency translation of overseas subsidiaries, remeasurement of defined benefit pension plans, and certain hedging and investment gains. Meridian carries accumulated OCI of $(7.0)m.

This matters because a company can have a good year on the income statement and a bad one in comprehensive income, or the reverse. Total comprehensive income is the honest measure of how much the owners' stake changed from performance, and it is reported one page after the number everyone quotes.

lessons.title: Earnings per share and the denominator problem
glossary: Net income attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares.
The same, adjusted for all potentially dilutive instruments — options, convertibles, restricted stock.
The convention for computing how many net new shares an option grant would create.
Shares outstanding weighted by the fraction of the period they existed.
An instrument that would increase EPS if converted, and is therefore excluded.

blocks.html: Earnings per share is net income divided by share count. It is the most quoted number in equity markets and the one most easily improved without improving anything.
Basic EPS = net income attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ weighted average ordinary shares

Both halves deserve attention. The numerator excludes income attributable to minority interests and to preference shareholders. The denominator is a weighted average, not a closing count: shares issued halfway through the year count for half.

Net income grew 36.3% but diluted EPS grew only 33.5%. The gap is share issuance from employee equity plans. Nothing improper has happened — but a shareholder's claim on each dollar of profit was diluted, and anyone tracking only EPS growth would attribute the whole 33.5% to the business.

blocks.text: Diluted EPS and the treasury stock method

blocks.html: Diluted EPS asks: if every instrument that could become a share did, what would EPS be? For options, the convention is the treasury stock method. It assumes the options are exercised and that the company immediately uses the exercise proceeds to buy back shares at the average market price. Only the net new shares count.

blocks.title: Worked example
steps: The grant
3.0m options with an exercise price of $12.
Average share price
$30 over the period.
Proceeds if exercised
Shares repurchasable with those proceeds
$36m ÷ $30 = 1.2m shares.
Net dilutive shares
3.0m − 1.2m = 1.8m added to the diluted denominator.

blocks.html: Two consequences follow. First, dilution from options depends on the share price: as the price rises, the proceeds buy back proportionally fewer shares and dilution grows. Second, options struck above the current price are anti-dilutive and are excluded — which means a falling share price makes diluted EPS look better by removing options from the count, at precisely the moment shareholders are doing worse.

blocks.q: A company grants 4m options at a strike of $20. The average share price for the year is $50. How many shares are added to the diluted count under the treasury stock method?
blocks.explain: Proceeds = 4m × $20 = $80m. At $50 that buys back 1.6m shares. Net dilution = 4.0m − 1.6m = 2.4m. Note that at a share price of $25 the same grant would add only 0.8m — dilution is a function of the share price, which is why option overhang matters most in exactly the years a company is doing well.

blocks.html: Repurchasing shares reduces the denominator, so EPS rises even if profit does not. Whether that creates value depends entirely on the price paid relative to intrinsic value — but the EPS effect appears regardless.

head: Before
After a $200m buyback at $25
rows: $97m — cash that was earning 2% pre-tax no longer does

blocks.label: The habit that protects you
blocks.html: Whenever EPS growth is quoted, ask what net income did. If net income grew 3% and EPS grew 11%, the difference came from the denominator, and the denominator cannot shrink forever. A company can also be buying back shares purely to offset the dilution from its own employee grants, in which case the buyback is not a return of capital at all — it is a cash cost of compensation, routed around the income statement.

Share-based compensation is an expense. It is recognised in the income statement at grant-date fair value, spread over the vesting period, with the credit going to equity. Meridian's charge was $4.0m, which is why share capital rose from $80.0m to $84.0m without a cash issuance.

Because no cash moves, it is added back in the cash flow statement, and a great many companies exclude it from their adjusted earnings on the argument that it is non-cash. The argument does not survive contact with the facts: the company obtained services and paid for them by issuing claims on itself. The cost fell on existing shareholders through dilution rather than through the bank account. It is one of the few adjustments where the standard-setters, most institutional investors and plain logic all agree, and where a large number of companies do it anyway.

blocks.label: How to handle it
blocks.html: If a company reports adjusted EPS excluding share-based compensation, add it back yourself. Then check whether buybacks roughly match the shares issued to employees. If they do, the "capital return" is funding compensation, and the free cash flow available to you as an owner is lower than the headline suggests by approximately the whole buyback.

questions.q: Under the five-step revenue model, when is revenue recognised?
options: As each performance obligation is satisfied
why: Signature creates a contract but transfers nothing. Step 1 is the beginning of the analysis, not the end.
Invoicing is an administrative act. Companies routinely recognise revenue before invoicing (contract assets) and after invoicing (deferred revenue).
Correct. Step 5: revenue is recognised as control passes, either at a point in time or over time.
That is the cash basis, which the accrual model exists to replace.
questions.explain: Contract, invoice and cash are three separate events, and revenue recognition is tied to none of them — it is tied to satisfying the promise.

questions.q: A ticketing platform switches from principal to agent presentation. Revenue falls from $900m to $110m. What has happened to the business?
options: Revenue collapsed and the business shrank by 88%
Nothing — only the presentation of the same transactions changed
It sold most of its operations
It lost most of its customers
why: The economics are unchanged. What fell is the gross-up, not the money kept.
Correct. As agent it reports only its commission. Gross profit and cash are identical under either presentation.
A disposal would be disclosed separately as discontinued operations.
Customer numbers are unaffected by a presentation conclusion under ASC 606 or IFRS 15.
questions.explain: Gross versus net turns on whether the company controls the good before transfer. It is one of the largest reported-figure effects in accounting with zero economic content, and it makes revenue multiples across a sector unusable without checking the basis.

questions.q: Meridian’s FY2 operating income is $109.2m, depreciation $32.0m and amortisation $6.0m. What is EBITDA, in $m?
questions.hint: Add back the two non-cash charges.
questions.explain: 109.2 + 32.0 + 6.0 = $147.2m. Note that against free cash flow of $29.3m, this figure is roughly five times larger — the gap is capital expenditure, working capital, interest and tax.

questions.q: Which of these would you strip out before using one year’s profit as a base for forecasting? Select all that apply.
options: A gain on the sale of a distribution centre
Restructuring charges from closing two plants
A one-off release of a legal provision
why: Strip it. A property disposal gain is real cash but says nothing about next year’s trading.
Strip it. Restructuring is genuinely a cost, but sizing next year on a year that included plant closures misstates the run rate.
Keep. This is the core operating cost of the business.
Strip it. A provision release is a reversal of a past estimate, not current-period performance.
Keep. Depreciation is a recurring cost of using assets, and removing it is exactly the EBITDA error.
questions.explain: The test is not "is it real?" but "will it recur?" One-off items are real and must be paid or received; they simply should not be extrapolated. Depreciation fails the test in the opposite direction — it is easy to remove and it recurs every year.

questions.q: A company grants 5m options with a $16 strike. The average share price for the year is $40. How many shares, in millions, does the treasury stock method add to the diluted count?
questions.hint: Proceeds buy back shares at the average price.
questions.explain: Proceeds = 5m × $16 = $80m. At $40 that repurchases 2m shares. Net dilution = 5m − 2m = 3m. If the share price were $20 instead, the proceeds would buy back 4m and dilution would be only 1m — dilution rises with the share price.

questions.q: Net income grew 4% while diluted EPS grew 13%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The share count fell, most likely through buybacks
why: A lower tax rate raises net income itself, so it would not create a gap between net income growth and EPS growth.
This would raise net income, again affecting both measures equally.
Correct. EPS growth exceeding net income growth is arithmetic: the denominator shrank.
Reducing depreciation raises net income, which lifts both figures together.
questions.explain: Any divergence between net income growth and EPS growth is a denominator story. It is not necessarily bad — buybacks below intrinsic value create real value — but it is not operating improvement and it cannot continue indefinitely.

questions.q: Why is share-based compensation a genuine expense despite involving no cash?
options: Because the tax authorities treat it as one
Because the company received services and paid for them by issuing claims on itself, diluting existing owners
Because it is usually reversed later
why: Tax treatment varies by jurisdiction and is not the reason for the accounting.
Correct. Value was transferred from existing shareholders to employees. The cost landed on the owners through dilution rather than through the bank account.
Conservatism is not the rationale; the rationale is that a cost was genuinely incurred.
It is not reversed. Unvested awards can be forfeited, but vested compensation stands.
questions.explain: Companies that exclude share-based compensation from adjusted earnings are asking you to treat labour paid in shares as free. Add it back, and check whether buybacks are quietly funding the dilution.

questions.q: Match each subtotal to the question it answers.
pairs: How much is left after making or buying the thing sold?
What did trading earn, before financing and tax?
What did trading plus financing plus one-offs earn?
What is left for the ordinary shareholders?
How much did the owners’ stake change from all performance?
questions.explain: Each subtotal exists because a different reader needs it. Choosing the wrong one is a common source of bad comparison — for example using net income to compare two companies with very different amounts of debt, when operating income is the neutral measure.

questions.q: A company’s effective tax rate falls from 25% to 12% for one year, lifting earnings sharply. What is the appropriate response?
options: Treat the higher earnings as the new base
Read the tax reconciliation footnote and normalise the rate before forecasting
Ignore it, since tax is not an operating item
Assume the company has moved its domicile
why: A one-year rate drop is usually a discrete benefit — a settled dispute, a released provision, a newly recognised deferred tax asset — and will not repeat.
Correct. The footnote reconciles statutory to effective rate line by line and shows exactly what caused the drop.
Tax is not operating, but it is unavoidable and directly determines earnings and cash available to shareholders.
Possible but rare, and a domicile change would be prominently disclosed rather than inferred.
questions.explain: The tax reconciliation is one of the most under-read footnotes. It converts an unexplained earnings jump into a specific, checkable cause.

questions.q: A software company reports revenue growth of 30% and receivables growth of 62% over the same year, while deferred revenue is flat. Set out what you would investigate, and what benign and adverse explanations each finding would support.
questions.model: The pattern is that billings are converting to cash more slowly and that customers are not prepaying more than before, which together weaken the usual quality signals for a software business. I would investigate five things. First, days sales outstanding for each of the last three years, computed consistently. If DSO has moved from roughly 60 to roughly 78 days, that is the whole story quantified, and the question becomes why. Second, the split between billed receivables and contract assets or unbilled receivables. Growth concentrated in unbilled amounts is materially worse, because it is revenue recognised before the customer has even been invoiced, which usually means percentage-of-completion or usage estimates rather than a collectable claim. Benign explanation: a shift toward larger enterprise contracts with milestone billing. Adverse: revenue recognised on progress that has been optimistically assessed. Third, the timing of revenue within the year. If the fourth quarter has grown as a share of the total, deals are closing at period end with extended payment terms, which is the classic quarter-end push. Benign: enterprise buying cycles genuinely cluster at year end. Adverse: terms are being given away to hit a number. Fourth, the flat deferred revenue against 30% revenue growth. For a subscription business this is the most concerning single fact on the page, because deferred revenue normally grows with the customer base. Benign: a deliberate move from annual upfront billing to monthly billing, which would be disclosed and would depress deferred revenue while improving nothing about demand. Adverse: growth is coming from one-off licence or services revenue rather than recurring subscriptions, so the reported growth rate is not repeatable. Fifth, the allowance for credit losses as a percentage of gross receivables, and the ageing analysis. A falling allowance percentage while receivables balloon suggests the provision is not keeping pace. To distinguish, I would compare operating cash flow growth with revenue growth over three years. If cash generation is tracking revenue, the receivables build is probably a mix or timing effect and will normalise. If operating cash flow is flat or falling while revenue grows 30%, the revenue is not turning into money, and the burden of proof shifts onto management.

modules.title: The Cash Flow Statement
modules.tagline: The statement nobody can argue with, and the one most people skip.
objectives: Explain what belongs in each of the three sections and why the classification itself carries information.
Reconstruct the indirect method line by line, identifying which entries are non-cash add-backs and which are working capital movements.
Compute free cash flow under at least two definitions and state what each one is fit for.
Use the ratio of operating cash flow to net income as a first-pass test of earnings quality, and name its limitations.

lessons.title: Three buckets and why the split matters
glossary: Cash generated by the trading business, including interest and tax under US GAAP.
Cash spent on or received from long-lived assets and acquisitions.
Cash raised from or returned to providers of capital.
Presenting operating cash flow as actual receipts and payments. Preferred by standard-setters, almost never used.
Starting from net income and reconciling to operating cash flow. Used by nearly everyone.

blocks.html: The cash flow statement is the youngest of the three. It became mandatory in the United States only in 1987, after a decade in which profitable companies kept failing and nobody could see it coming from the other two statements. Its purpose is narrow and valuable: to explain, in cash, how the balance of money changed over the year.

blocks.label: Why it resists manipulation
blocks.html: Cash is a fact. The closing balance is confirmable against a bank, and the statement must reconcile the opening balance to the closing balance exactly. That does not make it immune — the classification of a cash flow between the three sections is a judgement, and that judgement is where pressure lands. But the total cannot be argued with, which is more than can be said for net income.

head: Section
Contains
What it tells you
rows: Cash from customers, payments to suppliers and staff, interest and tax paid
Whether the business generates money by doing what it does
Capital expenditure, acquisitions, disposals, purchases and sales of securities
What the company is doing with money to build future capacity
Debt drawn and repaid, shares issued and repurchased, dividends paid
How the company is funded and what it returns to capital providers

blocks.html: The pattern across the three tells you where a company sits in its life. Learn to read the sign of each section as a sentence.

items.label: Operating + · Investing − · Financing −
items.html: A mature, self-funding business. It generates cash, reinvests some, and returns the rest to lenders and shareholders. Meridian is exactly this shape.

items.label: Operating − · Investing − · Financing +
items.html: An early-stage or high-growth company. It burns cash, invests heavily, and is funded by outside capital. Entirely normal for a young business; alarming for a thirty-year-old one.

items.label: Operating + · Investing + · Financing −
items.html: A business in retreat or harvest. It is selling assets and paying down debt. Could be a deliberate refocusing or the beginning of a wind-down; the disposals note tells you which.

items.label: Operating − · Investing + · Financing −
items.html: Distress. The company is losing money and selling assets to repay borrowings. This combination sustained for more than a year or two rarely ends well.

blocks.q: A twenty-year-old manufacturer reports negative operating cash flow, negative investing cash flow, and large positive financing cash flow, for the third consecutive year. What is the most likely reading?
options: A business that cannot fund itself and is being sustained by external capital
blocks.explain: The pattern is normal for a young company and worrying for a mature one. Three years of funding operations and capital expenditure entirely from new debt or equity means the trading business is not paying for itself, and the capacity of outside capital to keep filling the gap is finite.

blocks.text: Classification is where the judgement hides

blocks.html: Because operating cash flow is the number analysts watch, there is a standing incentive to move outflows out of it and inflows into it. Several legitimate options exist, and each one changes the operating figure without changing the total.

items: Interest paid. Under US GAAP it is operating. Under IFRS the company chooses operating or financing. Choosing financing lifts reported operating cash flow with no change in any payment.

Capitalised development or software. Money spent on building software can be an operating outflow (expensed) or an investing outflow (capitalised). Capitalising it raises operating cash flow and profit simultaneously.

Supply chain finance. A bank pays the supplier early and the company repays the bank later. Economically this is borrowing; if the balance stays in trade payables rather than debt, the cash flow appears in operating rather than financing. Carillion and Greensill made this a mainstream concern, and disclosure requirements have since tightened.
Securitising receivables. Selling receivables converts a working capital outflow into an immediate operating inflow. Sustainable only while the facility renews.

blocks.label: The defence
blocks.html: Read the accounting policy note for the classification choices, and watch for a step change in operating cash flow that is not matched by a step change in profit or working capital. If operating cash flow improves sharply while nothing else moves, something has been reclassified, refinanced or sold.

The direct method lists actual cash receipts and payments — cash from customers, cash to suppliers, cash to employees. It is more useful, it is what standard-setters have preferred for decades, and almost nobody uses it, because most accounting systems are built around accruals and producing it is genuine extra work.

The indirect method starts from net income and reconciles it to operating cash flow. It is what you will see in essentially every filing, and although it is harder to read, it has one great virtue: it makes the gap between profit and cash explicit, line by line. That reconciliation is the most analytically useful page in the annual report, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.title: The indirect method, line by line
glossary: An expense that reduced profit without any cash leaving — depreciation, amortisation, impairment, share-based compensation.
The cash effect of a change in receivables, inventory, payables or similar operating balances.
An item added to net income in the reconciliation because it never consumed cash.

blocks.html: Here is Meridian's cash flow statement in full. Every figure is derivable from the balance sheet and income statement you have already seen, which is the point of the exercise.

head: Meridian Tools plc — cash flow statement, FY2 ($m)

blocks.html: Everything between net income and operating cash flow falls into one of two families, and confusing them is the most common error in reading this statement.

tabs.label: Non-cash charges
tabs.html: Depreciation $32.0m, amortisation $6.0m and share-based compensation $4.0m all reduced profit without any money leaving. They are added back. This does not make them free. Depreciation is the accounting recognition of cash that left in earlier years to buy assets; share-based compensation is a cost borne by shareholders through dilution. Adding them back reverses a timing difference, not a real cost.

tabs.label: Working capital movements
tabs.html: Receivables rose $20.0m, so $20.0m of recognised revenue has not been collected — a cash outflow. Payables rose $8.0m, so suppliers financed $8.0m more than last year — a cash inflow. The rule is simple: an asset going up consumes cash; a liability going up provides it.

blocks.html: Working capital consumed $27.0m this year: receivables (20.0) + inventory (21.0) + prepaid (2.0) − payables 8.0 − accruals 5.0 − deferred revenue 3.0

blocks.text: Why the gain on disposal is subtracted

blocks.html: This is the line that confuses people most. Meridian sold a building for $14.0m and booked an $8.0m gain in the income statement. In the cash flow statement the gain is subtracted in the operating section. Has the company been penalised for a profitable sale?

No. The full $14.0m of proceeds appears in the investing section, where it belongs. If the $8.0m gain were left in net income at the top of the operating section, that $8.0m would be counted twice. Subtracting it removes the non-operating element from operating cash flow, leaving the whole cash effect in investing where a reader can see it as a disposal rather than mistake it for trading performance.

blocks.label: The general rule
blocks.html: Any gain or loss that is not an operating cash flow is reversed out of the operating section, and its full cash effect appears in investing or financing. Gains are subtracted, losses are added back. Once you see the reason — avoiding double counting and keeping each section honest — the sign stops being something to memorise.

blocks.q: A company records a $12m loss on the sale of equipment. How does this appear in the indirect cash flow statement?
options: Added back in operating activities, with the sale proceeds shown in investing
It does not appear at all
blocks.explain: The $12m loss reduced net income but consumed no cash on its own, so it is added back in operating. The actual proceeds from the sale — whatever they were — appear in investing. The same logic as a gain, with the sign reversed.

blocks.text: Reading the reconciliation as a diagnostic

blocks.html: The reconciliation answers the question "why did profit not turn into cash?" more directly than any ratio. For Meridian, net income of $79.3m became operating cash flow of $87.3m — cash exceeded profit by $8.0m, and the statement says exactly why: $42.0m of non-cash charges added back, less $27.0m absorbed by working capital, less the $8.0m disposal gain removed, plus $1.0m of deferred tax.

head: Diagnostic
What it means
Meridian FY2
rows: Operating cash flow > net income, driven by depreciation
Yes: D&A of 38.0 is the largest add-back
Growth is being funded out of the operating cycle
Yes: (27.0) this year — Module 6 examines whether this is sustainable
Operating cash flow < net income for several years
Earnings are not converting; investigate revenue quality
No, but the trend deserves watching
Often an impairment or provision; check whether it recurs annually

blocks.label: Recurring "one-offs"
blocks.html: Watch for companies that add back restructuring charges every year for five years. Each individual charge is presented as exceptional; the pattern says the cost is structural. When an add-back appears in every reconciliation, it is not an adjustment, it is an operating expense with better branding.

lessons.title: Free cash flow: a term with no fixed definition
glossary: Cash available after the investment needed to maintain the business. Defined differently by almost everyone.
The portion of capital expenditure needed to sustain current capacity, as opposed to growing it.
Buffett’s formulation: profit plus non-cash charges less the capital expenditure required to maintain competitive position.
Operating cash flow as a proportion of net income or EBITDA.

blocks.html: Free cash flow is the number most valuation ultimately rests on, and it is not defined by any accounting standard. Every practitioner computes it slightly differently, and companies exploit that latitude in their own disclosures. You must know which definition is on the page in front of you.

head: Definition
Calculation
Meridian FY2 ($m)
Fit for
rows: The default. Comparable across companies, easy to compute.
Operating cash flow + investing cash flow
Includes acquisitions and disposals. Lumpier, but honest about serial acquirers.
What is actually available to shareholders after servicing debt.

blocks.html: The three answers for the same company in the same year are $29.3m, $43.3m and $14.3m. None is wrong. The middle one is higher because it includes the $14.0m building sale, which will not repeat; the last one is lower because it recognises that $15.0m went to lenders.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.html: When a company quotes its own free cash flow figure, find the reconciliation and check three things: whether acquisitions are included, whether capitalised development costs are treated as capital expenditure, and whether lease payments are deducted. Excluding any of them inflates the number, and all three are excluded by someone.

Simple FCF deducts all capital expenditure, which understates the cash a business could distribute if it stopped growing. The conceptually right deduction is maintenance capex — enough to hold current capacity — but companies almost never disclose the split, and the distinction is genuinely blurry: a replacement machine is usually also a better machine.

Two rough approaches are standard. The first uses depreciation as a proxy for maintenance capex, on the theory that depreciation measures the consumption of capacity. Meridian's depreciation is $32.0m against capital expenditure of $58.0m, implying roughly $26.0m of growth investment and a maintenance-adjusted free cash flow near $55.3m. The second regresses capital expenditure against revenue over several years and treats the intercept as maintenance. Both are crude; the point is to bracket the answer rather than to find it.
Capex / depreciation = 58.0 / 32.0 = 1.81× — Meridian is investing well ahead of the rate at which its assets are being consumed.

That ratio is one of the most useful single numbers you can compute. Sustained above 1.0 it indicates a growing asset base; sustained below 1.0 it indicates a shrinking one, and a company running below 1.0 for years is either becoming genuinely less capital-intensive or borrowing capacity from its own future.

blocks.text: Cash conversion as an earnings quality test

blocks.html: Operating cash flow ÷ net income = 87.3 ÷ 79.3 = 1.10×

For a mature company this ratio should sit above 1.0, because depreciation adds back more than working capital typically absorbs. Persistently below 1.0 means reported profit is not becoming money, and the reconciliation will name the reason.

blocks.label: What the ratio cannot do
blocks.html: Cash conversion is a first-pass screen, not a verdict. It is legitimately below 1.0 for a fast-growing company building inventory and receivables — which is exactly the profile of a business worth owning. And it is legitimately above 1.0 for a declining company liquidating working capital, which is exactly the profile of one worth avoiding. Always read the ratio alongside revenue growth, and always over three years or more. A single year is dominated by timing.

blocks.q: Company A: revenue +35%, cash conversion 0.7×. Company B: revenue −8%, cash conversion 1.4×. Which has the better earnings quality?
options: Neither ratio settles it — the growth rates explain both
blocks.explain: A is growing fast, so receivables and inventory are absorbing cash; conversion below 1.0 is expected and not in itself a warning. B is shrinking, so working capital is being released, which flatters conversion temporarily and stops the moment the decline does. The ratios are consistent with the growth rates and neither is evidence of quality on its own. To judge either, you need three years and the reconciliation detail.

blocks.text: What Meridian looks like on this test

head: Measure
FY2
Reading
rows: Positive, but modest against $79.3m of profit
Investing for growth, not just replacing
Covered, but only just — a bad year would strain it
The main reason FCF is far below EBITDA of $147.2m

blocks.html: The picture is a healthy company investing ahead of depreciation and funding it internally, with one flag: dividends consume 66% of free cash flow, so there is little margin if working capital keeps absorbing cash at this rate. Module 6 asks whether it will.

questions.q: Why is a gain on the sale of an asset subtracted in the operating section of an indirect cash flow statement?
options: Because the gain is not real
Because the full proceeds appear in investing, so leaving the gain in operating would double count it
why: The gain is entirely real and was correctly recognised in the income statement.
Correct. The cash effect belongs in investing; removing the gain from operating prevents counting the same money twice.
A gain on disposal is not non-cash — cash was received. The issue is which section it belongs in.
Conservatism is not the driver; avoiding double counting and keeping the sections honest is.
questions.explain: Once you see that the whole disposal proceeds sit in investing, the subtraction in operating stops being an arbitrary rule and becomes obvious arithmetic.

questions.q: Net income $60m; depreciation $22m; receivables rose $14m; inventory fell $6m; payables rose $9m. What is operating cash flow, in $m?
questions.hint: An asset going up consumes cash; a liability going up provides it.
questions.explain: 60 + 22 − 14 + 6 + 9 = $83m. Inventory falling releases cash, so it is added; receivables rising consumes cash, so it is deducted. Getting the signs right is most of the skill in reading this section.

questions.q: A company reports operating cash flow +, investing cash flow −, and financing cash flow −. What does this pattern describe?
options: A start-up funded by venture capital
A mature business funding its own investment and returning the surplus
A company in distress selling assets
A business that has just completed an IPO
why: A start-up typically shows operating negative and financing positive.
Correct. It generates cash, reinvests part of it, and pays the rest to lenders and shareholders.
Distress usually shows operating negative and investing positive as assets are sold.
An IPO produces a large positive financing figure.
questions.explain: The signs of the three sections read as a sentence about where a company sits in its life. It is the fastest orientation available and takes five seconds.

questions.q: Which of these would increase reported operating cash flow without any improvement in the underlying business? Select all that apply.
options: Capitalising software development that was previously expensed
Classifying interest paid as financing under IFRS
Selling receivables to a bank under a factoring facility
Reducing the depreciation rate on plant
why: Yes. The spending moves from the operating section to the investing section, raising operating cash flow and profit simultaneously.
