Yes. IFRS permits the choice; moving interest to financing lifts operating cash flow with no change in any payment.
Yes. It converts a future collection into cash today. Sustainable only while the facility renews, and it usually costs a fee.
Yes. Payables rising is a cash inflow. It is real cash, but it is a one-time benefit from a level shift and it borrows from suppliers.
No. Depreciation is added back in full, so changing the rate alters profit and the add-back by identical amounts and leaves operating cash flow untouched.
questions.explain: The last option is the useful one: because depreciation is added straight back, depreciation policy cannot move operating cash flow. That immunity is precisely why the cash flow statement is a check on the income statement.

questions.q: Meridian’s operating cash flow is $87.3m and capital expenditure $58.0m. What is simple free cash flow, in $m?
questions.hint: The default definition deducts all capital expenditure.
questions.explain: 87.3 − 58.0 = $29.3m. Note this deducts growth investment as well as maintenance, so it understates what the business could distribute if it stopped expanding — which is why the maintenance capex question matters.

questions.q: A company’s cash conversion (operating cash flow ÷ net income) is 0.6× while revenue grows 40%. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: Working capital is absorbing cash to fund growth — expected, but it must be checked for sustainability
The company is about to fail
why: Possible but unsupported. Fast growth produces this pattern routinely without any wrongdoing.
Correct. Growth consumes working capital. The question is whether the absorption is proportionate to growth and whether it can be funded.
Conversion below 1.0 during rapid growth is normal. Failure risk depends on funding, not on this ratio.
Low depreciation would raise net income and lower the ratio, but it would not explain a 40% growth rate.
questions.explain: Cash conversion must always be read against growth. The same 0.6× would be a serious warning at a company growing 2% and is close to expected at one growing 40%.

questions.q: Place these in the order a company would normally prefer to fund an investment, from cheapest and least constrained to most.
items: Internally generated free cash flow
Existing undrawn credit facility
New bank debt
New public bond issue
New equity issue
questions.explain: The pecking order theory of capital structure predicts exactly this ranking, and it is consistent with observed behaviour: firms prefer internal funds, then debt, and issue equity last. The reason usually given is information asymmetry — issuing equity signals that management thinks the shares are not cheap, so the market marks them down on announcement.

questions.q: Which item is added back in the operating section but represents a genuine cost borne by shareholders?
why: Depreciation is also a genuine cost, but it is borne through cash that left in earlier years to buy the asset, not by shareholders through dilution.
Correct. The company obtained services and paid with shares. No cash left, so it is added back, but existing owners paid through dilution.
A payables increase is a source of cash, not a cost.
Interest paid is a cash outflow, not an add-back.
questions.explain: This is why excluding share-based compensation from adjusted earnings is indefensible: the add-back in the cash flow statement is correct, and the exclusion from earnings is not.

questions.q: What does supply chain financing do to the cash flow statement if the balance stays within trade payables?
options: It moves what is economically borrowing into the operating section, raising operating cash flow
It converts operating cash flow into investing cash flow
why: It has a material effect, which is exactly why disclosure requirements were tightened after several failures.
Correct. A bank pays the supplier early and the company repays the bank later. That is borrowing, but if it sits in payables the inflow appears in operating rather than financing.
The effect is the opposite: it raises operating cash flow.
Investing is not involved.
questions.explain: Carillion and the Greensill collapse made this mainstream. The tell is trade payable days rising sharply with no change in stated supplier terms, and both US and international standard-setters now require the arrangements to be disclosed.

questions.q: A company’s operating cash flow has exceeded net income by a widening margin for four years, while revenue is flat. Explain why this might not be good news, and what you would examine.
questions.model: Operating cash flow above net income is normally reassuring, but with flat revenue the widening gap needs explaining, and several of the explanations are unfavourable. Non-cash charges may be growing: rising impairments, provisions or restructuring accruals reduce profit without consuming cash in the period, so the gap widens while the business deteriorates. Recurring restructuring add-backs in particular suggest a structural cost being presented as exceptional. Working capital may be releasing cash because the business is shrinking in volume even if revenue is flat in value — receivables and inventory falling put cash in the door once, and that release stops the moment the decline stabilises. Deferred revenue could be falling, which would depress future revenue while doing nothing to current cash. Or the improvement could be a classification or financing effect rather than an operating one: supply chain finance lengthening payable days, receivables factoring, interest reclassified to financing under IFRS, or previously expensed development spending being capitalised, which lifts both operating cash flow and profit but moves the outflow to investing. I would examine the reconciliation itself first, because it names the drivers. Specifically: the trend in each non-cash add-back over four years, to see whether one is growing and whether it recurs; the working capital lines separately, distinguishing an inventory release from a payables extension, since the first is capacity being liquidated and the second is supplier credit being stretched; trade payable days against stated supplier terms, as the clearest supply chain finance signal; capitalised development costs and the capex line, since spending that moved from operating to investing flatters both statements; and the accounting policy note for any classification change. The decisive comparison is free cash flow rather than operating cash flow, because deducting capital expenditure neutralises the capitalisation effect. If free cash flow is flat or falling while operating cash flow rises, the improvement is a reclassification. If free cash flow is genuinely rising with flat revenue, the company is either becoming more efficient or harvesting its asset base, and the capex-to-depreciation ratio distinguishes those two.

modules.title: How the Three Statements Tie Together
modules.tagline: Not three reports but one system. Every figure appears twice, and the places they meet are where errors and distortions surface.
objectives: Name the four links that bind the three statements and verify each one against a published set of accounts.
Trace a single transaction through all three statements and state its effect on each.
Explain why the balance sheet balancing is a genuine check on a model and not merely a formality.
Build a simple forecast in which cash is the plug, and identify what has gone wrong when the balance check fails.

lessons.title: Articulation: every number appears twice
glossary: The property that the three statements are linked so that each derives from and constrains the others.
A schedule showing how an opening balance becomes a closing balance through the movements of the period.
The line in a model that absorbs the residual so the balance sheet balances — normally cash or a revolving facility.

blocks.html: People learn the three statements one at a time and then treat them as three documents. They are one document in three views. The income statement explains part of the change in the balance sheet; the cash flow statement explains another part; together they explain all of it.

blocks.label: The central property
blocks.html: The change in every balance sheet line between two dates is explained by a flow, and every flow appears somewhere in the income statement or the cash flow statement. This is called articulation. It is what makes the three statements a system rather than a collection, and it is the reason a competent analyst can reconstruct missing figures from those that are published.

head: Link
Where it comes from
Where it lands
rows: Top of the cash flow statement, and into retained earnings on the balance sheet
Bottom of the cash flow statement
Top line of the balance sheet
Inside the income statement, added back in operating cash flow
Accumulated depreciation and intangibles on the balance sheet
Financing section of the cash flow statement
Debt and share capital on the balance sheet

blocks.html: Now verify all four against Meridian, using only figures you have already seen.

blocks.label: Use this as a diagnostic, not a formality
blocks.html: When a check fails on real accounts, you have found something. If retained earnings does not roll forward, look for a prior-year restatement, a change in accounting policy taken to reserves, or a share buyback cancelled against retained earnings. If accumulated depreciation does not roll, there was a disposal, an impairment or a currency translation effect. Every failed check has a specific explanation somewhere in the notes, and finding it usually teaches you more than the check itself.

blocks.text: The PP&E roll-forward, which the notes must give you

blocks.html: Capital expenditure appears in the cash flow statement; depreciation appears in the income statement; the balance sheet shows only the closing position. The PP&E note joins them:
Closing net PP&E = opening 240.0 + capex 58.0 − depreciation 32.0 − NBV of disposals 6.0 = 260.0
Where a company does not disclose capital expenditure clearly, this identity lets you infer it. That is the practical value of articulation: it turns partial disclosure into complete information.

blocks.q: A company’s retained earnings rose by $140m. Net income was $180m and dividends were $25m. What is the most likely explanation for the $15m difference?
options: An arithmetic error in the accounts
A share buyback charged against retained earnings, or a prior-period adjustment
blocks.explain: 180 − 25 = 155, but retained earnings rose only 140, so $15m left retained earnings by some other route. The usual candidates are a buyback cancelled against reserves, a prior-period restatement, or an actuarial or policy adjustment taken directly to reserves. A share issue would increase share capital, not reduce retained earnings. The point is that the failed check tells you precisely where to look in the statement of changes in equity.

blocks.text: Why this matters for reading, not just for modelling

blocks.html: Articulation is the reason accounting fraud is hard to sustain. Inflating revenue creates a receivable that must eventually be collected or written off. Understating an expense creates a liability that must eventually be settled or released. Capitalising a cost creates an asset that must eventually be depreciated or impaired. Every distortion has to go somewhere, and it accumulates on the balance sheet until it becomes visible.

This is why the most reliable fraud signals are balance sheet signals rather than income statement ones — receivables growing faster than revenue for three years, inventory building against flat sales, an intangible asset that never amortises. The income statement can be flattered for a year. The balance sheet keeps the receipts.

lessons.title: Tracing one transaction through all three
glossary: One that changes the balance sheet and income statement without any cash movement.
An item that does not pass through the income statement, going directly to equity instead.

blocks.html: The fastest way to make articulation concrete is to take a single event and ask three questions: what does the income statement say, what does the balance sheet say, and what does the cash flow statement say? Work through these until the pattern is automatic.

head: Transaction
Income statement
Balance sheet
Cash flow statement
rows: Sell goods for $100 on credit; they cost $60
Operating: net income +40, receivables (100), inventory +60 → net cash effect nil
No effect — revenue was recognised at the sale
Operating: inventory (50), payables +50 → net effect nil
No effect at the moment of purchase
Operating: net income −20, add back +20 → nil
No effect — dividends are not an expense
Share capital +9, retained earnings −9 → equity unchanged
Operating: net income −9, add back +9 → nil
Write off a $12 receivable already provided for
No effect — the provision was taken earlier

items: A cash-neutral operating transaction shows up twice in the operating section and cancels. A credit sale adds profit and subtracts the receivable. Buying inventory on credit adds inventory and adds payables. The cash flow statement correctly reports that no money moved.

Capital expenditure never touches the income statement on the day it happens. It appears in investing, and enters the income statement over years as depreciation. This is why "we invested $200m" and "we spent $200m" mean different things to an accountant.

Dividends are not an expense. They are a distribution to owners, so they bypass the income statement entirely and appear in financing and in the statement of changes in equity. Anyone who deducts dividends to get to profit has confused a return of profit with a cost of earning it.

blocks.q: A company writes off a receivable of $8m that was fully provided for last year. What is the effect on this year’s profit?
options: It depends on the tax rate
blocks.explain: The cost was recognised last year when the allowance was created. The write-off simply removes the same amount from both gross receivables and the allowance, so net receivables and profit are unchanged. This is why the allowance balance is more informative than the write-off figure: the allowance is where the judgement was made, and the write-off is administration after the fact.

blocks.text: The transactions that appear nowhere in cash flow

blocks.html: Some economically significant events involve no cash at all and are disclosed only in a supplementary note. They are easy to miss and occasionally very large.

items: Acquiring a business by issuing shares. Assets and liabilities arrive on the balance sheet; nothing crosses the cash flow statement except any cash element of the consideration.
Entering a lease. A right-of-use asset and a lease liability are recognised together. The cash flows appear later, as lease payments.
Converting debt into equity. Debt falls, equity rises, no cash moves.
Revaluations and currency translation. Assets move, other comprehensive income absorbs it, cash is untouched.

blocks.label: Why this matters
blocks.html: A company that grows entirely by issuing shares for acquisitions can show a nearly empty investing section while transforming its balance sheet. Judging its capital allocation from the cash flow statement alone would miss the entire story. The non-cash investing and financing activities note, usually a few lines at the end of the cash flow statement, is where that story is told.

lessons.title: Building and checking a small three-statement link
glossary: A forecast in which the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement are linked so that the balance sheet balances.
The loop created when interest depends on debt, debt depends on cash, and cash depends on interest.
A test that a forecast implies plausible behaviour rather than merely arithmetic consistency.

blocks.html: Forecasting is not the subject of this course, but building a small linked forecast is the fastest way to prove you have understood articulation — because if you have not, the balance sheet will not balance and there is nowhere to hide.

blocks.title: Six steps
steps: Forecast the income statement from revenue
Grow revenue, then hold cost lines at a percentage of revenue unless you have a reason not to. Meridian at +8% gives revenue of $907.2m.
Forecast the balance sheet operating lines from activity ratios
Hold days sales outstanding, days inventory and days payable constant unless you are forecasting a change. This is the step that makes growth consume cash automatically.
Roll forward the fixed assets
Opening PP&E plus capex less depreciation. Opening intangibles less amortisation.
Roll forward equity
Opening retained earnings plus net income less dividends; share capital plus share-based compensation.
Build the cash flow statement from the two forecasts
Every line comes from either the income statement or a movement between the opening and closing balance sheet. Nothing is entered by hand.
Let cash be the plug and check that the balance sheet balances
If it does not, the error is always in step 5 — a movement has been counted twice or missed.

head: FY3 forecast ($m)
Value
Basis
rows: SG&A and R&D held at FY2 percentages of revenue
growth absorbs cash even at constant days
built entirely from the two forecasts

blocks.label: What the check proves
blocks.html: A balance check of zero does not mean the forecast is right. It means the forecast is internally consistent — that every assumption has been carried through to all three statements. Those are very different claims, and confusing them is how people build elegant models of impossible companies.

blocks.text: Notice what the model did on its own

blocks.html: Nobody entered a working capital assumption. Holding days constant and growing revenue 8% produced a cash absorption of $11.4m automatically. That is the mechanism behind the observation in Module 1 that a profitable, growing company can run out of money — and it emerges from the arithmetic rather than from any judgement about the business.
Growth of 8% consumed $11.4m of cash at unchanged efficiency. At 24% growth the absorption would be roughly three times as large, against operating cash flow that would rise far less.

head: Symptom
Almost always means
rows: Out by exactly the depreciation charge
Depreciation was expensed but not added to accumulated depreciation, or vice versa
Dividends deducted from retained earnings but not from cash, or the reverse
Out by a working capital line
A balance sheet line was moved without the corresponding cash flow entry
Capex added to PP&E but not deducted in investing
Out by a growing amount each year
An error in a roll-forward that compounds — usually retained earnings or accumulated depreciation
The same movement was entered in two sections

blocks.html: The last row is worth dwelling on. Being out by exactly twice a figure almost always means a flow was counted in both operating and investing, or both in the income statement and directly on the balance sheet. It is the single most common modelling error and the easiest to find once you know to look for the doubling.

blocks.q: A forecast balance sheet is out by exactly the amount of the year’s capital expenditure. What is the most likely cause?
options: Capex was added to PP&E but not deducted in the investing section
blocks.explain: An error equal to a specific line means that line was recorded once instead of twice. Capex must both increase PP&E on the balance sheet and reduce cash through the investing section; do one without the other and the imbalance equals the capex exactly. Diagnosing by the size of the gap is far faster than checking every formula.

blocks.html: In a fuller model, interest expense depends on the average debt balance, debt depends on how much cash the business generates, and cash depends on interest expense. That loop is genuine and is normally resolved either by iterating until it settles or by computing interest on the opening balance, which breaks the circle at a small cost in precision. It is worth knowing the loop exists so that a spreadsheet complaining about a circular reference reads as expected behaviour rather than a mistake.

blocks.label: The sanity checks that matter more than the balance check
blocks.html: Once it balances, ask whether the forecast implies anything absurd: a margin the industry has never achieved, receivable days that fall for no stated reason, a return on capital that rises indefinitely, or a cash balance that grows to exceed the company’s market value. A model can be perfectly articulated and still describe a company that cannot exist.

questions.q: Which figure links the income statement directly to the balance sheet?
why: Revenue affects receivables and cash, but it does not appear on the balance sheet itself.
Correct. Net income flows into retained earnings, which is why the equity section changes without any owner transaction.
Gross profit is a subtotal within the income statement and has no direct balance sheet counterpart.
Operating cash flow links the cash flow statement to cash, not the income statement to the balance sheet.
questions.explain: Closing retained earnings equals opening retained earnings plus net income less dividends. It is the hinge of the whole system.

questions.q: Opening PP&E net was $240m. Capex was $58m, depreciation $32m, and assets with a net book value of $6m were disposed of. What is closing net PP&E, in $m?
questions.hint: Add what came in, subtract what was consumed and what left.
questions.explain: 240 + 58 − 32 − 6 = $260m. This roll-forward is how you infer capital expenditure when a company discloses it poorly: every other term is available from the balance sheet and the depreciation note.

questions.q: A company sells goods for $100 on credit that cost it $60. What is the net effect on operating cash flow in that period?
why: Cash has not been received; the customer owes $100.
$40 of profit is added at the top of the operating section, but the $100 receivable and the $60 inventory release exactly offset it.
Correct. Net income +40, receivables (100), inventory +60. The three sum to zero.
Inventory falling is a source of cash, not a use.
questions.explain: A credit sale creates profit and no cash. The cash flow statement records this correctly by offsetting the profit with the working capital movements it created — which is exactly what articulation means in practice.

questions.q: Which of these change the balance sheet without appearing in the cash flow statement? Select all that apply.
options: Acquiring a company entirely for shares
Revaluing a foreign subsidiary at the closing exchange rate
why: Yes. Assets and liabilities arrive; no cash moves. Disclosed in the non-cash activities note.
Yes. A right-of-use asset and a lease liability are recognised together. Cash flows arise later as payments.
Yes. Debt falls, equity rises, no cash crosses.
No. A dividend is a cash outflow and appears in financing.
Yes. Translation moves assets and other comprehensive income with no cash effect.
questions.explain: The non-cash investing and financing note is where transformational events with no cash flow are disclosed. A company growing by share-funded acquisition can have an almost empty investing section.

questions.q: A forecast model is out of balance by exactly twice the dividend. What has most likely happened?
options: The dividend was deducted from retained earnings but not from cash
The dividend was deducted twice from the same place
The dividend was recorded in both financing and operating
why: That error would leave the model out by exactly one dividend, not two.
This would also produce an error of one dividend relative to the correct treatment in the other statement.
Correct. Recording the same outflow in two sections doubles its effect on cash while retained earnings moves only once.
A tax error would not produce a gap equal to a precise multiple of the dividend.
questions.explain: Diagnosing by the size of the imbalance is the fastest debugging technique there is. Out by one line means it was recorded once instead of twice; out by twice a line means it was recorded twice instead of once.

questions.q: Why do balance sheet signals tend to be more reliable indicators of accounting distortion than income statement signals?
options: Balance sheets are audited more thoroughly
Distortions accumulate on the balance sheet because every misstatement must go somewhere
Income statements are optional in some jurisdictions
Balance sheets are published more frequently
why: Both are covered by the same audit and the same materiality threshold.
Correct. Inflated revenue leaves a receivable; understated cost leaves a liability; capitalised expense leaves an asset. Each accumulates until it becomes conspicuous.
Both are required of any filer.
They are published together, at the same frequency.
questions.explain: This is the practical payoff of articulation. A single period can be flattered; a balance sheet keeps the record of every period, so a persistent distortion becomes a trend that is hard to hide.

questions.q: Match each transaction to where its cash effect appears.
questions.explain: Interest is the interesting one: US GAAP requires operating, while IFRS permits operating or financing. Because operating cash flow is the number analysts anchor on, that policy choice moves a widely used figure without any change to a single payment.

questions.q: Retained earnings opened at $173m and closed at $233m. Net income was $79.3m. What were dividends, in $m?
questions.hint: Rearrange the retained earnings roll-forward.
questions.explain: 173 + 79.3 − dividends = 233, so dividends = $19.3m. Working backwards through a roll-forward to recover an undisclosed figure is one of the most useful habits in statement analysis, and it works for capex, disposals, write-offs and buybacks as well as dividends.

questions.q: A forecast balances perfectly and shows operating margin rising from 13% to 31% over five years in a mature industry. What should you conclude?
options: The model is correct because it balances
The model is internally consistent but the assumption is implausible and needs defending
The balance check must be broken
Operating margin cannot rise in a mature industry
why: Balancing proves consistency, not realism. A model can be flawlessly articulated and describe a company that could not exist.
Correct. The arithmetic is fine; the economics need an argument. What would let this firm more than double its margin while competitors do not respond?
Nothing about an aggressive margin assumption breaks the balance check.
It can, following a genuine change in mix, scale or cost structure — but it requires a reason, not an assumption.
questions.explain: The balance check is a necessary condition and a very weak one. The sanity checks — implied margins, implied returns on capital, implied working capital days, implied market share — are where a forecast is actually tested.

questions.q: You have a company’s income statement and its balance sheets for two years, but the cash flow statement page is missing. Explain how you would reconstruct operating, investing and financing cash flow, and what you would be unable to determine.
questions.model: Almost all of it is recoverable, because articulation means every balance sheet movement corresponds to a flow. For operating cash flow I would start from net income and add back the non-cash charges I can identify: depreciation and amortisation, which I can derive from the movement in accumulated depreciation and in intangibles if the notes give the disposal element, plus share-based compensation, which usually equals the increase in share capital or additional paid-in capital where there was no cash issue. I would then compute the movement in each operating balance sheet line — receivables, inventory, prepayments, payables, accruals, deferred revenue — and apply the rule that an asset increase consumes cash and a liability increase provides it. I would also add the movement in deferred tax balances and reverse any gain or loss on disposal shown in the income statement. For investing, capital expenditure comes from the PP&E roll-forward: closing gross equals opening gross plus additions less the cost of disposals, so if the note gives disposals I can solve for additions. Disposal proceeds equal the net book value disposed of plus any gain recognised in the income statement. Acquisitions would show up as a jump in goodwill and in the acquired asset lines. For financing, debt movements come from the change in current and long-term borrowings, dividends from the retained earnings roll-forward as opening plus net income less closing, and share issuance from the change in share capital less the share-based compensation credit. Finally the whole reconstruction is testable: the three sections must sum to the actual change in cash on the balance sheet, and if they do not, one of the inferred figures is wrong. What I cannot determine is anything where a single balance sheet movement is the net of two offsetting flows. I would see net debt repayment but not gross drawings and repayments, which matters for judging revolver usage. I would see net capital expenditure but could not separate maintenance from growth. Acquisitions net of cash acquired, and any non-cash transactions such as leases entered or shares issued as consideration, would be invisible or would corrupt the roll-forwards. Currency translation on the balances of foreign subsidiaries would also distort every movement, since part of the change in each line is translation rather than a flow. And I could not split working capital movements caused by an acquisition from those caused by trading. The reconstruction is therefore reliable in aggregate and unreliable in exactly the places a company with something to hide would prefer.

modules.title: Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle
modules.tagline: The arithmetic behind the oldest way to go bankrupt: growing profitably.
objectives: Explain mechanically why growth absorbs cash, and compute how much.
Calculate days sales outstanding, days inventory outstanding, days payables outstanding and the cash conversion cycle, and state the flow each is measured against.
Decompose a working capital movement into the portion caused by growth and the portion caused by a change in efficiency.
Interpret a change in each component as a business signal rather than an accounting one, and compute a sustainable growth rate.

lessons.title: Why growth consumes cash
glossary: Receivables plus inventory less payables — the cash tied up in the trading cycle.
The number of days between paying for inventory and collecting from the customer.
Growing faster than the business can fund, leading to failure despite profitability.
The growth a company can fund from retained profit without new external finance.

blocks.html: Module 1 asserted that a profitable, growing company can go bankrupt. This lesson proves it with arithmetic, because the claim is repeated so often that it has become a slogan, and slogans are easy to nod at and hard to act on.

blocks.text: The mechanism, in one worked example

blocks.html: A distributor buys a widget for $70 and sells it for $100. It pays its supplier in 40 days and its customers pay in 70 days. It sells 1,000 units in month one, and volume grows 20% a month. Gross margin is 30% and every sale is profitable. Follow the cash.

blocks.title: One unit, one cycle
steps: Day 0 — receive stock
Inventory rises $70. No cash moves; the supplier is owed.
Day 25 — sell it
Revenue $100, profit $30 recognised. Still no cash. A receivable of $100 exists.
Day 40 — pay the supplier
$70 leaves. The company is now $70 out of pocket on a sale it has already booked as profitable.
Day 95 — the customer pays
$100 arrives. Cash is finally positive by $30.
The gap
For 55 days the company funded $70 per unit out of its own pocket, on a transaction the income statement recorded as a $30 profit on day 25.

blocks.label: The trap
blocks.html: At flat volume this is manageable — the cash from old sales funds the new ones. At 20% monthly growth it is not, because each month requires more funding than the previous month returns. Profit accrues at the moment of sale; cash accrues 70 days later; and the funding requirement scales with the growth rate. The faster the growth, the wider the hole, which is why the businesses that fail this way are usually the ones that look most successful.
Cash absorbed by growth ≈ increase in revenue × (operating working capital ÷ revenue)

Meridian's operating working capital — receivables plus inventory less payables — was $194.0m on revenue of $840.0m, or 23.1% of sales. Every extra dollar of revenue therefore requires about 23 cents of funding before it produces any cash at all.

Compare that with its operating margin of 13.0%. Each extra dollar of revenue generates 13 cents of operating profit and consumes 23 cents of working capital. The company can grow, but growth is cash-negative in the year it happens and only pays back later.
A minority of businesses have negative working capital: customers pay before suppliers are paid. For them, growth releases cash, and the effect is a genuine and durable competitive advantage.

head: Model
Why working capital is negative
Consequence
rows: Customers pay at the till; suppliers are paid in 30 to 60 days; stock turns in weeks
Growth generates cash. Historically this funded expansion without external capital.
Annual fees collected up front; costs incurred monthly
Deferred revenue funds the business interest-free.
Premiums collected before claims are paid
The float can be invested. This is the core of Berkshire Hathaway’s structure.
Dell built its 1990s advantage on exactly this.

blocks.label: The mirror image
blocks.html: Negative working capital is a wonderful engine in growth and a brutal one in decline. If sales fall, the cycle reverses: suppliers must still be paid for goods already sold while new customer cash no longer arrives. Several large retailers have failed this way, and the collapse is far faster than the profit-and-loss deterioration would suggest, because working capital unwinds all at once.
How fast can a company grow without raising new capital? The standard approximation is:
g = return on equity × (1 − payout ratio)

For Meridian: return on equity of 25.6% and a payout ratio of 24% give a sustainable growth rate of 19.4%. Actual revenue growth was 10.2%, comfortably inside that limit, which is consistent with what the cash flow statement shows: the company funded its growth and its capital expenditure internally and still repaid debt.

blocks.label: Treat it as a boundary, not a target
blocks.html: The formula assumes constant margins, constant asset intensity and constant leverage. It is a sanity check, not a forecast: a company growing well above its sustainable rate for several years must be raising debt, raising equity, or improving efficiency, and knowing which of the three is happening tells you a great deal about the durability of the growth.

blocks.q: A profitable distributor grows revenue 45% and reports its first ever negative operating cash flow. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Working capital absorbed more cash than operations generated — the classic overtrading pattern
It paid an unusually large dividend
blocks.explain: Growth of 45% at unchanged efficiency requires roughly 45% more receivables and inventory. If operating working capital is a substantial share of revenue, that requirement can exceed the entire year’s operating profit. Nothing improper needs to have happened — but the company must fund the gap, and if the facility is not there, a profitable business fails. Dividends are financing, not operating, so the last option cannot explain it.

lessons.title: DSO, DIO, DPO and the cycle
glossary: Days sales outstanding — how long customers take to pay.
Days inventory outstanding — how long stock sits before being sold.
Days payables outstanding — how long the company takes to pay suppliers.
DSO plus DIO less DPO. Also called the cash conversion cycle.

blocks.html: Absolute balances mean nothing without the flow they relate to. Converting each into days makes them comparable across years, across companies and across sizes.

head: Measure
Formula
Flow it uses
Why that flow
rows: Receivables arise from sales, and are recorded at selling price.
Inventory is carried at cost, so it must be compared with a cost figure, not revenue.
Payables arise from purchases, which are at cost. Using revenue would flatter DPO by the whole gross margin.

blocks.label: The most common mistake
blocks.html: Using revenue as the denominator for DIO or DPO. Because inventory and payables are recorded at cost while revenue includes the margin, this understates both figures by the gross margin percentage — for Meridian, by 36%. It is an error that appears in published research, and it makes companies with high gross margins look far more efficient than they are.
Cash conversion cycle = 60.0 + 103.2 − 65.2 = 98.0 days

Meridian now waits 98.0 days between paying for a component and collecting from the customer who buys the finished tool, 9.6 days longer than a year ago. Every one of those days must be financed by someone — the company's own cash, its bank, or its shareholders.

Working capital consumed $27.0m this year. Some of that was unavoidable: the company grew 10.2% and a larger business needs more stock and carries more receivables. The rest is a deterioration in efficiency. Separating the two is the single most useful piece of analysis in this module.

head: Component
$m
What it means
rows: Absorption from growth alone, at last year’s days
The cost of being 10.2% bigger. Expected and, if the growth is profitable, worth paying.
The cost of collecting later and holding stock longer. Not inherent to growth, and reversible.
As reported in the cash flow statement

blocks.html: So roughly 58% of the cash absorbed by working capital had nothing to do with growth. Recovering last year's days would release about $15.6m — over half of this year's free cash flow of $29.3m — without selling a single extra tool.

blocks.label: The question this reframes
blocks.html: "Why is cash flow weak?" is a vague question that invites a vague answer. "Why did receivable days rise 3.4 days and inventory days rise 6.2 days?" is a specific one that a management team must answer specifically. It is the most useful question you can ask on an earnings call.

Every ratio above mixes a balance sheet figure, which is a snapshot, with an income statement figure, which is a period total. Strictly the balance should be an average of opening and closing. For Meridian, DSO on average receivables is 55.6 days rather than 60.0 — a meaningful difference.

Use closing balances when you want to know where the company stands today, and averages when you want a fair measure of the year's performance. What matters most is consistency: never compare a closing-balance figure at one company with an average-balance figure at another.

blocks.q: A company reports revenue of $600m, COGS of $390m, inventory of $130m and payables of $80m. What is DIO, to the nearest day?
blocks.explain: 365 × 130 ÷ 390 = 121.7, so 122 days. Using revenue instead of COGS would give 365 × 130 ÷ 600 = 79 days — the wrong answer, and the one that appears whenever someone reaches for the revenue line out of habit. Inventory is carried at cost, so it must be measured against a cost flow.

blocks.html: For a seasonal business, year-end days are close to meaningless. A garden centre closing in December has almost no inventory and almost no receivables; the same business in April is carrying both at their peak. Quarterly data, or the average of five quarter-end balance sheets, gives a far truer picture. Where only annual figures exist, comparing the same company year on year is still valid because the distortion is consistent — but comparing it to a peer with a different year end is not.

lessons.title: Reading working capital as a signal
glossary: Selling receivables to a third party for immediate cash at a discount.
A bank pays suppliers early on the buyer’s behalf; the buyer repays the bank later.
Deliberately paying suppliers more slowly to conserve cash.
Stock held by distributors that has been recognised as sold by the manufacturer.

blocks.html: Each component of the cycle is a different business signal. Learning to read them separately turns working capital from an accounting topic into a source of information about demand, customer quality and negotiating power.

blocks.title: What each movement is telling you

tabs.label: Rising DSO
tabs.html: Usually a revenue quality signal. Either customers are in difficulty, or the company loosened credit terms to close sales, or revenue is being recognised earlier relative to billing. Check the receivables ageing and the split between billed and unbilled amounts. A rise concentrated in the over-90-day bucket is the worst case; a rise spread evenly usually means terms changed.

tabs.label: Rising DIO
tabs.html: Usually a demand signal. Stock is not moving as fast as it was. Check the split between raw materials, work in progress and finished goods: a build in raw materials can be deliberate buying ahead of price rises or supply disruption, while a build in finished goods means product is not selling. Then check the obsolescence provision — if inventory is rising and the provision is not, a write-down is being deferred.

tabs.label: Rising DPO
tabs.html: Ambiguous, and worth resolving. It can mean growing negotiating power — a large buyer imposing terms on smaller suppliers — or it can mean the company is short of cash and stretching. The tell is whether DSO and DIO are also deteriorating: rising DPO alone is usually strength; rising DPO alongside rising DSO and DIO is usually stress. Also check for supply chain financing, which lengthens payable days without any change in agreed terms.

tabs.label: Falling DIO with falling revenue
tabs.html: Often the least understood. Cash flow improves, conversion looks excellent, and the business is shrinking. Working capital release in a decline is a one-time benefit that flatters exactly the companies that least deserve it. Always read cash conversion against revenue growth.

items: Factoring or securitising receivables. Converts a receivable into cash today. Legitimate and common, but it improves DSO and operating cash flow without any change in customer behaviour. The disclosure is usually in the financial instruments note.

Supply chain finance. Lengthens payable days while suppliers are paid on time by a bank. Economically it is borrowing. After Carillion and the Greensill collapse, both US and international standard-setters introduced explicit disclosure requirements — but the arrangements are still easy to miss if you do not look.

Year-end pushes. Discounts offered in the last week to pull sales forward. Revenue and receivables both rise; the following quarter is weaker. Look at the fourth quarter as a share of the year, over several years.
Delaying supplier payment runs. Simply not running the payment batch until after the year end. Costs nothing, improves the closing cash balance, and reverses within days.

blocks.label: The test that cuts through all of it
blocks.html: Compute the cash conversion cycle for five consecutive years and plot it. Every technique above shifts one component or one year; almost none of them can hold a five-year trend flat. A cycle that has lengthened steadily for five years is telling you something structural about the business, whatever any individual year’s presentation suggests.
If the cycle absorbs cash, something must supply it. In practice there are four sources, in roughly ascending order of concern.

head: Source
Cost
What it signals
rows: The business funds its own growth. Meridian is here.
Interest on drawings plus a commitment fee
Normal and expected. Watch the headroom and the covenants.
Receivables factoring or supply chain finance
A discount or fee, often 1–4% annualised
Fine in itself. The concern is dependence: these facilities can be withdrawn quickly, and withdrawal creates an immediate cash crisis.
Raising equity to fund working capital, rather than investment, usually means the operating cycle is out of control.

head: Observation
Reading
rows: A real deterioration, worth about $15.6m of cash
Ask whether terms were loosened to support the 10.2% growth
Ask for the finished goods split and the obsolescence provision
Not stretching suppliers — so the cash pressure has not yet been passed down the chain
Free cash flow still positive at $29.3m
The deterioration is affordable this year
Another year like this one and the dividend is not covered

blocks.html: The conclusion is neither alarm nor comfort. Meridian is growing profitably and funding itself, but it is getting slower at converting sales into cash, and it has little cushion left before that starts to constrain the dividend or require borrowing. That is a specific, checkable conclusion — and it came entirely from three ratios and a decomposition.

blocks.q: A company’s DPO rises from 45 to 78 days while DSO and DIO are unchanged and revenue grows 6%. Which explanation should you consider first?
options: It has gained negotiating power over suppliers, or has entered a supply chain finance arrangement
blocks.explain: DPO rising alone, with the other two components stable, is usually strength or a financing arrangement rather than distress — distress normally shows all three deteriorating together. The two candidates are genuine buying power and supply chain finance, and they are distinguished by the financial instruments and payables notes. A 33-day extension is large enough that it should be explained somewhere.

questions.q: Revenue $900m, COGS $585m, receivables $150m, inventory $160m, payables $105m. What is the cash conversion cycle, in days?
questions.hint: Receivables against revenue; inventory and payables against COGS.
questions.explain: DSO = 365×150÷900 = 60.8. DIO = 365×160÷585 = 99.8. DPO = 365×105÷585 = 65.5. Cycle = 60.8 + 99.8 − 65.5 = 95.1 days. Using revenue for the last two would give 64.9 and 42.6, and a cycle of 83.1 — wrong by 12 days, all of it the gross margin.

questions.q: Why is cost of goods sold, rather than revenue, the correct denominator for days inventory outstanding?
options: Because inventory is carried at cost, so it must be compared with a cost flow
why: It is smaller, but that is a consequence of the reason rather than the reason itself.
Correct. Comparing a cost-based balance with a price-based flow embeds the gross margin in the ratio and understates the days held.
Returns reduce revenue but are not the issue here.
No standard prescribes ratio formulas; the reason is dimensional consistency.
questions.explain: The same logic applies to payables, which arise from purchases at cost. Getting this wrong makes high-margin companies look dramatically more efficient than they are, and it is a genuinely common error.

questions.q: A supermarket chain has negative working capital. What happens to cash if sales fall sharply?
options: Cash improves, because less inventory is needed
Cash deteriorates rapidly, because suppliers must still be paid while customer cash slows
Nothing — negative working capital is stable
why: Inventory does fall, but the payables balance falls with it and payables are the larger number in a negative working capital model.
Correct. The cycle that generated cash on the way up consumes it on the way down, and it unwinds faster than the profit decline suggests.
It is highly unstable in reverse. This is precisely how several large retailers failed faster than their reported results implied.
It is affected substantially and in the unfavourable direction.
questions.explain: Negative working capital is a powerful engine in growth and a trap in decline. Any assessment of a negative working capital business should model what happens if volumes fall, because that is the scenario the structure handles worst.

questions.q: Which of these would raise reported days payables outstanding without any change in agreed supplier terms? Select all that apply.
options: Entering a supply chain finance arrangement
Delaying the year-end payment run by a week
Negotiating longer terms with the largest supplier
why: Yes. A bank pays the supplier on time; the company repays later. Terms with the supplier are unchanged; the payable balance is longer.
Yes. A pure timing effect at the balance sheet date, reversing within days, and it costs nothing.
No. This is a genuine change in terms, which is exactly what DPO is supposed to measure.
No. Reclassifying to debt would reduce payables and therefore reduce DPO.
questions.explain: The two that qualify are the two that change the measured number without changing the underlying relationship, which is why the payables note and the financial instruments note both need reading when DPO moves sharply.

questions.q: A company has return on equity of 18% and pays out 40% of earnings as dividends. What is its sustainable growth rate, as a percentage?
questions.hint: Return on equity times the retention ratio.
questions.explain: 18% × (1 − 0.40) = 10.8%. Growing meaningfully faster than this for several years requires new debt, new equity, or an improvement in efficiency — and identifying which of the three is happening tells you whether the growth can continue.

questions.q: Inventory days rise from 70 to 95 while raw materials are flat and finished goods have doubled. What is the most likely conclusion?
options: The company is buying ahead of a price increase
Product is not selling, and a write-down may be pending
Suppliers have shortened their lead times
Cost of goods sold was understated
why: That would show as a build in raw materials, which are flat.
Correct. A build concentrated in finished goods means output is not converting into sales.
Shorter lead times would reduce raw material holdings, not increase finished goods.
Understated COGS would raise inventory arithmetically, but it would not concentrate the increase in finished goods specifically.
questions.explain: The composition of an inventory build is more informative than its size. Raw materials suggest a purchasing decision; work in progress suggests a production issue; finished goods suggest a demand problem, which is the most serious of the three.

questions.q: A company’s cash conversion improves sharply while revenue falls 12%. How should this be read?
options: As working capital being released by the contraction — a one-time benefit that stops when the decline does
As a sign the company is about to grow
why: Possible, but a 12% revenue decline is a sufficient explanation and must be ruled out first.
Correct. Shrinking releases receivables and inventory. The cash is real, and it arrives once.
It may be well managed, but the cash improvement here is a consequence of contraction rather than of management.
Nothing in the data supports a turn to growth.
questions.explain: This is the mirror of the growth trap and it fools people in the opposite direction. Cash conversion must always be read against revenue growth, because the same ratio means opposite things at +30% and −12%.

questions.q: Place these working capital funding sources in order from least concerning to most concerning as a company’s primary source.
items: Operating cash flow
An undrawn revolving credit facility
Receivables factoring
Supply chain finance at scale
New equity raised to fund the operating cycle
questions.explain: The ranking reflects both cost and fragility. Internal cash cannot be withdrawn. A committed facility can be, but only on a covenant breach. Factoring and supply chain finance can be pulled at short notice, which converts a working capital problem into a liquidity crisis overnight. Raising equity to fund an operating cycle, rather than investment, usually means the cycle is out of control.

questions.q: Operating working capital is 24% of revenue. If revenue grows from $500m to $650m, roughly how much cash does growth absorb, in $m?
questions.hint: The increase in revenue times the working capital intensity.
questions.explain: ($650m − $500m) × 24% = $36m. Compare that against the operating profit on the incremental revenue: at a 10% margin the extra $150m of sales earns $15m, so growth is cash-negative by roughly $21m in the year it occurs. That gap is the whole reason profitable companies fail.

questions.q: A manufacturer reports revenue growth of 18%, a rise in DSO from 52 to 71 days, DIO flat, DPO up from 40 to 58 days, and operating cash flow up 4%. Assess what is happening and what you would want to see next.
questions.model: The headline is respectable growth with barely improved cash generation, and the components explain why. DSO rising 19 days on 18% revenue growth is the dominant fact. Customers are paying substantially later, and the coincidence with accelerating growth suggests the two are connected: the most economical explanation is that credit terms were loosened, or that the growth came from a customer segment with weaker payment behaviour or larger contracts with milestone billing. The alternative, that existing customers are deteriorating financially, would normally show up as a shift in the ageing profile rather than an even lengthening. DIO flat during 18% growth is genuinely good and slightly at odds with the rest of the picture — it suggests production and demand are in balance, which argues against the growth being a channel stuffing exercise, since stuffing usually shows up as flat or falling reported inventory at the manufacturer while distributor inventory swells invisibly. DPO up 18 days is the piece that makes me most cautious, because the company has funded much of the receivables increase by paying its own suppliers later. That is a finite lever. Either it reflects new negotiating power, which an 18% larger buyer might plausibly have, or it reflects supply chain finance, or it is stretching. The near-perfect symmetry between the DSO extension and the DPO extension makes me suspect the third or the second: the company appears to have passed its collection problem down the supply chain rather than solved it. Operating cash flow up only 4% against 18% revenue growth confirms that the working capital cycle absorbed most of the incremental profit. What I would want next: the receivables ageing analysis and the allowance as a percentage of gross receivables, to distinguish loosened terms from deteriorating customers; the disclosure of any supply chain financing or reverse factoring arrangement, and the payables note; the split of revenue growth between existing and new customers, and between geographies, since a push into a market with different payment norms explains the DSO move benignly; the fourth quarter as a share of annual revenue over three years, to test for quarter-end pushes; and the revenue recognition policy, particularly any growth in contract assets or unbilled receivables, which would indicate revenue recognised ahead of billing rather than merely collected late. Finally I would compute the cash conversion cycle for five years. If it has lengthened steadily, this is structural and the 18% growth is being bought. If this is a single-year step, it may be one large contract with unusual terms, which is a much more benign story and one management should be able to name.

modules.title: Ratios That Mean Something
modules.tagline: A small number of ratios carry almost all the information. The rest are arithmetic.
objectives: Decompose return on equity using the three-step and five-step DuPont identities and say which lever is driving a change.
Compute return on invested capital and compare it against a cost of capital to judge whether growth creates or destroys value.
Assess leverage using both stock and flow measures, and explain why coverage matters more than gearing.
State the limitations of liquidity ratios and what to use instead.

lessons.title: Margins, turns and the DuPont identity
glossary: A decomposition of return on equity into margin, asset turnover and leverage.
Revenue divided by total assets — how much sales each dollar of assets generates.
Total assets divided by equity — a measure of leverage.
Net income divided by pre-tax profit — the fraction of profit kept after tax.
Pre-tax profit divided by operating profit — the fraction of operating profit kept after financing.

blocks.html: There are hundreds of published financial ratios and perhaps a dozen that repay the effort. This module covers those, and the organising insight is that most of them are related to one another rather than independent.

blocks.text: Return on equity, and why it is not enough on its own

blocks.html: Return on equity = net income ÷ shareholders’ equity = 79.3 ÷ 310.0 = 25.6% (FY1: 23.7%)

Return on equity is the headline measure of what the owners earn on what they have. Its weakness is that it can be raised in three quite different ways, two of which are improvements in the business and one of which is simply borrowing more. Read on its own it cannot distinguish them, which is why it needs decomposing.
ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier

Each term is a different question. Net margin asks how profitable each sale is. Asset turnover asks how much sales the asset base produces. Equity multiplier asks how much of the asset base was funded by other people.

blocks.label: What the decomposition just told us
blocks.html: Meridian's return on equity rose from 23.7% to 25.6% despite reducing leverage. Margin improvement more than offset the deleveraging. That is a materially better story than the headline number alone: a company that raises return on equity by borrowing has bought the improvement, while one that raises it while repaying debt has earned it.
Splitting net margin into its components isolates operations from financing and tax:
ROE = tax burden × interest burden × operating margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier

head: Term
Formula
FY2
FY1
What changed
rows: Improved — less debt, and the disposal gain

blocks.html: This version separates two things the three-step form conflates. Operating margin rose from 11.92% to 13.00% — a genuine trading improvement. Interest burden improved from 0.844 to 0.956, but part of that came from the one-off disposal gain, not from operations. Splitting them prevents crediting the business with something the property market provided.

blocks.q: Company A raises ROE from 12% to 18% by doubling its debt. Company B raises ROE from 12% to 18% by improving operating margin. Are these equivalent?
options: Yes — the shareholder return is identical
No — A has raised risk as well as return, and the improvement is not repeatable
No — B is worse because margin gains erode
Yes, provided interest rates stay low
blocks.explain: Leverage raises expected return and raises the variance around it. A shareholder in A now bears materially more risk for the same headline return, and the trick can only be repeated until the covenants bind. B improved the underlying economics. This is precisely the distinction DuPont exists to expose, and it is invisible in the ROE number itself.

head: Margin
Meridian FY2
What it is sensitive to
rows: Pricing power and input costs. The most informative over long periods, the least comparable across companies because COGS definitions differ.
Operating efficiency including overhead. The best single measure for comparing two companies with different capital structures.
Everything, including financing, tax and one-offs. Useful to shareholders, poor for comparison.
Widely used in covenants and multiples. Ignores capital intensity entirely.

blocks.label: The habit
blocks.html: When a margin moves, always ask at which level it moved. A gross margin decline with flat operating margin means the company cut overhead to defend profit — a defensive move that cannot repeat indefinitely. A flat gross margin with rising operating margin means operating leverage: fixed costs spread over more revenue, which is the healthiest form of margin expansion there is.

lessons.title: Return on invested capital and the cost of capital
glossary: Net operating profit after tax — operating income taxed at the effective rate, ignoring financing.
Weighted average cost of capital — the blended required return of debt and equity holders.
(ROIC − WACC) × invested capital. Value created above the cost of the money used.

blocks.html: Return on equity is distorted by leverage. Return on assets is distorted by operating liabilities that suppliers provided for free. Return on invested capital avoids both, and it is the closest thing financial analysis has to a single measure of business quality.
ROIC = NOPAT ÷ invested capital, where NOPAT = operating income × (1 − tax rate)

Note that ROIC uses operating income, so it is unaffected by how the business is financed. Two identical companies with different debt loads report different returns on equity and the same return on invested capital, which is exactly what you want when the question is "is this a good business?" rather than "is this a good share?"

A return means nothing until it is compared with what the capital cost. The weighted average cost of capital blends the required return of lenders and shareholders in proportion to how much of each the company uses. Estimating it properly is a course of its own; for now take an illustrative 8.5% for a business of Meridian's risk and leverage.
Economic profit = (ROIC − WACC) × invested capital = (16.34% − 8.5%) × 508.0 = $39.8m

blocks.label: The single most important idea in this module
blocks.html: Growth only creates value when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital. If a company earns 16.3% on capital that costs 8.5%, every dollar it reinvests adds value and growth is worth funding. If ROIC were 6.0% against the same 8.5% cost, every dollar reinvested would destroy value, and the company would create more wealth by shrinking and returning cash. Growth is not good in itself. Growth is a multiplier on the spread.

This is why the combination of high growth and low returns on capital is the most dangerous profile in investing, and why it is so often celebrated. Revenue rises, the story is exciting, and value is quietly consumed with every reinvested dollar.

blocks.q: Company X earns 6% ROIC against a 9% cost of capital and grows 20% a year. Company Y earns 22% ROIC against the same 9% cost and does not grow at all. Which is creating more value?
options: Y, because every dollar it employs earns well above its cost while X destroys value on each dollar reinvested
blocks.explain: X reinvests heavily at a return three points below the cost of that capital, so each dollar of growth destroys roughly three cents of value per year, and faster growth destroys more. Y earns a 13-point spread on its existing capital. Growth multiplies the spread — and multiplying a negative spread makes things worse. The correct action for X is to stop growing and return the cash.

items: Goodwill. Including goodwill measures the return on what was actually paid, including for acquisitions; excluding it measures the return the operating assets generate. Both are legitimate and they answer different questions. Compute both, and be explicit about which you are quoting — the gap between them is a direct measure of how much acquisition premium has been paid.

Operating leases. Since IFRS 16 and ASC 842 these are on the balance sheet, which has made ROIC far more comparable between companies that lease and companies that buy. Pre-2019 comparisons need adjusting.

The internal intangibles problem. A company that expensed thirty years of brand building carries almost no capital for it, so its ROIC can appear implausibly high. This is not a measurement triumph; it is the balance sheet omission from Module 2 reappearing in a ratio.
Averages. Use the average of opening and closing invested capital where the base moved materially during the year, particularly after an acquisition.

blocks.label: A very high ROIC is a question, not an answer
blocks.html: Returns of 60% or more usually mean the denominator is missing something rather than that the business is extraordinary. Look for internally generated intangibles, heavy use of negative working capital, assets held in joint ventures, or a business that outsources its entire asset base. Sometimes the return is genuinely that good. More often the capital is somewhere the balance sheet does not show it.

lessons.title: Leverage, coverage and liquidity
glossary: Debt as a proportion of equity or of total capital. A stock measure.
The number of times profit or cash covers interest or debt. A flow measure.
Current assets divided by current liabilities.
Cash plus receivables divided by current liabilities — inventory excluded.
The distance between a current ratio and the level at which it breaches a loan agreement.

blocks.html: Leverage can be measured as a stock — how much debt relative to capital — or as a flow — how comfortably profit services it. Lenders care far more about the flow, and so should you, because companies default when they cannot pay, not when a ratio looks high.

Net debt to EBITDA is the measure that matters most in practice, because it is the one written into loan agreements. Investment-grade industrial companies typically sit below 2.5×; covenants commonly bind at 3.0× to 3.5×. Meridian at 1.35× has real headroom, and it improved from 1.72× as debt was repaid and EBITDA grew.

head: Measure
Formula
Meridian FY2
Comfortable level
rows: Above 4×; the strictest of the three

blocks.label: Why coverage beats gearing
blocks.html: A company with debt at five times equity and interest covered fifteen times is safer than one with debt at one times equity and interest covered 1.4 times. The first has a lot of cheap, long-dated debt against strong cash generation. The second cannot survive a bad quarter. Gearing describes the balance sheet; coverage describes whether the payments can be made, and it is the payments that cause defaults.

head: Ratio
Meridian FY2
What it claims to measure
rows: Whether short-term assets cover short-term obligations

blocks.html: The traditional rule that a current ratio should exceed 2.0 is close to useless. A supermarket typically runs below 1.0 and is entirely safe, because its inventory turns in days and its customers pay instantly. A shipbuilder may run above 3.0 and be in serious trouble, because its current assets are half-built vessels.

blocks.label: What a high current ratio can conceal
blocks.html: Current assets include inventory that may be obsolete and receivables that may be uncollectable. A company can raise its current ratio by failing to write down either. The ratio treats a 200-day-overdue invoice and a bank deposit as equivalent, which is why the quick ratio — and better still the ageing analysis and the inventory composition — carries more information than the current ratio ever will.

The more useful liquidity question is not a ratio at all: what will the company have to pay in the next twelve months, and where is that money coming from? Answering it requires the debt maturity ladder, the undrawn facility disclosure, the covenant thresholds and the cash conversion cycle from Module 6. Those four together beat any liquidity ratio.

head: Dimension
Measure
FY2
FY1
Reading
rows: Well above an estimated 8.5% cost of capital
Positive but thin against the dividend

blocks.html: Seven ratios, one clear story: a good business getting better at trading and worse at collecting, with enough balance sheet strength that the second problem is not yet urgent. Note how little the number of ratios matters — adding twenty more would not have changed the conclusion, and the one that generated the only negative finding was the least conventional of the set.

blocks.q: Which pair of companies is more likely to default within two years?
options: The one with more debt, always
blocks.explain: Interest cover of 1.3× means a 25% fall in operating profit leaves the company unable to pay its interest. Debt to equity of 4.0× with 12× cover describes a business with a lot of cheap debt and strong cash generation — a utility, typically, and one of the safest credit profiles there is. Defaults are caused by missed payments, so the flow measure dominates.

questions.q: Net margin 8%, asset turnover 1.4×, equity multiplier 2.5×. What is return on equity, as a percentage?
questions.hint: The three-step DuPont identity is a product.
questions.explain: 0.08 × 1.4 × 2.5 = 0.28, so 28%. Note that a third of this return comes from the equity multiplier — remove the leverage and ROE falls to 11.2%. That decomposition is the entire point of the identity.

questions.q: A company’s return on equity rises from 14% to 21% while its equity multiplier rises from 1.8× to 2.9×. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The increase came largely from additional leverage
why: Possible, but the equity multiplier rose 61% while ROE rose 50% — leverage alone more than accounts for the change.
Correct. Leverage rose by a factor that fully explains the ROE improvement, so the underlying business may not have improved at all.
Asset turnover is not given, and the leverage move already explains the result.
A tax change would show in the tax burden term, not the equity multiplier.
questions.explain: ROE rising alongside a sharply rising equity multiplier is the classic false positive. Decomposing separates borrowed return from earned return, and the shareholder now bears more risk for that higher headline number.

questions.q: Operating income $150m, effective tax rate 25%, equity $400m, total debt $350m, cash $50m. What is ROIC, as a percentage?
questions.hint: NOPAT over equity plus debt less cash.
questions.explain: NOPAT = 150 × 0.75 = $112.5m. Invested capital = 400 + 350 − 50 = $700m. ROIC = 112.5 ÷ 700 = 16.1%. Using total assets instead of invested capital would include operating liabilities supplied free by suppliers and understate the return.

questions.q: A company earns 7% ROIC against a 10% cost of capital and is growing 25% a year. What should it do?
options: Stop growing and return capital to shareholders, unless returns can be raised above the cost of capital
Raise more debt, since debt is cheaper than equity
why: Growing faster destroys value faster. Every reinvested dollar earns three points less than it costs.
Correct. Growth multiplies the spread between ROIC and the cost of capital, and here the spread is negative.
Cheaper debt lowers the cost of capital somewhat but also raises risk; it does not fix a three-point negative spread.
A positive accounting return that is below the cost of capital still destroys value, because the capital had a better alternative use.
questions.explain: Growth is a multiplier on the spread, not a good in itself. This is the most consequential idea in the module and the one most often ignored in practice, because growth is easy to celebrate and the cost of capital is invisible.

questions.q: Which of these would raise return on invested capital without improving the underlying business? Select all that apply.
options: Writing off goodwill from a failed acquisition
Selling a factory and leasing it back, if the lease stayed off balance sheet
Paying a large special dividend funded from cash
why: Yes. Impairment shrinks invested capital, so the same NOPAT divides into a smaller base. Returns improve because a past mistake was recognised.
Yes under pre-2019 accounting, which is why the lease standards were changed. Under IFRS 16 and ASC 842 the right-of-use asset comes back on and the effect largely disappears.
Yes. Cash is deducted from invested capital, but paying out excess cash also removes it from the balance sheet entirely and can raise measured returns.
No. A price increase raises NOPAT, which is a genuine improvement in the business.
questions.explain: ROIC is a ratio, and a ratio can be improved from either end. Always check whether the denominator moved, and why — a return that improves because capital shrank is a different event from one that improves because profit grew.

questions.q: Why does the traditional guidance that the current ratio should exceed 2.0 have so little value?
options: Because it was never meant for public companies
Because the appropriate level depends entirely on how fast inventory turns and customers pay
Because current liabilities are hard to measure
why: It was applied to public companies for decades; the problem is the rule itself, not its audience.
Correct. A supermarket safely runs below 1.0; a shipbuilder can be distressed above 3.0. The right level is a function of the operating cycle.
Current liabilities are among the more straightforward figures on the balance sheet.
Ignoring long-term debt is deliberate — it is a short-term liquidity measure — and is not the reason the threshold fails.
questions.explain: A single threshold across all business models cannot work. The debt maturity ladder, undrawn facilities, covenant headroom and the cash conversion cycle answer the liquidity question far better than any of the three liquidity ratios.

questions.q: Match each ratio to the question it answers best.
pairs: Does the company have pricing power over its input costs?
Is this a good business, regardless of how it is financed?
Is the debt load within what lenders will tolerate?
Can the company keep paying its lenders if profit falls?
How long is cash tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers?
questions.explain: Choosing the ratio that matches the question is most of the skill. Almost every misuse of financial ratios comes from applying one built for a different question — most commonly using ROE to judge business quality when leverage differs.

questions.q: A company reports ROIC of 78%. What should you check first?
options: Nothing — it is an exceptional business
Whether the denominator is missing capital, such as internally generated intangibles or leased assets
Whether the tax rate is unusually low
why: Some businesses genuinely earn returns like this, but the base rate for a measurement problem is far higher than for a genuinely extraordinary business.
Correct. Expensed brand and R&D spending, negative working capital and outsourced asset bases all shrink invested capital without shrinking the economics.
Growth is relevant to value but does not explain an implausible return level.
Tax affects NOPAT modestly; it cannot produce a 78% return on its own.
questions.explain: Extreme ratios are usually measurement artefacts. Investigating the denominator before celebrating the number is the difference between analysis and screening.

questions.q: A company has ROIC of 14%, a weighted average cost of capital of 9%, and invested capital of $620m. What is its economic profit, in $m?
questions.hint: The spread times the capital.
questions.explain: (14% − 9%) × $620m = $31m of value created above the cost of the money employed. If the company could reinvest a further $100m at the same 14%, it would add another $5m a year — which is why growth is worth funding here and would not be if ROIC were 7%.

questions.q: Two companies in the same industry both report 20% return on equity. Company P has an equity multiplier of 1.4× and ROIC of 15%. Company Q has an equity multiplier of 3.6× and ROIC of 7%. Both are growing 12% a year and the cost of capital for the industry is about 9%. Compare them.
questions.model: The identical returns on equity conceal opposite economics. P earns 15% on its invested capital against a 9% cost, a positive spread of six points, and uses modest leverage. Its 20% return on equity is therefore mostly earned rather than borrowed, and because ROIC exceeds the cost of capital, its 12% growth creates value — every dollar reinvested adds roughly six cents a year of economic profit. Q earns 7% on invested capital against the same 9% cost, a negative spread of two points, and reaches the same 20% return on equity only by employing an equity multiplier of 3.6 times. Its growth is destroying value: each reinvested dollar earns two points less than it costs, so faster growth makes Q worse, not better, and the 12% growth rate is actively harmful. The risk profiles differ as sharply as the returns. P at 1.4 times has substantial capacity to absorb a downturn and to borrow if an opportunity appears. Q at 3.6 times has little of either; a moderate fall in operating profit would take it toward its covenants, and because its returns are already below the cost of capital it cannot easily grow its way out. Q is also more exposed to interest rates, since a rise raises its cost of capital and widens an already negative spread. What I would check before concluding. First, whether the ROIC difference is real or a measurement artefact — whether P has internally generated intangibles that shrink its capital base, or whether Q carries goodwill from acquisitions that P grew organically, since that alone can account for a large gap. Computing ROIC both including and excluding goodwill for each would settle it. Second, the trajectory of both returns over five years rather than one, since a single year can be distorted by one-offs. Third, Q’s coverage ratios and covenant headroom, because at that leverage the flow measures matter more than the stock measure. Fourth, whether Q’s leverage is structural to a subsegment it operates in — property, financing arms and leasing operations legitimately carry more debt. On the evidence given, P is the better business and the safer one, and the equal returns on equity are exactly the false equivalence the DuPont decomposition exists to break.

modules.title: Where Statements Mislead
modules.tagline: Not fraud — mostly. The specific, legal, disclosed places where a true set of accounts gives a false impression.
objectives: Identify the four timing levers — recognition, capitalisation, provisioning and classification — and describe how each flatters reported results.
Evaluate a non-GAAP or adjusted earnings reconciliation and decide which adjustments to accept.
Compute an accrual ratio and explain the evidence behind it, including its limitations.
Describe what the major accounting failures had in common and which signals were visible beforehand.

lessons.title: Recognition, capitalisation and the timing levers
glossary: Recording a cost as an asset to be expensed over future periods, rather than expensing it now.
An over-provision created in a good year and released to flatter a bad one.
Taking an unusually large charge in an already bad period so that later periods look better.
Shipping more product than distributors can sell in order to recognise revenue early.

blocks.html: Very little of what misleads readers of financial statements is fraud. Most of it is judgement exercised consistently in one direction, disclosed in a footnote nobody reads, by people who would pass a lie detector test. That makes it harder to detect than fraud, not easier, because there is nothing to confess.

blocks.label: The four levers
blocks.html: Almost every distortion is one of four things: recognising revenue earlier, recognising cost later, moving an item to a different line, or moving cash to a different section. Learn the four and every specific technique becomes an instance of one of them.

Covered in Module 3, and the most consequential of the four because revenue sits at the top.
