The techniques are channel stuffing, bill and hold, aggressive percentage-of-completion, under-provision for returns, and treating a bundle as one obligation delivered up front rather than several delivered over time.
The common consequence is that a receivable or contract asset grows faster than revenue. Revenue pulled forward always leaves a trace on the balance sheet, because the cash has not arrived.

head: Technique
How it works
Where it shows
rows: Spending becomes an intangible asset instead of an expense
Intangibles grow; the capitalisation rate rises in the accounting policy note
Interest is added to the asset rather than charged to profit
Disclosed in the borrowing costs note; raises both profit and PP&E
Implied life from gross PP&E ÷ depreciation rises with no change in asset mix
Less of the cost is depreciated
A change in estimate, disclosed but rarely prominent
Under-providing for warranties, returns or bad debts
Estimated future costs are set low
Provision as a percentage of the relevant base falls year on year
A real economic cost is simply postponed
Nothing in the accounts. Capex-to-depreciation below 1.0 for years is the only trace

blocks.label: Capitalisation is the most seductive of these
blocks.html: It improves profit and operating cash flow simultaneously — the expense leaves the income statement and the payment leaves the operating section for the investing section. It is therefore invisible to the cash conversion test that catches most other distortions. The only reliable checks are free cash flow, which deducts capital expenditure, and the trend in capitalised costs as a percentage of total spending, which the policy note discloses.

blocks.text: Lever three — move it to a different line

blocks.html: Reclassification changes no total but changes every subtotal a reader might anchor on. Moving costs from cost of goods sold into SG&A raises gross margin. Moving recurring costs into a "restructuring" line raises adjusted operating profit. Moving a loss below operating income makes the operating line look clean.

The tell is a step change in a subtotal without a corresponding change in the total, and the accounting policy note is required to disclose reclassifications and restate comparatives. Companies that reclassify without restating are making comparison impossible, which is worth noticing on its own.

blocks.text: Lever four — move cash to a different section

blocks.html: Covered in Module 4: capitalising spending, choosing the financing classification for interest under IFRS, supply chain finance, and receivables factoring all raise operating cash flow without any change in the total cash generated.
Provisions are the only lever that works in both directions, which makes them the instrument of choice for smoothing.

tabs.label: The cookie jar
tabs.html: In a strong year, over-provide for restructuring, warranties or litigation. Profit is reduced now — when there is plenty of it — and the excess sits on the balance sheet. In a weak year, release the provision. Profit rises with no trading improvement, and the release may be disclosed only as a movement in a provisions table. This is how a genuinely volatile business reports smooth earnings.

tabs.label: The big bath
tabs.html: A new chief executive arrives, or a year is already lost. Take an enormous charge covering every conceivable future cost — restructuring, impairment, write-downs. The market forgives it as a clean-up, the prior management is blamed, and the following years look transformed because their costs were already charged. Watch for large charges in the first year of a new management team.

blocks.q: A company’s warranty provision falls from 3.1% of revenue to 1.8% over three years while product complaints rise. What is the effect on reported profit, and what should you do?
options: Profit is flattered by the reduced charge — recompute earnings at the original provisioning rate
blocks.explain: A lower provisioning rate means a smaller charge to the income statement, so profit rises without any operating improvement — and rising complaints suggest the true rate should be going the other way. Recomputing at 3.1% of revenue shows how much of the reported profit growth is provisioning. Cash flow is unaffected, which is exactly why comparing profit growth with cash flow growth catches this.

blocks.text: The one that leaves no trace

blocks.html: Deferred maintenance and deferred investment are the hardest to detect because nothing appears anywhere. A company that stops replacing equipment, cuts research, or lets its stores decay reports higher profit and higher cash flow immediately, and the cost arrives years later as lost competitiveness.

The only visible signals are indirect: capital expenditure running below depreciation for several years, research as a percentage of revenue declining against peers, or an ageing asset base implied by accumulated depreciation approaching gross cost. None of these is proof. Together, sustained over five years, they are a pattern worth naming.

lessons.title: Adjusted earnings and the non-GAAP problem
glossary: Any financial measure not defined by the applicable accounting framework.
EBITDA further adjusted for items management considers non-recurring.
The required bridge from the standardised figure to the adjusted one.
Figures presented as if a transaction had occurred at an earlier date.

blocks.html: Every large company now reports two sets of earnings: the ones the standards require, and the ones management prefers. The second set is presented first, in larger type, and is what most headlines quote.

blocks.label: Why adjusted figures exist at all
blocks.html: The case for them is real. Standardised earnings include items that genuinely obscure underlying performance — the amortisation of intangibles created by an acquisition years ago, a one-off legal settlement, currency movements on translation. An analyst forecasting next year is right to strip those out. The problem is not the practice; it is that the adjustments are chosen by the party being measured.

Adjustments overwhelmingly increase reported earnings rather than decrease them. That asymmetry is the single most useful fact about the whole area: if adjustments were an honest attempt to reveal underlying performance, they would go both ways roughly equally, and they do not.

head: Adjustment
Verdict
Reasoning
rows: A non-cash charge arising from purchase accounting on a deal that may be a decade old. But note that the cash was spent, and a serial acquirer adjusting this out every year is hiding the cost of its strategy.
A genuine cost of labour paid in equity. Excluding it treats staff as free. The dilution is real and permanent.
A genuine one-off from a discrete programme.
If it happens annually it is an operating cost with better branding. Check five years of adjustments before deciding.
Non-cash and non-recurring, so exclude it from a run rate — but it is direct evidence about past capital allocation and should shape your view of management.
One large settlement, accept. A company that settles something every year is in a business where litigation is an operating cost.
Constant-currency growth is a legitimate way to see volume and price. Do not let it disappear from the actual reported result.
A category with no accounting definition, frequently used for recurring spending.
Excluding the cost of the premises you operate from is not a measure of anything.

blocks.q: A company reports adjusted EPS of $2.40 and standardised EPS of $0.95. The largest adjustment is share-based compensation of $0.80. What should you conclude?
options: Adjusted EPS is the better measure of underlying performance
The gap is largely a genuine cost being excluded, and adjusted EPS overstates earnings by roughly that amount
blocks.explain: Share-based compensation is a real cost of obtaining labour, settled in equity rather than cash, and it dilutes existing owners permanently. Adding $0.80 back inflates the picture by that amount. A gap of more than 2.5× between adjusted and standardised earnings is itself a warning sign regardless of composition, and warrants reading every line of the reconciliation.

blocks.title: Five steps
steps: Start from the standardised figure, never the adjusted one
Anchoring matters. Read the reconciliation from the bottom up.
List every adjustment and its sign
Note how many increase earnings and how many decrease them. Anything close to all in one direction is informative.
Check each one against five years
Pull the same reconciliation from five annual reports. Anything appearing in four or five is recurring by definition.
Rebuild your own adjusted figure
Accept the adjustments you agree with, reject the rest, and use your number rather than either published one.
Compare the result with free cash flow
If your adjusted earnings figure is far above free cash flow year after year, the adjustments are not describing economic reality.

blocks.label: What regulators require
blocks.html: In the US, Regulation G requires that any non-GAAP measure be reconciled to the most directly comparable GAAP measure, and that the GAAP measure be presented with equal or greater prominence. The SEC has brought enforcement actions over prominence and over misleading adjustments. Similar guidance exists from the European Securities and Markets Authority. The rules mean the reconciliation must exist — they do not mean the adjustments are reasonable.

Over a five-year window, add up standardised net income and add up free cash flow. For a mature business the two should be broadly similar, because accruals reverse over time. Then add up adjusted earnings. If adjusted earnings are far above both, the adjustments are not correcting for noise — they are systematically removing costs.
Meridian, one year: net income $79.3m · free cash flow $29.3m · no adjusted measure presented

Note that Meridian's free cash flow is well below its net income, driven by capital expenditure of $58.0m against depreciation of $32.0m. Over a longer window those converge as the investment programme completes — which is exactly why the five-year test is more reliable than a single year in either direction.

lessons.title: Accrual quality and the limits of forensic screens
glossary: The difference between accounting earnings and cash flow.
Accruals scaled by average total assets.
An eight-variable model estimating the probability that earnings have been manipulated.
The underlying frequency of an event, which determines how many false positives a screen produces.

blocks.html: Several quantitative screens attempt to flag distorted accounts. They are genuinely useful and they are routinely oversold, so it is worth understanding both what they capture and why they cannot be used mechanically.
Accrual ratio = (net income − operating cash flow) ÷ average total assets

The logic is direct. Accruals are the part of earnings not backed by cash. They are a normal and necessary part of accounting, but they reverse: a receivable is collected or written off, a provision is used or released. Earnings composed mostly of accruals are therefore less likely to persist than earnings composed mostly of cash.
A negative ratio means cash exceeded earnings, which is the favourable direction. Meridian's -1.10% is comfortable. High positive values — earnings well above cash — are the concern.

blocks.label: The evidence
blocks.html: Richard Sloan's 1996 paper in The Accounting Review documented that firms with high accruals subsequently underperformed those with low accruals, and that the market appeared not to distinguish between the cash and accrual components of earnings. The accrual anomaly became one of the most replicated findings in accounting research. It has weakened since publication — as documented anomalies generally do once they are widely known and traded — but the underlying logic, that cash-backed earnings persist better than accrual-backed earnings, remains sound.

Messod Beneish's model combines eight ratios — covering receivables, gross margin, asset quality, sales growth, depreciation, SG&A, leverage and total accruals — into a single score. A value above roughly −1.78 flags a company as more likely to have manipulated earnings. It is best known for the Cornell student project that flagged Enron in 1998, before its collapse.

head: Component
What it captures
rows: Deteriorating margin, which raises the incentive to manipulate
A rising share of assets that are neither PP&E nor current — where capitalised costs hide
Growth itself, since high-growth firms face more pressure to sustain it
Rising leverage, which tightens covenant pressure

blocks.label: Why you cannot use this mechanically
blocks.html: Manipulation is rare. Suppose it occurs in 2% of company-years and a screen catches 70% of cases with a 10% false-positive rate. Out of 1,000 companies, 20 are manipulators and the screen catches 14 of them — while also flagging 98 honest companies. Under one in eight flagged companies is a genuine manipulator. The screen is doing real work, but a flag is the beginning of an investigation, not a conclusion. This is the base rate problem, and it defeats every low-prevalence screen ever built.

blocks.text: What the major failures had in common

head: Case
Mechanism
Visible signal beforehand
rows: Special purpose entities holding debt off balance sheet; mark-to-model gains on long contracts
Earnings far above operating cash flow; related-party disclosures involving the CFO; incomprehensible structure
Line costs capitalised as assets rather than expensed
Capital expenditure rising with no corresponding capacity; margins far above peers
Commercial income disclosure vague; payable days and rebate accruals moving oddly
Aggressive contract profit recognition; supply chain finance treated as trade payables
Payable days far above peers; profit high against consistently weak cash conversion
€1.9bn of cash in escrow that did not exist
Cash held in unusual jurisdictions; persistent short-seller allegations; auditor never confirmed balances directly
Store-level economics implausible against reported volumes

blocks.html: Three features recur. Earnings persistently exceeded cash flow. A balance sheet line grew without a business reason — receivables, capitalised costs, payables or an implausible cash balance. And the structure was more complicated than the business required, which is itself information: complexity is expensive, and companies do not pay for it without a reason.

blocks.label: The most practical screen there is
blocks.html: Plot cumulative net income against cumulative operating cash flow over five years on the same axis. In a healthy company the lines track each other. In almost every case above they diverged and kept diverging. It takes two minutes, requires no model, and catches most of what the sophisticated screens catch.

blocks.q: A screen flags 12% of a 1,200-company universe. Historical base rates suggest about 2% of companies manipulate earnings in a given year. Roughly what share of flagged companies are likely to be manipulators?
blocks.explain: 144 companies are flagged. At a 2% base rate only about 24 manipulators exist in the whole universe, and a screen will not catch all of them — perhaps 17. So at most around 17 of 144 flagged, roughly 12%, are genuine. Screens are useful for ordering a research queue and useless as verdicts, and this arithmetic is why.

blocks.text: What to do with all of this

items: Compare earnings with cash over five years, not one. Single years are dominated by timing; five years reveals whether accruals are reversing as they should.

Read the accounting policy note for changes. A change in useful life, capitalisation threshold, provisioning basis or revenue policy must be disclosed, and each one moves reported profit without moving the business.
Rebuild adjusted earnings yourself. Accept the adjustments you agree with, reject the rest, and never use management's figure unexamined.
Treat screens as a queue, not a verdict. Use them to decide what to read first.

Take complexity as evidence. When a structure is more complicated than the business requires, ask what the complexity is for. Sometimes the answer is tax, or regulation, or history. Sometimes it is the answer.

questions.q: Why is capitalising an operating cost harder to detect than most other distortions?
options: It improves both profit and operating cash flow, so the usual cash conversion check does not catch it
It only affects the balance sheet
It is illegal and therefore concealed
why: The capitalisation policy must be disclosed in the accounting policy note; the difficulty is that the effect is invisible in the usual screens.
Correct. The expense leaves the income statement and the payment moves from the operating section to investing, so profit rises and operating cash flow rises together.
It affects the income statement, the balance sheet and the classification of cash flow.
Capitalisation within the rules is entirely legal, which is precisely why it is common.
questions.explain: Free cash flow is the defence, because deducting capital expenditure neutralises the reclassification. Comparing capitalised costs as a percentage of total spending across years is the second check.

questions.q: Net income $180m, operating cash flow $95m, average total assets $1,400m. What is the accrual ratio, as a percentage?
questions.hint: The gap between earnings and cash, scaled by the asset base.
questions.explain: (180 − 95) ÷ 1,400 = 6.07%. A positive value of this size means most of the profit growth is not backed by cash. It is not proof of anything, but it puts the company high in the queue for a closer look at receivables, inventory and capitalised costs.

questions.q: A new chief executive takes a $900m charge in her first quarter covering restructuring, impairment and inventory write-downs. What is this pattern called and what is its effect?
options: A cookie jar reserve; it smooths earnings downward
A big bath; future periods look better because their costs have been charged now
A prior-period adjustment; it restates history
why: A cookie jar is an over-provision built quietly in good years, not a single large charge on arrival.
Correct. The charge is attributed to prior management, and future results improve because costs that would have fallen in those periods have already been taken.
A prior-period adjustment restates comparatives, which is a different mechanism.
Real charges were taken; totals changed.
questions.explain: Large first-year charges by incoming management are common enough to be a recognised pattern. They are often partly justified — a fresh view can identify genuine impairment — which is exactly what makes the technique durable.

questions.q: Which of these adjustments to earnings would you generally reject? Select all that apply.
options: Restructuring costs that have appeared in each of the last five years
"Business transformation" costs in year four of a transformation
Amortisation of intangibles from an acquisition six years ago
why: Reject. A genuine cost of labour, settled in equity, permanently diluting existing owners.
Reject. Five consecutive years of restructuring is an operating cost with a different label.
Reject. A cost recurring for four years is structural, and the category has no accounting definition.
Generally accept. A discrete one-off, provided the company is not in a business where litigation recurs.
Often accept for forecasting. Non-cash and arising from purchase accounting — though note that a serial acquirer excluding this every year is hiding the cost of its strategy.
questions.explain: The organising test is recurrence. Anything appearing in four or five of five years is not exceptional, whatever it is called, and pulling the same reconciliation from five annual reports settles most cases in ten minutes.

questions.q: What did Enron, Worldcom, Carillion and Wirecard have in common as a detectable signal?
options: All were audited by the same firm
Earnings persistently exceeded operating cash flow
All were in the same industry
why: They were audited by different firms.
Correct. In each case reported profit ran ahead of cash generation for years before the failure, and the gap widened rather than reversed.
They span energy, telecoms, construction and payments.
Several reported healthy equity right up to collapse.
questions.explain: Plotting cumulative net income against cumulative operating cash flow over five years is the single highest-yield forensic check available, and it requires no model at all.

questions.q: A forensic screen flags 15% of companies. Manipulation occurs in roughly 2% of company-years. What does this imply about a flagged company?
options: It is worth investigating, but most flagged companies are honest
why: At a 2% base rate, most of the 15% flagged must be false positives — there are not enough manipulators to fill the flag list.
Correct. Screens are for ordering a research queue, not for reaching conclusions.
It has real value: it concentrates the true cases into a much smaller pool than the universe.
Acting on a screen alone, given this base rate, means being wrong the large majority of the time.
questions.explain: This is the base rate problem, and it defeats every screen for a rare event. The screen raises the probability from 2% to perhaps 12% — a genuine sixfold improvement, and still a long way from a conclusion.

questions.q: Match each technique to the lever it uses.
pairs: Moving recurring costs into a restructuring line
Move it to a different line
Supply chain finance kept in trade payables
Move cash to a different section
Releasing an over-provision in a weak year
Recognise cost earlier, then reverse it
questions.explain: Reducing the whole field to four levers makes new techniques easy to classify. Whenever you meet an unfamiliar one, ask which of the four it is, and the appropriate check follows immediately.

questions.q: A company’s implied average asset life, calculated as gross PP&E divided by the annual depreciation charge, rises from 12 years to 17 years with no change in the type of assets held. What has happened?
options: Depreciation has been slowed, raising reported profit without any economic change
why: Newer equipment of the same type would not change the implied life, which depends on the depreciation rate rather than asset age.
Correct. A longer assumed useful life means a smaller annual charge, so profit rises with no change in the business.
An impairment would reduce carrying value and typically raise the charge, not lower it.
Higher capital expenditure raises gross PP&E but would also raise the depreciation charge over time.
questions.explain: Changes in accounting estimates must be disclosed, but they appear in a note rather than in the results commentary. Computing the implied life each year is a two-second check that surfaces them.

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest argument in favour of allowing companies to present adjusted earnings?
options: They are easier for investors to understand
Standardised earnings genuinely include items that obscure underlying performance, such as amortisation of long-past acquisitions
why: Simplicity is not the argument, and adjusted measures are frequently harder to compare, not easier.
Correct. An analyst forecasting next year is right to exclude a genuinely non-recurring item, and standardised earnings do not distinguish recurring from non-recurring.
That is the objection, not the argument in favour.
Regulators require reconciliation and equal prominence; they do not encourage the measures.
questions.explain: The case for adjusted figures is real, which is why they are permitted. The problem is that the party being measured chooses the adjustments, and the resulting asymmetry — adjustments almost always increase earnings — is the evidence that the discretion is being used self-servingly.

questions.q: A company has grown revenue 20% a year for four years. Over the same period, operating cash flow has been flat, capitalised development costs have risen from 15% to 45% of total research spending, days sales outstanding has risen from 55 to 84, and adjusted EBITDA excludes share-based compensation that now equals 19% of revenue. Assess the quality of the reported earnings and set out what would change your mind.
questions.model: Each fact on its own has an innocent explanation; together they describe earnings that are substantially an accounting construction rather than a cash result, and the combination is the concern rather than any single item. Flat operating cash flow against four years of 20% compound revenue growth is the central fact. Revenue has roughly doubled while cash generation has not moved, so essentially none of the incremental revenue has converted into cash. The capitalisation shift explains part of the gap and is the most serious item, because tripling the capitalised share of research spending both raises profit, by removing the expense, and raises operating cash flow, by moving the payment to investing. It therefore flatters the very metric I would normally use as a check, which means flat operating cash flow is worse than it appears: without the capitalisation change it would likely have declined. The correct measure here is free cash flow, and I would expect it to be materially negative. The rising days sales outstanding is the second item. Twenty-nine additional days on a doubled revenue base is a large absolute increase in receivables, and it means revenue is being recognised well ahead of collection. The benign reading is a shift toward larger enterprise contracts with milestone billing; the adverse reading is loosened credit terms used to sustain the growth rate, or revenue recognised on progress rather than delivery. The split between billed receivables and contract assets would distinguish them, as would the ageing analysis and the trend in the credit loss allowance as a percentage of gross receivables. Share-based compensation at 19% of revenue, excluded from adjusted EBITDA, means adjusted EBITDA is not a measure of anything an owner receives. Nearly a fifth of revenue is being paid to employees in equity, diluting shareholders permanently, and then presented as though it were free. I would add it back and recompute every margin and multiple. I would also check whether buybacks approximate the shares issued to staff, in which case the company is spending cash on compensation while routing it through the financing section. What would change my mind. Evidence that the capitalisation change followed a genuine change in the development process — a shift from research to a defined product with demonstrated technical and commercial feasibility — with the policy note explaining the threshold and the comparatives restated. Evidence that the receivables increase is concentrated in a small number of named large contracts with disclosed milestone terms, rather than spread across the book. A cohort or contracted-revenue disclosure showing that the growth is recurring and that customers renew, since durable revenue justifies more patience with the cash timing. Free cash flow that is negative but improving, with a credible path to positive, rather than deteriorating. And a share-based compensation charge that is falling as a percentage of revenue, indicating a transition from equity to cash compensation as the company matures. Absent those, my working conclusion is that reported profit growth substantially exceeds economic profit growth, and that the gap is widening rather than closing.

modules.title: Capstone: Reading a Company End to End
modules.tagline: Where the numbers live, which footnotes change the answer, and a workflow you can repeat on any company in three hours.
objectives: Navigate an annual report or 10-K and know which section answers which question.
Identify the six footnotes most likely to change a conclusion, and what to look for in each.
Execute a repeatable analysis workflow from first open to written view.
Produce a written analysis of a real company supported by computed figures and specific citations to the filing.

lessons.title: A map of the annual report
glossary: The annual report US-listed companies file with the SEC.
Management’s discussion and analysis — the narrative explanation of the results.
The SEC’s free public filing database.
Disclosure of results broken down by business line or geography.

blocks.html: A 10-K runs to a hundred pages or more and almost nobody reads it front to back. That is fine — it is a reference document, not a narrative. What matters is knowing which part answers which question, so you can go straight there.

head: Section (US 10-K)
What it contains
Read it when
rows: What the company actually does, its markets, customers, competition
First time you look at a company. Skim thereafter for changes in wording, which are deliberate.
Everything that could go wrong, in management’s own words
Every year. Mostly boilerplate, but changes year on year are highly informative.
Always. A single case can exceed the market value.
Buybacks by month, share count, dividend history
When assessing capital returns and dilution.
Management’s explanation of the results, segment performance, liquidity
Always, second. It tells you what management wants emphasised.
Sensitivity to rates, currency and commodities
For any leveraged or international business.
The three statements plus every footnote
Always, first. This is the audited part.
The internal control opinion and any material weakness
Always. A material weakness is a leading indicator of a restatement.
Executive pay and the metrics it is based on
Always. What management is paid to maximise predicts what they will maximise.

blocks.label: Read in this order
blocks.html: Statements and notes first, MD&A second, press release last or never. Reading the narrative before the numbers lets someone else frame your view of figures you have not yet seen. Reading the numbers first means you arrive at the narrative with your own questions already formed, and you can notice which of them management chose not to address.

blocks.text: Risk factors: read the diff, not the list

blocks.html: Risk factors are written by lawyers to be comprehensive rather than informative, and the base list barely changes. What is informative is what was added this year, what was removed, and what moved up the ordering — companies generally list what they consider most significant first. A newly added risk factor is a disclosure decision somebody argued about.
Comparing two years of risk factors takes ten minutes with any text comparison tool, and it is one of the highest-yield ten minutes available in the whole document.

blocks.text: The proxy statement, which most people never open

blocks.html: Executive compensation is disclosed in a separate filing, and it answers a question the financial statements cannot: what is management actually trying to maximise?

items: Bonus on adjusted EPS tells you why the adjustments look the way they do, and why buybacks may be timed as they are.
Bonus on revenue growth with no return-on-capital condition predicts acquisitions and margin dilution.
Long-term awards on relative total shareholder return against a peer group are among the better designs, though the choice of peer group is itself a decision worth checking.
Bonus on EBITDA in a capital-intensive business creates a standing incentive to under-invest, because capital expenditure does not reduce EBITDA.

blocks.q: A company’s annual bonus is 70% weighted to adjusted EBITDA and the business is heavily capital-intensive. What behaviour should you expect?
options: A bias toward under-investing in capital expenditure and toward classifying costs as exceptional
blocks.explain: Capital expenditure does not reduce EBITDA, so deferring it raises the bonus with no immediate reported cost. Classifying costs as exceptional removes them from the adjusted figure with the same effect. Neither is fraud; both are the predictable result of the incentive. Reading the pay design tells you which balance sheet lines to watch.

head: Jurisdiction
Source
Cost
rows: SEC EDGAR — full text search across all filings
Companies House for all registered companies, including private ones
National registers and the ESAP framework; issuer investor relations pages
The company’s own investor relations page, which usually holds ten years of reports

blocks.label: The most underused free resource
blocks.html: UK Companies House holds filed accounts for private companies, not just listed ones. If you are assessing a supplier, a customer, a competitor or a potential employer, the accounts are usually there. Small-company filings are abbreviated, but a balance sheet and a director’s report tell you a great deal that no public source will.

lessons.title: The footnotes that change the answer
glossary: The description of the methods used, always the first substantive note.
Results disaggregated by business line or geography.
Obligations and possible liabilities not recognised on the balance sheet.
Dealings with directors, major shareholders or entities they control.

blocks.html: The statements are four pages. The notes are forty. Almost everything that changes a conclusion is in the notes, and six of them do most of the work.

blocks.text: 1 · Accounting policies, and changes to them

blocks.html: Always the first substantive note. Read it for revenue recognition, inventory costing, depreciation lives, capitalisation thresholds and provisioning basis. Then read last year's version and compare. A change in policy or estimate moves reported profit without moving the business, and it will be disclosed here in careful language and nowhere else prominently.

A consolidated income statement can hide two businesses moving in opposite directions. The segment note gives revenue, profit and often assets by division, which lets you compute margin and return by segment.

Two things to watch. A company that changes its segment definitions is making historical comparison difficult, and it usually does so when one segment is deteriorating. And an unallocated corporate cost line that grows faster than revenue is where overhead goes to be invisible.

Required under ASC 606 and IFRS 15. It splits revenue by type, timing and geography — point in time versus over time, product versus service, recurring versus one-off. This is where you learn that a company describing itself as a subscription business has 60% one-off licence revenue.

Also here: contract assets and contract liabilities, and the amount of revenue recognised in the period that was in deferred revenue at the start. That last figure lets you separate genuinely new business from the unwinding of last year's bookings.

The maturity ladder, interest rates, security, and — most importantly — covenants. A company with modest leverage and a covenant three inches away is in a different position from one with high leverage and abundant headroom. If the covenant thresholds are not disclosed, that is itself informative.
Meridian: net debt / EBITDA of 1.35× against a typical 3.0× covenant — EBITDA could fall 55% before the test binds.

Purchase commitments, guarantees, litigation, environmental obligations and take-or-pay contracts. None of it is on the balance sheet, and any of it can be larger than equity. This is the note where a company's real fixed cost base is sometimes visible for the first time.

Transactions with directors, major shareholders, or entities they control. Most are mundane — a property leased from a founder, a service bought from an affiliate. But this note has appeared in the history of nearly every major accounting failure, and the effort of reading it is two minutes.

blocks.label: The pattern to be alert to
blocks.html: Related party transactions become serious when they involve the transfer of assets or revenue at prices nobody else set, when a director is on both sides, or when a special purpose entity holds obligations the group has effectively guaranteed. Enron’s structures were disclosed in this note. They were disclosed in language that made them hard to follow, which is a different problem, and one worth treating as a signal in itself.

head: Note
What it can change
rows: The rate reconciliation explains an unexplained earnings jump; unrecognised deferred tax assets indicate management doubts future profits
Discount rate and mortality assumptions move a deficit enormously; a small change is a large number
Maturity profile of lease liabilities; the discount rate used
Where factoring, supply chain finance and hedging appear
Grant volumes, vesting conditions, and the dilution pipeline
Anything material that happened after the year end but before signing

blocks.q: A company changes its reporting segments for the third time in four years. What is the most reasonable inference?
options: The business is genuinely reorganising frequently
Historical comparison is being made difficult, and it is worth asking which segment the change obscures
blocks.explain: Reorganisations do happen and sometimes require re-segmentation. But three changes in four years makes multi-year comparison nearly impossible, and re-segmentation most often follows deterioration in a division that was previously visible. The check is to rebuild the old segmentation from the restated comparatives, which companies are required to provide, and see what the previously separate line was doing.

lessons.title: A repeatable analysis workflow
glossary: The typical value of a measure for the industry, used as a reference point.
A conclusion stated so that specific future evidence would show it to be wrong.

blocks.html: What follows is a workflow, not a checklist to be completed. It takes about three hours on an unfamiliar company and gets faster with practice. The order matters: it is designed so that you form your own questions before you read anyone else's answers.

blocks.title: Nine steps
steps: Understand the business in plain language
Item 1 and the revenue disaggregation note. Write two sentences: what does it sell, and to whom? If you cannot, stop — you cannot analyse what you cannot describe.
Pull five years of the three statements
Not one year. Almost every technique in this course requires a trend, and single years are dominated by timing.
Plot cumulative net income against cumulative operating cash flow
Two minutes. If the lines diverge and keep diverging, that is now the central question of the whole analysis.
Compute the ratio set
Gross and operating margin, ROIC, the cash conversion cycle, net debt to EBITDA, interest cover, capex to depreciation. Seven numbers, five years, one table.
Decompose what moved
Use DuPont for return on equity and the growth-versus-efficiency split for working capital. Do not accept a movement without knowing which component caused it.
Read the six footnotes
Policies, segments, revenue, debt, commitments, related parties. Note anything that would change a number you computed.
Rebuild adjusted earnings yourself
Take management’s reconciliation, accept what you agree with, reject the rest, and use your figure.
Read MD&A and the risk factor changes
Now, and not before. You have your own questions; see which ones management addresses and which it does not.
Write a falsifiable view
One page. What you believe, the two or three numbers it rests on, and what would prove you wrong.

blocks.label: Why step 9 is the one that matters
blocks.html: "The business looks healthy" is not a view; it cannot be wrong, so it cannot be useful. "Operating margin will hold above 12% because the gross margin gain came from mix rather than price, and I will be wrong if the segment note shows the mix reverting" is a view. It commits, it names its evidence, and it tells you in advance what would change your mind. Most analytical failure is failure to have done this.

blocks.text: Meridian, worked through the whole thing

head: Step
Finding
rows: A tool manufacturer and distributor. Revenue $840.0m, growing 10.2%.
Net income $79.3m against operating cash flow $87.3m — cash ahead of profit, which is the reassuring direction.
ROIC 16.3%, well above a plausible cost of capital. Growth here creates value.
Cash conversion cycle 98 days, up from 88. The clear negative.
Of the $27.0m absorbed by working capital, more than half came from slower days rather than from growth.
Net debt / EBITDA 1.35×, interest cover 7.8×. Comfortable, and improving.
A $8.0m property disposal gain, 7.7% of pre-tax profit. Strip it before extrapolating.
Free cash flow $29.3m against dividends of $19.3m — 66% covered. Thin.

blocks.html: A falsifiable view. Meridian is a good business getting better at trading and worse at collecting. Operating margin improvement of 1.1 points is real and, on the evidence, driven by mix rather than one-off pricing. The dividend is the pressure point: at 66% of free cash flow, another year of 3.4-day receivable slippage would leave it uncovered and require borrowing. I would be wrong if the next annual report shows the cash conversion cycle flat or improving, in which case the working capital movement was a one-year timing effect and free cash flow should step up sharply.

blocks.label: Note what that view does not claim
blocks.html: It says nothing about whether the shares are cheap. Statement analysis tells you what a business is and how it is performing; valuation is a separate discipline with separate tools, and conflating them is the most common error made by people who have just learned to read accounts. Knowing that a company is excellent does not tell you what to pay for it.

items: Analysing one year. Nearly every technique here needs a trend. One year is timing.
Accepting management’s adjusted figures. They were chosen by the party being measured.
Comparing across accounting frameworks without adjustment. LIFO versus FIFO, capitalised versus expensed development, gross versus net revenue.
Treating a ratio as a conclusion. Every ratio has a numerator and a denominator, and both can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the business.
Reading the narrative first. It frames your view of numbers you have not yet seen.
Confusing quality with value. A wonderful business at a terrible price is a terrible investment.

blocks.q: The workflow puts read MD&A and the risk factors at step 8, after the ratios, the decomposition and the footnotes. Why so late?
options: Management’s narrative is usually inaccurate, so it is worth little
Reading it first frames your view of numbers you have not yet computed, so you end up testing management’s questions rather than your own
The MD&A repeats the footnotes, so it adds nothing new
Regulators require the statements to be read in filing order
blocks.explain: The narrative is written by the party being measured and is usually accurate — that is not the problem. The problem is anchoring: read it first and its framing becomes the lens for every figure you go on to compute, and you spend the analysis answering management’s questions instead of your own. Computing first gives you a list of things you want explained; the MD&A then becomes a test of which of them management chooses to address.

blocks.title: Capstone assignment: a full analysis of a real company
blocks.brief: Choose a listed company whose most recent annual report is publicly available, and whose business you can describe in two sentences. Avoid banks and insurers for a first attempt — their statements follow different conventions. Pull five years of financial statements and produce a written analysis of no more than three pages. Every figure you quote must be computed by you from the filings and must be traceable to a specific statement or note. State clearly that this is your own educational analysis and not investment advice.
items: A two-sentence description of what the company sells and to whom, drawn from Item 1 and the revenue disaggregation note.
A five-year table of the seven core measures: gross margin, operating margin, ROIC, cash conversion cycle, net debt to EBITDA, interest cover, and capital expenditure to depreciation.
A chart or table comparing cumulative net income with cumulative operating cash flow over the five years, and a paragraph explaining any divergence.
A DuPont decomposition of return on equity for the first and last year, identifying which component drove the change.
A working capital decomposition splitting the latest movement into the portion caused by growth and the portion caused by a change in days.
A review of the company’s adjusted earnings reconciliation: which adjustments you accept, which you reject, and your own adjusted figure with the reasoning.
Findings from at least four of the six key footnotes, each with a specific note reference and a statement of whether it changed a number you computed.
A note on what the executive compensation design rewards, drawn from the proxy or remuneration report, and what behaviour that predicts.
A one-paragraph falsifiable view: what you believe, the two or three figures it rests on, and the specific future evidence that would prove you wrong.
An explicit list of what you could not determine from the filings and what you would need in order to determine it.

blocks.html: Write the analysis before reading any broker research or press commentary on the company. Read those afterwards, and note every place where your conclusion differs from theirs and why. That comparison, done a dozen times, is how the skill in this course turns into judgement.

questions.q: In what order should the sections of an annual report be read?
options: Press release, MD&A, then the statements
Statements and notes first, then MD&A, then the press release
why: This is the most common order and the worst. It lets management frame your view of figures you have not seen.
Correct. Forming your own questions from the audited numbers first means you can notice which of them the narrative avoids.
Risk factors are valuable, but mainly as a year-on-year comparison rather than as a starting point.
The order materially changes what you notice, because anchoring is powerful and largely involuntary.
questions.explain: The statements are audited; the press release is not, and leads with figures management selected. Reading in the reverse order is the single cheapest improvement most people can make.

questions.q: Why is a change in reporting segments worth investigating?
options: It is prohibited without regulatory approval
It makes multi-year comparison difficult, and often follows deterioration in a division that was previously visible
why: Companies may change segments when the internal management structure changes; no approval is required.
Correct. Re-segmentation is legitimate but disproportionately follows a division starting to look bad on its own.
It is far too common to be a fraud indicator on its own.
Total revenue is unchanged; only its disaggregation moves.
questions.explain: Companies must restate comparatives when segments change, so the old view can usually be partially rebuilt. Doing so, and seeing what the previously separate line was doing, is the check.

questions.q: What does the executive compensation disclosure tell an analyst that the financial statements cannot?
options: What management is being paid to maximise, and therefore what it will maximise
why: The tax reconciliation note covers this.
Correct. Incentive design predicts behaviour — bonuses on EBITDA predict under-investment; bonuses on adjusted EPS predict adjustments and buybacks.
Share count is in the statements and in Item 5.
Debt maturities are in the debt note.
questions.explain: The proxy or remuneration report is the most reliably informative document that most people never open. It tells you which lines of the accounts to watch most closely at this particular company.

questions.q: Which of these belong in the six footnotes to read first on any company? Select all that apply.
options: Accounting policies and changes to them
why: Yes. A policy change moves profit without moving the business, and this is where it is disclosed.
Yes. Consolidated figures can conceal two divisions moving in opposite directions.
Yes. Covenant headroom determines whether a bad quarter is an inconvenience or a crisis.
Interesting as a governance signal — a large non-audit fee raises independence questions — but it rarely changes a number you computed.
Yes. This note has featured in the history of nearly every major accounting failure and takes two minutes.
questions.explain: The six are policies, segments, revenue disaggregation, debt, commitments and contingencies, and related parties. Auditor remuneration is worth a glance but belongs in the second tier.

questions.q: Which statement is a falsifiable view rather than an observation?
options: The company has a strong balance sheet
Gross margin will hold above 34% because the gain came from mix rather than price; I am wrong if the segment note shows the mix reverting
why: "Strong" is undefined and no evidence could contradict it.
True but backward-looking. It is a fact, not a view.
Correct. It commits to a threshold, names the reason, and specifies the evidence that would refute it.
A fact about the past. Necessary input, but not a view.
questions.explain: A conclusion that cannot be wrong cannot be useful. Naming in advance what would change your mind is what separates analysis from description, and it is the discipline most often skipped.

questions.q: What is the most useful thing to do with risk factors?
options: Read the full list carefully each year
Compare this year’s against last year’s and focus on what was added, removed or moved up
why: The list is written to be comprehensive rather than informative and changes little year to year.
Correct. Additions and reordering are deliberate disclosure decisions that someone argued about.
Not boilerplate in the changes, only in the base list.
Length correlates with legal caution rather than with risk.
questions.explain: A text comparison of two years takes ten minutes and surfaces the disclosures management felt newly obliged to make. It is among the highest-yield ten minutes in the whole filing.

questions.q: Place these analysis steps in the order the workflow recommends.
items: Describe the business in two sentences
Pull five years of statements
Plot cumulative earnings against cumulative operating cash flow
Compute the core ratio set
Read the six key footnotes
Read MD&A and the risk factor changes
Write a falsifiable view
questions.explain: The narrative comes late deliberately. By the time you reach MD&A you have your own questions, and the useful information is as much in which of them management declines to address as in what it says.

questions.q: Statement analysis has established that a company is excellent. What does that tell you about whether to buy the shares?
options: Very little on its own; quality and price are separate questions
Sell, since quality is priced in
Nothing can be inferred from financial statements
why: A wonderful business at a sufficiently high price is a poor investment, and quality alone cannot tell you which case you are in.
Correct. Statement analysis establishes what a business is and how it performs; valuation is a separate discipline.
Sometimes quality is fully priced and sometimes it is not — that is precisely the question analysis cannot answer alone.
A great deal can be inferred about the business; the limitation is specifically about price.
questions.explain: Conflating business quality with investment merit is the most common error made by people who have just learned to read accounts. This course teaches the first; the second requires valuation, which is a separate course.

questions.q: Why does the workflow insist on five years of statements rather than one?
options: Single years are dominated by timing effects, and almost every technique in the course depends on a trend
It makes the analysis look thorough
why: US filers present five years of selected data but the reason for using it is analytical, not regulatory.
Correct. Accruals reverse over time, one-offs average out, and a persistent divergence is meaningful in a way that a single year never is.
Older data is not more accurate; it is more contextual.
Thoroughness for appearance is not the point — a single-year conclusion is frequently simply wrong.
questions.explain: Cash conversion, accrual quality, capex to depreciation and the cash conversion cycle are all close to meaningless in a single year and highly informative over five.

questions.q: You have three hours and an unfamiliar mid-cap industrial company. Set out exactly what you would do, in order, and what you would have at the end.
questions.model: First twenty minutes: understand the business. Item 1 of the most recent 10-K or the strategic report, plus the revenue disaggregation note, until I can write two sentences saying what it sells and to whom. If I cannot write those sentences I stop, because there is no point computing ratios for a business I cannot describe. I would also note the segment structure and the revenue split by geography and by product versus service. Next forty minutes: assemble the data. Five years of income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement into one sheet. This is mechanical and it is the foundation for everything else; doing it by hand rather than downloading it is worth the time on a first pass because it forces me to see the line items the company actually uses. Next twenty minutes: the two fastest diagnostics. Plot cumulative net income against cumulative operating cash flow across the five years. Compute free cash flow each year. If the lines diverge persistently, that becomes the central question of the whole exercise and I reorder everything that follows around it. Next forty minutes: the ratio set and the decompositions. Gross margin, operating margin, ROIC, cash conversion cycle, net debt to EBITDA, interest cover, capex to depreciation — seven measures, five years. Then a DuPont decomposition of return on equity for the first and last year to see whether any change came from margin, turnover or leverage, and a working capital decomposition splitting the latest movement into growth and efficiency. At this point I know what moved and I have a specific list of things I do not understand. Next forty minutes: the footnotes, targeted at that list. Accounting policies and any change to them, compared against the prior year. Segments, to see whether the consolidated picture is hiding divergent divisions. Revenue disaggregation, for the recurring versus one-off split and the contract asset balance. Debt, for the maturity ladder and covenant headroom. Commitments and contingencies. Related parties. I would also pull the tax rate reconciliation if the effective rate moved and the share-based payment note if dilution looked material. Next fifteen minutes: rebuild adjusted earnings. Take management’s reconciliation, pull the same reconciliation from three or four prior years, identify which adjustments recur, accept what I agree with, reject the rest, and compute my own figure. Next fifteen minutes: only now, MD&A and a comparison of this year’s risk factors against last year’s, plus a skim of the compensation design to see what management is paid to maximise. I am reading these with my own questions already formed, so what matters is which of them are addressed and which are not. Final ten minutes: write the view. One page. What I believe, the two or three computed figures it rests on, and the specific future evidence that would prove me wrong. What I would have at the end: a five-year figure table, two decompositions, my own adjusted earnings number, a list of footnote findings with references, and a one-page falsifiable view. What I would explicitly not have: a valuation, a price target, or a recommendation — those require a separate discipline and a separate set of tools, and three hours of statement analysis does not produce them. I would also have a written list of what I could not determine from the filings, which is usually the most useful page for deciding whether to spend another three hours.

questions.q: What problem does accrual accounting exist to solve?
options: Allocating continuous economic activity to discrete reporting periods
why: Accrual accounting arguably creates more opportunity for distortion than cash accounting, not less.
Correct. Businesses run continuously; reporting is periodic, and someone must decide which period each item belongs to.
Taxable profit is computed under statute and often differs from accounting profit.
It is substantially more complex than cash accounting.
questions.explain: The artificial period boundary is the source of every estimate in accounting — useful life, collectability, percentage complete — and therefore of both its usefulness and its manipulability.

questions.q: A gym sells 500 annual memberships at $840 each on 1 April. What revenue is recognised by 31 December, in $?
questions.hint: Nine of twelve months have been delivered.
questions.explain: 500 × $840 = $420,000 total. Nine months of twelve elapsed, so $420,000 × 9/12 = $315,000 recognised, with $105,000 remaining as deferred revenue — a liability, because the gym still owes three months of access.

questions.q: A company buys a $9m machine for cash. What is the immediate effect on total assets?
options: It depends on the depreciation method
why: Nothing new entered the business; cash was exchanged for equipment.
A purchase is not an expense. The $9m has been converted, not consumed.
Correct. Cash falls $9m and equipment rises $9m — a change in composition only.
Depreciation affects later periods, not the moment of purchase.
questions.explain: Capital expenditure is an asset swap on the day it happens and becomes a cost over subsequent years through depreciation. This is why "we invested" and "we spent" mean different things.

questions.q: An unmodified audit opinion does NOT assert which of the following?
options: That the statements comply with the applicable framework
That the statements are free of all error
That the statements present fairly in all material respects
That sufficient audit evidence was obtained
why: It does assert compliance with GAAP or IFRS.
Correct. Immaterial errors are known to exist and are deliberately not pursued. Absolute accuracy has never been the standard.
This is the core of the opinion.
The auditor must state that the evidence obtained was sufficient and appropriate.
questions.explain: Materiality is set at a small percentage of profit, revenue or assets, and the audit is designed around it. A clean opinion is a floor, not a ceiling.

questions.q: Cash $88m, receivables $210m, inventory $260m, trade payables $170m, current debt $40m, long-term debt $390m. What is net debt, in $m?
questions.hint: Only borrowings count.
questions.explain: (40 + 390) − 88 = $342m. Trade payables are an operating liability that arises from trading and are excluded. Including them would give $512m and materially overstate leverage — the most common error in this calculation.

questions.q: Which of these appear on a conventional balance sheet? Select all that apply.
options: A brand developed internally over twenty years
A right-of-use asset for a leased building
A guarantee given to a subsidiary’s lender
why: Appears. The excess of purchase price over identifiable net assets is recognised.
Does not appear. Internally generated brands are expensed as incurred.
Appears. IFRS 16 and ASC 842 require lessees to recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
Does not appear as a number unless an outflow is probable and measurable; otherwise it is disclosed in the contingencies note.
questions.explain: Purchase and contract create recognition; internal creation and uncertainty do not. That asymmetry is the main reason book value diverges from economic value in the modern economy.

questions.q: Deferred revenue rose from $180m to $250m at a subscription business. How should this be read?
options: As a deterioration, since liabilities grew
As customers prepaying for future service — interest-free financing and a leading indicator of revenue
As evidence revenue was recognised too early
why: The obligation is to deliver a service already paid for, not to repay cash.
Correct. More cash collected in advance, and more contracted future revenue.
The opposite: deferred revenue exists because revenue was not recognised on receipt of cash.
It carries no interest and is settled by delivering service.
questions.explain: Deferred revenue is customer-funded working capital. A decline in it is a warning about future revenue long before reported revenue turns.

questions.q: Gross PP&E is $840m and the annual depreciation charge is $56m. What average useful life, in years, is implied?
questions.hint: Gross cost divided by the annual charge.
questions.explain: 840 ÷ 56 = 15 years. The value of this crude estimate is comparative: against a peer with the same equipment, or against the company’s own prior years. A lengthening implied life with no change in asset mix means depreciation has been slowed, raising profit for no economic reason.

questions.q: A marketplace reclassifies from principal to agent. Revenue falls from $1.2bn to $180m. What has changed economically?
options: Nothing — the same transactions are presented net rather than gross
It disposed of most of its business
why: Nothing was lost; the gross-up was removed.
Correct. Gross profit and cash are identical under either presentation.
A disposal would appear as discontinued operations.
Customer numbers are unaffected by a presentation conclusion.
questions.explain: This is among the largest reported-figure effects in accounting with zero economic content, and it makes revenue multiples across a sector unusable unless the basis has been checked for each company.

questions.q: A company grants 6m options at a $15 strike. The average share price for the year is $45. How many shares, in millions, does the treasury stock method add to the diluted count?
questions.hint: The proceeds buy back shares at the average price.
questions.explain: Proceeds = 6m × $15 = $90m, which repurchases 2m shares at $45. Net dilution = 6m − 2m = 4m. At a share price of $22.50 the same grant would add only 2m — dilution rises as the share price rises.

questions.q: Net income grew 3% while diluted EPS grew 14%. What explains the gap?
why: A tax change raises net income itself, so both measures move together.
Same issue: it lifts both figures equally.
Correct. Any divergence between net income growth and EPS growth is a denominator effect.
Lower depreciation raises net income and therefore both figures.
questions.explain: Buybacks below intrinsic value do create real value, so the gap is not necessarily bad — but it is not operating improvement, and a share count cannot shrink indefinitely.

questions.q: Why is excluding share-based compensation from adjusted earnings indefensible?
options: The company received services and paid for them by issuing claims on itself, permanently diluting existing owners
why: Regulators require reconciliation and prominence; they do not prohibit the adjustment.
Correct. Value transferred from existing shareholders to employees. The cost landed through dilution rather than the bank account.
It involves no cash, which is precisely the argument companies make for excluding it.
At many technology companies it exceeds 15% of revenue.
questions.explain: The add-back in the cash flow statement is correct, because no cash moved. The exclusion from earnings is not, because a real cost was incurred.

questions.q: Operating income $220m, depreciation $65m, amortisation $18m. What is EBITDA, in $m?
questions.hint: Add back the two non-cash charges.
questions.explain: 220 + 65 + 18 = $303m. Whether that figure is useful depends entirely on capital intensity: if capital expenditure is also around $65m a year, EBITDA overstates distributable cash by roughly a quarter before interest and tax are even considered.

questions.q: Net income $110m, depreciation $40m, receivables up $28m, inventory down $12m, payables up $15m, gain on disposal $9m. What is operating cash flow, in $m?
questions.hint: Assets up consume cash; liabilities up provide it; gains are reversed out.
questions.explain: 110 + 40 − 28 + 12 + 15 − 9 = $140m. The gain is subtracted because the full disposal proceeds appear in investing; leaving it in operating would count the same money twice.

questions.q: A company reports operating cash flow negative, investing cash flow negative, and financing cash flow strongly positive, for a fourth consecutive year. It is thirty years old. What is the reading?
options: The trading business does not fund itself and is being sustained by external capital
why: This pattern is normal for a start-up and worrying for a mature business.
Correct. Four years of funding both operations and investment from new capital means the business has not been paying for itself.
Seasonality does not persist across four full years.
Cost control would show in operating cash flow, which is negative.
questions.explain: The signs of the three sections read as a sentence about where a company sits in its life. The same pattern is unremarkable at year three and serious at year thirty.

questions.q: Which of these raise reported operating cash flow without improving the business? Select all that apply.
options: Classifying interest paid as financing under IFRS
why: Yes. The outflow moves from operating to investing, and profit rises too.
Yes. IFRS permits the choice; the payment is unchanged.
Yes. It converts a future collection into cash today, at a fee, and improves DSO as well.
No. Depreciation is added straight back, so changing the rate alters profit and the add-back identically and leaves operating cash flow untouched.
questions.explain: That immunity to depreciation policy is exactly why the cash flow statement is a useful check on the income statement — and why capitalisation, which evades the check, is the most seductive distortion.

questions.q: Why is a gain on disposal subtracted in the operating section of an indirect cash flow statement?
options: Because the full proceeds appear in investing, so leaving the gain in operating would double count
why: The gain is real and correctly recognised.
Correct. Removing it keeps each section honest and avoids counting the same money twice.
Cash was received on the disposal; the issue is which section reports it.
Conservatism is not the driver.
questions.explain: Losses are added back for the same reason with the sign reversed. Once the double-counting logic is clear the sign stops being something to memorise.

questions.q: Retained earnings opened at $486m and closed at $551m. Net income was $92m. What were dividends, in $m?
questions.hint: Rearrange the roll-forward.
questions.explain: 486 + 92 − dividends = 551, so dividends = $27m. Working backwards through a roll-forward to recover an undisclosed figure works equally well for capital expenditure, disposals, write-offs and buybacks.

questions.q: Opening net PP&E $410m, capital expenditure $95m, depreciation $62m, net book value of disposals $8m. What is closing net PP&E, in $m?
questions.hint: Add what came in, subtract what was consumed and what left.
questions.explain: 410 + 95 − 62 − 8 = $435m. Where a company discloses capital expenditure poorly, this identity lets you solve for it, since every other term is available from the balance sheet and the depreciation note.

questions.q: A company sells goods for $200 on credit that cost $120. What is the net effect on operating cash flow?
why: No cash has been received.
The $80 profit is added at the top, but the $200 receivable and the $120 inventory release exactly offset it.
Inventory falling is a source of cash, not a use.
questions.explain: A credit sale creates profit and no cash, and the cash flow statement records that correctly by offsetting the profit against the working capital movements it created.

questions.q: A forecast balance sheet is out by exactly the year’s depreciation charge. What is the most likely cause?
options: Depreciation was expensed but not added to accumulated depreciation, or the reverse
why: A tax error would not produce a gap equal to a specific line item.
Correct. An imbalance equal to one line means that line was recorded once instead of twice.
Growth assumptions do not break the balance check; they are carried through consistently.
That would produce a gap equal to the dividend, not to depreciation.
questions.explain: Diagnosing by the size of the gap is far faster than checking every formula. Out by one line means recorded once; out by twice a line means recorded twice.

questions.q: Which change the balance sheet without appearing in the cash flow statement? Select all that apply.
options: An acquisition paid for entirely in shares
why: Yes. Assets and liabilities arrive with no cash movement.
Yes. A right-of-use asset and lease liability are recognised together; cash flows come later as payments.
Yes. Debt falls, equity rises, no cash crosses.
No. That is a financing outflow.
questions.explain: The non-cash investing and financing note is where these are disclosed. A company growing by share-funded acquisition can have an almost empty investing section while transforming its balance sheet.

questions.q: Revenue $1,200m, COGS $780m, receivables $205m, inventory $230m, payables $130m. What is the cash conversion cycle, in days?
questions.hint: Receivables against revenue; inventory and payables against COGS.
questions.explain: DSO = 365×205÷1200 = 62.4. DIO = 365×230÷780 = 107.6. DPO = 365×130÷780 = 60.8. Cycle = 62.4 + 107.6 − 60.8 = 109.2 days. Using revenue for the last two would understate both by the gross margin.

questions.q: Why must days inventory outstanding use cost of goods sold rather than revenue?
options: Inventory is carried at cost, so it must be measured against a cost flow
why: COGS is smaller, and that is a consequence rather than the reason.
Correct. Comparing a cost-based balance against a price-based flow embeds the gross margin and understates the days held.
Returns reduce revenue but are not the issue.
No standard prescribes ratio formulas.
questions.explain: The same logic applies to payables. Getting this wrong makes high-margin companies look dramatically more efficient than they are, and the error appears in published research.

questions.q: Operating working capital is 30% of revenue. Revenue grows from $400m to $520m. Roughly how much cash does growth absorb, in $m?
questions.hint: The revenue increase times the working capital intensity.
questions.explain: $120m × 30% = $36m. If the operating margin is 9%, the incremental revenue earns about $10.8m — so growth is cash-negative by roughly $25m in the year it happens. This gap is why profitable companies fail.

questions.q: A supermarket with negative working capital sees sales fall 15%. What happens to cash?
options: It improves, since less inventory is needed
It deteriorates rapidly, because suppliers must still be paid while customer cash slows
why: Inventory does fall, but payables — the larger balance in a negative working capital model — fall with it.
Correct. The cycle that generated cash on the way up consumes it on the way down, faster than the profit decline implies.
The effect is substantial.
Falling payables are a use of cash, not a source.
questions.explain: Negative working capital is a powerful engine in growth and a trap in decline. Several large retailers failed far faster than their reported results suggested for exactly this reason.

questions.q: Inventory days rise from 62 to 88 while raw materials are flat and finished goods have doubled. What is the likeliest conclusion?
options: Buying ahead of a price increase
Product is not selling, and a write-down may be pending
why: That would build raw materials, which are flat.
Correct. A build concentrated in finished goods means output is not converting into sales.
Shorter lead times reduce raw material holdings.
Understated COGS would raise inventory arithmetically but would not concentrate it in finished goods.
questions.explain: The composition of an inventory build matters more than its size. Raw materials suggest purchasing; work in progress suggests production; finished goods suggest demand, which is the most serious.

questions.q: Net margin 6%, asset turnover 1.8×, equity multiplier 2.2×. What is return on equity, as a percentage?
questions.hint: The three-step DuPont identity is a product.
questions.explain: 0.06 × 1.8 × 2.2 = 0.2376, so 23.76%. Remove the leverage and the return falls to 10.8%, which is the decomposition doing its job: it separates borrowed return from earned return.

questions.q: Operating income $180m, effective tax rate 22%, equity $520m, total debt $410m, cash $90m. What is ROIC, as a percentage?
questions.hint: NOPAT over equity plus debt less cash.
questions.explain: NOPAT = 180 × 0.78 = $140.4m. Invested capital = 520 + 410 − 90 = $840m. ROIC = 140.4 ÷ 840 = 16.7%. Using total assets instead would include operating liabilities supplied free by suppliers and understate the return.

questions.q: A company earns 8% ROIC against an 11% cost of capital and grows 30% a year. What should it do?
options: Stop growing and return capital, unless returns can be raised above the cost of capital
Borrow more, since debt is cheaper
why: Growing faster destroys value faster; every reinvested dollar earns three points less than it costs.
Correct. Growth multiplies the spread, and here the spread is negative.
Cheaper debt lowers the cost of capital marginally and raises risk; it does not fix a negative spread.
A positive accounting return below the cost of capital still destroys value, because the capital had a better use.
questions.explain: Growth is a multiplier on the spread between ROIC and the cost of capital, not a good in itself. High growth with low returns on capital is the most dangerous profile in investing and the most often celebrated.

questions.q: Which pair of companies is more likely to default within two years?
options: Always the one with more debt
why: A lot of cheap debt against strong cash generation. This is a typical utility profile and among the safest credits there is.
Correct. Interest cover of 1.4× means a 30% fall in operating profit leaves the company unable to pay its interest.
The flow measure differs by nearly an order of magnitude.
Gearing describes the balance sheet; coverage describes whether the payments can be made, and payments cause defaults.
questions.explain: Coverage beats gearing because companies default when they cannot pay, not when a ratio looks high.

questions.q: A company reports ROIC of 84%. What should you check first?
options: Whether the denominator is missing capital, such as internally generated intangibles or leased assets
why: Some businesses genuinely earn this, but the base rate for a measurement artefact is far higher.
Correct. Expensed brand and research spending, negative working capital and outsourced asset bases all shrink invested capital without shrinking the economics.
Growth is relevant to value but does not explain an implausible return level.
Audit quality is not what produces an extreme ratio.
questions.explain: Extreme ratios are usually measurement artefacts. Investigating the denominator before celebrating the number is the difference between analysis and screening.

questions.q: Match each ratio to the question it answers best.
pairs: Does the company have pricing power over its input costs?
Is this a good business, regardless of how it is financed?
Can it keep paying lenders if profit falls?
How long is cash tied up between paying suppliers and collecting?
How much of the asset base was funded by other people?
questions.explain: Almost every misuse of financial ratios comes from applying one built for a different question — most commonly using return on equity to judge business quality when leverage differs between the companies being compared.

questions.q: Net income $240m, operating cash flow $130m, average total assets $1,800m. What is the accrual ratio, as a percentage?
questions.hint: The gap between earnings and cash, scaled by the asset base.
questions.explain: (240 − 130) ÷ 1,800 = 6.1%. A positive value of this size means most of the profit is not backed by cash. It is not proof of anything, but it places the company high in the queue for a closer look at receivables, inventory and capitalised costs.

questions.q: Why is capitalising an operating cost harder to detect than most distortions?
options: It raises both profit and operating cash flow, so the usual cash conversion check misses it
It only affects the balance sheet
It is concealed because it is illegal
why: The capitalisation policy must be disclosed; the difficulty is that the effect evades the standard screens.
Correct. The expense leaves the income statement and the payment moves from operating to investing.
It affects all three statements.
Capitalisation within the rules is entirely legal, which is why it is common.
questions.explain: Free cash flow is the defence, because deducting capital expenditure neutralises the reclassification. Tracking capitalised costs as a percentage of total spending is the second check.

questions.q: Which adjustments to earnings would you generally reject? Select all that apply.
options: Restructuring charges present in each of the last five years
"Transformation costs" in year five of a transformation
why: Reject. A genuine cost of labour paid in equity, permanently diluting owners.
Reject. Five consecutive years makes it an operating cost with a different label.
Generally accept, provided the company is not in a business where litigation recurs.
Reject. A cost recurring for five years is structural, and the category has no accounting definition.
questions.explain: The organising test is recurrence. Pulling the same reconciliation from five annual reports settles most cases in ten minutes.

questions.q: A screen for accounting manipulation flags 14% of companies. Manipulation occurs in roughly 2% of company-years. What follows?
options: Most flagged companies are honest, but the flag is worth investigating
Flagged companies should be sold immediately
why: At a 2% base rate there are not enough manipulators in the universe to fill a 14% flag list.
Correct. The screen concentrates the true cases into a smaller pool, which is genuine value, but a flag is not a verdict.
It raises the probability several-fold, which is useful for ordering a research queue.
Acting on the flag alone means being wrong the large majority of the time.
questions.explain: This is the base rate problem, and it defeats every screen for a rare event. Screens tell you what to read first, not what to conclude.

questions.q: What did Enron, Worldcom, Carillion and Wirecard share as a detectable signal?
options: Reported earnings persistently exceeding operating cash flow
why: They were audited by different firms.
Correct. In each case profit ran ahead of cash for years, and the gap widened rather than reversed.
They span energy, telecoms, construction and payments.
Several reported healthy equity until collapse.
questions.explain: Plotting cumulative net income against cumulative operating cash flow over five years is the highest-yield forensic check available, and it requires no model at all.

questions.q: A company’s warranty provision falls from 2.9% to 1.6% of revenue while product returns rise. What has happened to reported profit?
